The US midterms were an historic election: the largest swing in the last fifty years of American elections. Voters in every part of the country, voters of all ages, and voters of all racial and ethnic backgrounds have shifted away from the Republican Party. We have asked three of our colleagues in Washington DC to zoom out and think about what these Midterm results might mean for their respective fields of expertise.

How can the new Congress support a just peace deal for Ukraine?
Jason C. Moyer, Program Director, Foreign and Security Policy

The Trump administration has resumed negotiations with Russia to end the conflict in Ukraine after a lengthy pause. In recent weeks, a flurry of diplomatic activity has led to concerns that the United States will seek a speedy end to the conflict, potentially tilting the terms of a peace deal to favor Russia. This would be detrimental to Europe and European security more broadly. As a result of the historic shift in U.S. politics in the midterms, Congressional Democrats will have the opportunity to provide a countervailing force in U.S. foreign policy in support of Ukraine.

Congressional Democrats will have the opportunity to provide a countervailing force in U.S. foreign policy in support of Ukraine.

For starters, Democrats can leverage the “power of the purse” of Congress to provide security material to strengthen Ukraine’s negotiating stance. The new Congress can also demand oversight and offer input on any proposed peace deal to ensure it is equitable and just for Ukraine. They also can hold accountable some of the private citizens negotiating on behalf of the U.S. government, ensuring their personal interests do not directly benefit from any proposed deal.

The new Congress can also keep up pressure on Russia. The recent decision to allow the sale of Russian diesel to lower costs for American consumers was met with some pushback by the current U.S. Congress, however, the new Congress can ramp up pressure on Russian energy exports. With the latest bilateral negotiations between Russia and the United States, a sweeping, revamped European security architecture could embolden Russia. It is more important than ever that the new Congress continues its support for Ukraine. The future of Ukraine is the future of Europe, and ensuring a fair deal that respects Ukrainian territorial integrity and imposes costs on Russia for its aggression will be vital for the continent’s long-term security.

What do the midterm election results mean for U.S. foreign assistance and international development?
Mariama Baldé, Program Director, Global Dialogue

With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress from January 2027, U.S. aid funding is likely to become more stable, and oversight of foreign assistance programs will increase. While this will not restore USAID or reverse recent cuts, Congress will have greater capacity to investigate decisions made over the past two years, including the restructuring of federal agencies and the dismantling of USAID. Democrats can use hearings, subpoenas, and budget negotiations to strengthen accountability and reaffirm development assistance as a tool for advancing U.S. interests and global stability. 

Congress is also likely to support funding for multilateral institutions such as the World Bank and regional development banks. However, the executive branch will continue to control disbursement decisions, and growing pressure on multilateral funding means competition for resources will remain intense. Rebuilding U.S. bilateral aid architecture will take years, while expanding support through multilateral institutions offers a faster and politically feasible path to restoring U.S. leadership in development assistance. 

A Democratic Congress can slow or limit further cuts to foreign aid.

Overall, a Democratic Congress can slow or limit further cuts to foreign aid and strengthen oversight, but it cannot recreate the pre-2024 aid system. The most likely outcome is a smaller aid budget focused on fewer priorities and countries, reflecting a broader global decline in development assistance.

The 2026 Midterms, Implications for Democracy, and What’s Next For Democrats
Katharina Obser, Democracy Program Director

It was never a given that these U.S. midterm elections would pass without anti-democratic interference. That elections are run at a state and local level proved a key safeguard against the Trump administration’s repeated efforts to undermine them. Fair elections were possible, thanks to extraordinary efforts: by states, whose election officials and attorneys general went to court again and again; by civil society, who challenged anti-democratic measures and courts that repeatedly ruled against the administration; and by voters, who rallied through historic “No Kings” and other protests.  

Democrats now have an opportunity to restore the congressional oversight that Republicans abdicated over the past two years. Trump continues to hold enormous power, and he elevated hardliner Stephen Miller, architect of the immigration enforcement policies so many voters rejected, as his Chief of Staff. But a new Congress can work to hold government agencies to account, propose conditions to spending measures on issues like the Iran War or immigration, and show voters Democrats’ legislative priorities by proposing bills on health care and affordability, even if Trump rejects them. 

Democrats also gained hundreds of seats in state legislatures and won governorships and attorney general posts. They won flipped state legislative chambers – in some cases took control of governorships and legislature both – and broke Republican supermajorities, offering countless new chances to demonstrate governance outside of DC.  

The election results are, firstly, a clear repudiation of Trump’s policy and Republican governance.

The midterms saw an historic wave of Democratic wins, despite Republican-led attempts to gerrymander a more favorable map. On November 3, voters elected the first Black woman governor, the first Native American women governor and Senator, the first Muslim Senator, the first Black Senator from Mississippi since the Reconstruction Era, new Hispanic governors, and the first openly gay man elected Senator, to name a few. The election results are, firstly, a clear repudiation of Trump’s policy and Republican governance. But they also reflect an electorate that chose decency over hatred in campaigns from Michigan to Ohio to Texas.
items.title: US-Midterm Elections: What they mean for Security, Development and Democracy Analysis While the Democrats’ historic victory in the U.S. midterm elections will not bring the Trump era to an end, it will limit the president’s power and enable governance outside of Washington, D.C. We take a look at the implications in three areas. Jason C. Moyer, Mariama Baldé

These needs shape our work at Callas Foundation, a community organisation on the Cape Flats in Cape Town. These experiences shape how I understand the theme proposed for this 25 November article:

 “Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity.” 

We must judge these commitments by what changes in women’s daily lives in our city.

I write as an African feminist, a survivor and a community activist. Over three decades of work against gender-based violence have taught me to listen beyond the first request. A woman may ask for food while carrying fears she cannot yet share. Another may seek court support while worrying about returning home.

Our response must make room for the whole person. Justice becomes harder to reach when we treat hunger, safety and healing as separate concerns. These concerns remain with us after meetings end and campaigns close. For me, feminism means paying attention to whose needs are overlooked and whose labour keeps others going. It means asking women what would help, then working alongside them to make that support possible.

I live and work in the community I serve. The Cape Flats is home to diverse communities shaped by colonialism, apartheid forced removals, migration and resistance. Our neighbourhoods have different histories, languages and ways of organising. Many share the lasting effects of inequality and exclusion. We face unemployment, hunger, violence and gaps in services. We also have strong traditions of solidarity and care.

Where food and safety meet

I founded Callas Foundation in 2018 in Bridgetown. Our work combines court accompaniment, rights advocacy, psychosocial support and prevention programmes with a community kitchen. We work in communities where poverty and violence place heavy demands on families.

Food is part of this work because people need to eat while seeking safety. Hunger does not pause during a police investigation. Children still need meals when their mother spends a day at court. A survivor cannot build a secure future without meeting her daily needs.

Telling a woman to leave offers little help unless safe, practical options exist.

Access to food can also become a means of control. A partner may withhold money for groceries or threaten to stop supporting the children. Leaving may mean losing the household’s only income. Telling a woman to leave offers little help unless safe, practical options exist.

Poverty never excuses abuse. Responsibility belongs to the person who chooses violence. Yet financial hardship can narrow a survivor’s choices and make seeking help more difficult.

Our kitchen helps us meet immediate needs and build relationships within the community. This takes hard work on the frontline. Alongside food, we provide psychosocial support and help survivors access safety and other services. Trust matters when someone is deciding whether it is safe to speak. Receiving food must never depend on disclosing abuse. Support should respect each person’s privacy and choices.

Since we began serving our community, I have watched the need for food grow. Behind each request is a household trying to cope. Our work and research on food insecurity and violence have deepened our understanding of their connections. Food support can widen a survivor’s choices. I want government to recognise that securing the right to food belongs within a response to violence. Community care carries us through today while we organise for lasting change.

Justice must be reachable

Court accompaniment is an important part of our work. Standing alongside a survivor can help her navigate an unfamiliar and intimidating process. It also helps us understand the practical obstacles between a right and its use.

Repeated court visits require transport, childcare and time away from work. Each postponement brings costs and uncertainty. People supporting survivors must take these pressures seriously.

Ensuring justice means building services that women can actually reach. Police should receive complaints respectfully and investigate them properly. Survivors need clear information about their cases and available support. Courts and care services should coordinate so women do not carry the burden of navigating everything alone.

A woman should not need an influential contact to receive proper assistance.

Ending impunity means holding perpetrators accountable through fair, effective processes. It also requires action when officials neglect their duties or mistreat survivors. Institutions need clear complaint routes and consequences for failures. A woman should not need an influential contact to receive proper assistance.

We should measure progress through people’s experiences. Could she reach the service? Did someone explain the next step? Was her safety taken seriously?

Survivors must shape the response

A survivor-centred approach starts with listening and respecting choice. It means explaining options clearly, protecting privacy and seeking consent. It means recognising that the survivor knows things about her circumstances that others may miss.

We cannot demand a particular decision before offering care. Someone may need time to consider reporting, leaving or seeking further help. Her choices may reflect fears about children, housing, income or retaliation. Support must help her assess those concerns without taking control away from her.

Survivors also hold knowledge that should shape policies and services. They can identify where referrals break down or procedures cause further harm. Participation requires more than an invitation to tell a painful story. It requires influence over decisions and respect for people’s time.

Survivors should never have to disclose their experiences publicly to be heard. Their privacy matters across websites, languages and social media.

Prevention starts early and across the gender spectrum

At Callas Foundation, our boys programme is known as BBB Boys. It works with boys aged eight to sixteen. Our wider prevention work includes school Human Rights Clubs and training community responders. This work creates opportunities to discuss respect, rights and the use of power.

Working with boys matters because ideas about masculinity develop early. Boys need space to discuss emotions and question beliefs that link manhood with control. They need adults who show respect in everyday relationships. They also need to learn that care does not entitle anyone to obedience.

Men have a responsibility to challenge abuse among peers and in their own behaviour. Women should not carry the work of prevention alone. Partnerships with men must remain accountable to women’s rights and survivors’ safety.

Prevention also belongs in workplaces and online spaces. Employers need trusted reporting routes and protection against retaliation. Digital platforms must take threats and harassment seriously. A woman’s ability to earn, speak or organise should never require accepting abuse.

The call to unite: what solidarity should deliver

Various frameworks guide action in response to violence against women. The United Nations Declaration on the Elimination of Violence against Women calls for state action including preventing, investigating and punishing violence through national law. The World Health Organization and UN Women, the United Nations gender equality entity, have worked to develop the RESPECT women framework – a violence prevention framework that identifies the necessity for the existence of various mechanisms and programmes to prevent violence and support women including the provision of services, women’s empowerment programmes, poverty reduction and changing harmful attitudes. 

South Africa’s National Strategic Plan on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide provides another useful framework. Its six pillars connect accountability, prevention, justice, survivor support, economic power and research.

Actions and responsibilities to address and prevent violence need to equally extend to private individuals from families and neighbours to community workers – abuse within a home should be a matter of public responsibility. A survivor’s protection, however, cannot depend entirely on families, neighbours, volunteers or an overstretched local organisation.

A policy has practical value when people can use it to secure change.

Action Plans and Frameworks need to ensure adequate funding for those providing violence prevention and response. And there must be clear delineated responsibilities. Communities need to know who will act, by when and with what resources. They also need a way to challenge failures. A policy has practical value when people can use it to secure change.

My work has taken me from community spaces into national policy discussions. I carry the same questions into both. What will this decision mean for the woman who needs help today? Who will listen when the service fails her? Women must help shape those answers. Their experience belongs wherever decisions about their lives are made.

Community organisations connect people with services and help make institutional failures visible. This work needs reliable funding. Counselling, transport, staff time and safe spaces all carry costs. Expecting women to sustain these services through unpaid labour places another burden on them.

Funders should listen to local organisations. Short projects can leave essential work without continuity. Sustained, flexible support helps us respond to needs that cross funding categories.

Women sustaining community care need support.

For me, the call to unite means sharing responsibility while keeping women’s rights at the centre. Government must fulfil its duties. Community organisations need resources and a meaningful voice in decisions. Survivors must have choices, care and routes to justice that they can use.

On 25 November, I want our commitments to reach beyond statements of concern. I want them to reach a woman waiting for help in her own community. Can she find safety, feed her children and pursue justice without facing those challenges alone? Our work should always make that possible.
items.title: Fighting for justice and safety for women in the Cape Flats Comment What do women need to truly escape violence? On the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25, an African feminist from South Africa explains why justice alone is not enough - and what needs to change. Caroline Peters

More than four years after the onset of the full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine on February 24, 2022 - and over a decade since the aggression began in 2014 - the Ukraine and the international community face one of the most complex legal and diplomatic challenges of our time. How can a just, sustainable and lasting peace  with Russia be built that fulfills the fundamental pillars of justice, human rights, and accountability under international law? A failure to prosecute war crimes fosters a culture of impunity that normalizes military aggression as an instrument of politics, undermines the global security architecture, and drastically increases the risk of future wars of aggression. 

The Dilemma: Short-Term Cessation of Hostilities vs. Long-Term Integrity of International Law

Every attempt to end the Russian war of aggression through negotiations is confronted with a fundamental tension. On the one hand, there is the urgent humanitarian imperative to bring the daily loss of life on the frontlines, the ongoing Russian air strikes against civilians, and the destruction of critical infrastructure (which regularly triggers humanitarian crises, particularly ahead of the winter months) to an end as quickly as possible. Furthermore, the Charter of the United Nations (UN Charter) obliges to settle disputes by peaceful means and foster peaceful relations among states. 

At the same time, international law and its institutions have not been able to put a halt to the Russian aggression. With a view to a negotiated end of the Russian aggression a similar tension arises. The law of state responsibility mandates that Russia immediately cease its internationally wrongful acts. This requires a complete withdrawal of troops from the entire sovereign territory of Ukraine (including Crimea), guarantees of non-repetition, comprehensive reparations for the damage caused, and the criminal prosecution of those responsible for the crime of aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.

These requirements of international law and the military-diplomatic situation diverge. Russia remains committed to its maximalist goals - the destruction of Ukraine as an independent, sovereign state, or respectively, the legal recognition of its territorial claims  alongside sweeping impunity for its leadership and armed forces. At present, a peace settlement seems conceivable only with considerable compromises to the solution required under international law.

A flawed peace achieved at the expense of justice does not pacify the aggressor.

Herein lies the core problem: Any departure from fundamental principles of international law not only impairs the sovereign rights of Ukraine, but also threatens the entire post-1945 international legal order. If an aggressor succeeds in permanently securing the fruits of its illegal war of aggression through an international treaty, international law transforms from a shield protecting the sovereign equality of all states into an instrument of hegemonic power politics. The experience with the Minsk Agreements of 2014/2015, which provided for sweeping amnesties and sidelined questions of accountability, painfully demonstrated to Ukrainian society that a flawed peace achieved at the expense of justice does not pacify the aggressor, but merely invites preparation for the next stage of escalation.

Political and Practical Obstacles to Peace and Accountability

Alongside this structural dilemma, achieving peace and accountability is complicated by a series of acute political and practical factors.

The Problem of “Paper Justice”

Since 2022, Ukraine and the international community have built an unprecedented architecture for criminal prosecution and the redress of damages. This includes over 253,900 open domestic investigations in Ukraine, arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC), the initiative to establish a Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression, as well as the Register of Damage and the International Claims Commission established under the auspices of the Council of Europe. Yet all of these mechanisms face anenforcement deficit: The overwhelming majority of suspects remain outside the custody of the Ukrainian and international judiciary  and the Russian Federation refuses any cooperation. Moreover, member states of the ICC have not complied with international arrest warrants, which creates further difficulties for the enforcement of justice. Without innovative transnational enforcement strategies, hundreds of thousands of investigations and in absentia trials risk becoming symbolic “paper justice.” Precisely for this reason, the issue of accountability will inevitably have to become a central subject of future peace negotiations.

Geopolitical Fault Lines and Diplomatic Pressure

The diplomatic framework for a human rights-based peace is under considerable pressure. In the United States there is a danger that short-term agreements will be forced through at Ukraine’s expense. A prime example of this was a US proposal in November 2025 (drafted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, among others) that envisaged sweeping amnesties and a waiver of reparation claims, standing in stark contrast to European and Ukrainian counterproposals. This is compounded by a US diplomacy that at times actively obstructs international prosecution mechanisms such as the ICC or threatens them with sanctions.

Headwinds are also growing within Europe and Germany: In the European Union, a growing number of governments are questioning long-term support for Ukraine. In the German discourse, parties such as the AfD and the BSW occupy a populist “peace” narrative that in essence amounts to subjugating Ukraine to Russian dictates. For democratic actors - including the German Green Party - this creates an urgent need to put forward constructive peace proposals that uphold international law.

Legal Limits and Red Lines in Peace Negotiations

A central academic contribution of the project consists in defining the legal guardrails that international law establishes for peace negotiations. While sovereign states generally enjoy freedom of contract under international law, this freedom is decisively constrained in the context of an ongoing war of aggression.

Russia seeks a legally binding treaty in order to permanently legalize its unlawful occupation of Ukrainian territory, lift sanctions, and shield its leadership from criminal prosecution. Under Article 52 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), however, a treaty is void if its conclusion has been procured by the threat or use of force in violation of the UN Charter.

These are rights and obligations that are not at the free disposition of states. International law sets a framework for peace that places justice and the sustainability and durability of a peace agreement at its core.  In particular, international law prevents a hasty dictated peace that would leave Ukraine defenseless and provoke future wars.

Every attempt to end the Russian war of aggression through negotiations is confronted with a fundamental tension. At the same time, international law and its institutions have not been able to put a halt to the Russian aggression. With a view to a negotiated end of the Russian aggression a similar tension arises. The law of state responsibility mandates that Russia immediately cease its internationally wrongful acts. These requirements of international law and the military-diplomatic situation diverge. Russia remains committed to its maximalist goals - the destruction of Ukraine as an independent, sovereign state, or respectively, the legal recognition of its territorial claims  alongside sweeping impunity for its leadership and armed forces. At present, a peace settlement seems conceivable only with considerable compromises to the solution required under international law.

items.content_html:
On 11 September 2025, Mikalai Statkevich, who stood in Belarus's 2010 presidential election, was pardoned and taken to the Lithuanian border. He refused to cross and instead turned back towards Belarus, where he was detained and returned to prison. In January 2026, he suffered a stroke. He was released again the following month.

Ten years earlier, Statkevich had been pardoned alongside five other political prisoners, although he had not asked for clemency. In 2015, he was able to return home and continue his opposition activities. In September 2025, however, his release was effectively conditional on leaving the country. Statkevich refused to leave Belarus and was sent back to prison.

The two pardons, a decade apart, show how the terms of negotiations over political prisoners have changed. The September release was part of the second of five rounds of talks between Washington and Minsk since June 2025. During that period, 464 people were released from Belarusian prisons, with four rounds accompanied by an easing of US sanctions against Lukashenko's government.

Washington has judged the success of the talks largely by the number of prisoners released. After the December 2025 negotiations, US special envoy John Coale said that around 1,000 political prisoners still in jail could be freed within months. In return, he said, the US could lift most of its sanctions. Coale described the proposed deal as “a fair trade”.

But while Washington and Minsk negotiated the terms of the releases, Lithuania and Poland had to receive the prisoners expelled from Belarus. Some were deported without passports, while others remained in Belarus under surveillance. Meanwhile, political repression continued. Following the September 2026 talks, the human rights group Viasna reported that 886 political prisoners were still being held in Belarus.

The East German Precedent

In four of the five rounds of talks in 2025 – 2026 — June, September and December 2025, and September 2026 — all political prisoners who were released were deported to Lithuania or Ukraine. They included key people associated with the 2020 protests: Ales Bialiatski, Siarhei Tsikhanouski, Viktar Babaryka and Maria Kalesnikava. In September 2020, Kalesnikava tore up her passport at the Ukrainian border to avoid deportation. Yet after five years in prison, she too was expelled from Belarus.

The practice is often compared to East Germany's programme of buying the freedom of political prisoners (Häftlingsfreikauf). They all received West German passports, voting rights and social assistance under a special law for former prisoners. West Germany also negotiated their release and received them on its own territory.

Mikita Zalatarou, 22, was arrested on politically motivated charges when he was 16, and he spent most of his teenage time behind bars. Upon his release, Mikita was deported to Lithuania. His health had deteriorated significantly during his imprisonment, leaving him unable to undertake physically demanding work. He is now looking for a job in Vilnius that does not require physical labour. Nikita’s family remains in Belarus, where his father is still imprisoned. Nikita has declined psychological support, saying the only thing that could bring him peace of mind is his father's release.

Older exiles face a parallel crisis over their pensions. According to Vesna Centre, some former-prisoners pensioners remained in Belarus, stopped receiving payments after their release in June 2025. Others, living in exile, have been cut off from pensions and social benefits because their bank accounts have been frozen and their property seized. In Lithuania and Poland, pension eligibility depends partly on contribution records and existing social security agreements. For those expelled from Belarus without documents or access to their own money, claiming a pension becomes an agonising task. 

In March 2026, following a referral by Lithuania, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court opened an investigation into the deportation and persecution of opponents of the Belarusian government as possible crimes against humanity.

Belarus is not the first country to use such measures. In February 2023, the Nicaraguan authorities sent 222 political prisoners on a flight to Washington. They were subsequently stripped of their citizenship.

Freedom Under Tight Control

During the talks on 19 March 2026, only 15 of the 250 prisoners granted pardons were forcibly taken to Lithuania. The remaining 235 were allowed to stay in Belarus.

US special envoy John Coale acknowledged that the fate of the 235 had been a point of disagreement with Minsk. He said those allowed to stay had been convicted of less serious offences, including some who were nearing the end of their sentences. Human rights defenders Marfa Rabkova and Nasta Loika, Viasna deputy chairman Valiantsin Stefanovich and protester Mikita Zolatarou were forcibly transferred to Lithuania. Political analyst Valeria Kostyugova was released in Belarus the following day. Referring to those expelled, Lukashenko said: "We don't need them here in this country." He ordered the KGB to monitor those who remained.

In Belarus, a pardon removes the obligation to serve the rest of a prison sentence but does not overturn the conviction. Under Article 97 of the Belarusian Criminal Code, a criminal record for a serious offence is cleared five years after release, and for a particularly serious offence after eight years.

Former political prisoners remain on the Interior Ministry's list of "extremists" under Article 18 of the Law on Countering Extremism. This restricts their right to teach, work in publishing or hold public office. Special financial monitoring continues until their criminal record is cleared and for a further five years. For journalists, researchers and teachers, the restrictions can amount to a ban on working in their profession for up to 13 years.

Contact with independent media or international human rights organisations can be treated by the authorities as "participation in an extremist organisation" or "facilitating extremist activity", exposing former prisoners to the risk of another arrest.

Notably, US negotiators also had an interest in the released prisoners avoiding public activity. Following the March pardons, Coale said US representatives had advised those freed to "stay home and keep quiet for a while" to avoid complicating negotiations over the remaining prisoners. In effect, maintaining the political status quo inside Belarus became an unspoken condition for continuing talks with Lukashenko.

Between June 2025 and September 2026, the number of political prisoners recorded by Viasna fell by just 301, from 1,177 to 876. In 2025 alone, Belarusian courts handed down at least 1,254 politically motivated criminal sentences.

As Ales Bialiatski put it after his deportation in December 2025: "With one hand, the authorities release people, while with the other, they imprison new political prisoners."

The Limits of US Diplomacy

The current agreement marks a change from previous periods of improved relations between Washington and Minsk. In 2008, under OFAC General Licence No. 1, and again in 2015, under General Licence No. 2, the US Treasury suspended sanctions for limited periods of between three and 18 months. Belarusian companies remained on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, and the restrictions automatically took effect again when the licences expired, unless Washington renewed them. The approach was similar to that used by the US towards Nicolae Ceausescu's Romania in 1983, when annual extensions of trade preferences under the Jackson–Vanik amendment served as a means of pressure.

In 2025 and 2026, the Trump administration began removing major Belarusian companies from the sanctions list without setting an expiry date. The state airline Belavia was removed in November 2025. On 26 March 2026, Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company were taken off the list. The US also revoked Directive No. 1 and authorised transactions with Belinvestbank. In September, the Lakokraska paint manufacturer and the Bellesbumprom industrial group were removed.

The White House and the US Treasury can legally reimpose these sanctions, but doing so has become more politically costly. Previously, Minsk had to meet US conditions to secure each extension of sanctions relief. Now that trade has resumed, renewed restrictions could also affect American companies. In September, Trump announced plans to buy Belarusian potash, five days after Minsk released 25 political prisoners, rather than the 200 that had been expected.

But even if Washington lifts all its sanctions, Minsk still faces a major economic obstacle. The US has largely used sanctions as leverage in negotiations over political prisoners. The European Union has different priorities. Its sanctions, extended until 28 February 2027, are also linked to Belarus's role in Russia's war against Ukraine and to hybrid activities, including the use of migrants to put pressure on neighbouring EU borders. Releasing political prisoners alone would therefore not be enough to secure the removal of EU sanctions. Any change would require the agreement of all member states.

Washington can allow American companies to buy Belarusian potash, but it cannot force Lithuania to reopen the export route through its port of Klaipėda. Before 2022, around 12 million tonnes of fertiliser passed through the port each year under an agreement with Lithuanian Railways. Belaruskali also owned a 30 percent stake in one of its terminals. But in January 2022, Lithuania terminated the transport contract, citing national security concerns. Belaruskali's subsequent international arbitration claim for more than 12 billion US dollars has made any change in Lithuania's position more difficult.

The first shipment of Belarusian potash to reach the US in four years, 30,000 tonnes delivered to New Orleans on 14 October 2026, travelled through the Russian port of Bronka, near St Petersburg, bypassing the EU.

According to the US Fertilizer Institute, the shipment represented just 0.24 percent of annual American imports. Canada supplies 85 – 90 percent of US potash needs, benefiting from established rail connections. Belarusian producers could capture an estimated 8 – 12 percent of the import market, equivalent to between one million and 1.5 million tonnes a year.

Without the shorter route through Klaipėda, Belarus must use Russian railways and ports to reach the American market. This means paying Russian companies for transport and becoming more dependent on Moscow's infrastructure.

Lithuania, at the same time, has managed to adapt to the loss of Belarusian transit. In 2025, the Klaipėda port authority reported a net profit of 24.2 million euros, while the Lithuanian railway group LTG made 43.3 million euros. Although the lost Belarusian business has not been fully replaced, LTG has been expanding freight operations in Poland and Germany. Klaipėda port also plans to invest 775 million euros in infrastructure by 2029.

Lithuania's economic ties with the US are considerably more valuable than its former earnings from Belarusian freight. By the end of 2025, American direct investment in Lithuania had reached 2.8 billion euros. Vilnius therefore has reason to avoid a dispute over Klaipėda that could damage relations with Washington. But there is no evidence so far that the Trump administration is prepared to make economic cooperation with Lithuania dependent on reopening the Belarusian transit route.

Trump also faces potential opposition in Congress. If Republicans fail to confirm John Coale's nomination as special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with the rank of ambassador, before the new Congress takes office on 3 January, a Democratic majority could block his appointment and subject the Belarus deal to greater scrutiny. Efforts to persuade Lithuania to resume potash transit have also met with opposition within the US administration itself.

The Democrats' victory in the congressional elections could make Trump's Belarus policy harder to pursue, although the president would retain broad powers over sanctions. For now, Lithuania has little economic incentive to change its position.

The result is that US sanctions relief has not reduced Belarus's dependence on Russian transport routes, while the release of political prisoners has done little to stop repression at home.

In Deir al-Balah, in the Gaza Strip, displaced farmers have been rebuilding something that can fit inside a handful: the seeds of future harvests. Before Israel’s war on Gaza, the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Khan Younis, established by agronomist Salama Ayesh Muhanna in 2017, held an estimated 70 tonnes of seed covering 42 crops. Its premises were destroyed, in Al-Qarara town, during the Israeli war on Gaza Strip, in ​early 2024. Yet, the initiative survived in a different form. Muhanna, his daughter Hanadi and other farmers began recovering seeds kept by families, multiplying them and lending them to growers. By September 2026, they had recovered approximately 32 local varieties. [1]

The story reveals two things at once: the extraordinary vulnerability of agricultural systems under military destruction, and the profound resilience of the knowledge and genetic resources dispersed among farming communities. A destroyed building may be reconstructed; a lost local crop variety, selected over generations and adapted to particular soils and (micro) climates, may be impossible to recover. For Palestinians, the question is therefore not simply how to store seeds safely, but who holds the power to keep Cultivating them.

When seeds become instruments of power

A seed begins the agricultural production cycle, but it also defines relationships between farmers, markets, and institutions. Can farmers save part of their harvest for the following season? Must new seed be purchased every year? Who selects varieties, sets standards, controls access to genetic material, and benefits from improvements? These are questions of political economy, not merely agronomy.

Globally, the seed industry has become increasingly concentrated. According to a 2025 analysis by ETC Group and GRAIN, four corporations—Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta and BASF—controlled approximately 56 percent of the commercial seed market and 61 percent of the pesticides market. The figures concern commercial markets, not the entirety of farmers’ own seed systems. Nevertheless, they indicate the influence a handful of companies can exercise over the technologies, inputs and choices available to growers. [2]

This concentration does not make every commercial or hybrid variety inherently undesirable. Some varieties deliver valuable agronomic performance. The problem arises when farmers’ choices narrow, seed saving becomes economically or legally constrained, and agricultural production depends on purchasing a package of seed, pesticides and other inputs. Seed sovereignty, by contrast, is about keeping farmers’ capacity to conserve, select, improve, multiply, and exchange seed—as well as to participate in deciding how agricultural genetic resources are governed.

These concerns are acute in Palestine, where market dependence is layered onto occupation, restrictions on land and water, and fragmented geography. According to UN Comtrade data accessed through the World Bank’s WITS database, the occupied Palestinian territory imported US$9.18 million in seeds, fruits and spores for sowing under tariff heading HS 1209 in 2023. Imports recorded from Israel accounted for US$5.79 million, or approximately 63 percent of the total. The figures identify a recorded trading partner, not necessarily the genetic origin or corporate ownership of every seed. Still, they illuminate the weight of one route through which Palestinian agricultural inputs are supplied. [3]

The corporate landscape is interconnected as well. Hazera, with operations in Israel, is part of the French-based Limagrain Group, while Swiss agribusiness company Syngenta announced its acquisition of Israeli seed producer Zeraim Gedera in 2007. These links show how the local seed market is embedded in transnational networks of plant breeding, investment and distribution; they do not, by themselves, establish which branded varieties individual Palestinian farmers purchase. [4]

The 1994 Paris Economic Protocol adds a structural dimension. It established trade and customs arrangements under which Palestinian autonomy to import goods is subject to specified lists, procedures and restrictions. The agreement does not directly prohibit farmers from saving traditional seeds. Rather, it limits the space for an independent trade policy and influences the ability to diversify sources of agricultural inputs. [5] Dependency here is neither simply a consumer preference nor a purely technical outcome; it is also produced by the rules governing the economy.

Local seeds, living knowledge

Palestine’s varied ecological zones—from the humid highlands to the semi-arid eastern slopes and the Jordan Valley—have long supported diverse cropping practices. Traditional baladi seeds are not relics preserved unchanged in a museum. Farmers have selected and adapted them through repeated cultivation, observing germination, taste, seasonal performance and suitability for local conditions. Their value resides both in genetic diversity and in the knowledge of how to grow, save and use them.

This is why agroecology has political meaning beyond reducing chemical inputs. It combines ecological practices with cooperation, locally situated knowledge and stronger farmer agency. Saving seed can reduce some recurring purchases, but community-based production also entails costs, including labour, irrigation, testing, storage and distribution. Romanticising it as effortless or automatically cheaper would obscure the investment needed to sustain it.

Palestinian farmers and organisations have nevertheless developed practical alternatives. The Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC) established its local seed-bank programme in the Hebron area in 2003, collecting, conserving and multiplying traditional varieties. Its model encourages farmers to plant locally supplied seeds and return part of the resulting seed harvest, allowing stocks to circulate beyond a single growing season. [6]

A significant step came in October 2024, when UAWC deposited 23 seed samples representing 21 species of vegetables, legumes and herbs in Norway’s Svalbard Global Seed Vault. The deposit is a safeguard against the loss of collections, rather than a substitute for growing and exchanging seeds in Palestinian fields. [7] A seed preserved abroad remains only a potential harvest until land, water, agricultural expertise and farmers can bring it back into use.

Other initiatives pursue complementary approaches. The Palestine Heirloom Seed Library, founded by Vivien Sansour, reconnects traditional varieties with the stories, foods and relationships carried by them. [8] Om Sleiman Farm in Bil’in links agroecological production with community-supported agriculture. Research organisations and community seed banks in places such as Jenin, Nablus and Bethlehem have experimented with conservation, participatory multiplication and seed-lending schemes. Earlier research on Palestinian food sovereignty documented an emerging network of farms and initiatives whose common premise was that farmers should rely more on local resources and have greater control over production. [6]

These initiatives are not interchangeable: a research genebank, a community seed library, and a farm producing vegetables perform different functions. Nor can the existence of small projects alone transform the food economy. Yet, their combined experience provides the ingredients for a wider system—scientific conservation, local multiplication, cultural transmission, community management and farmer-to-farmer exchange.

War on seeds: What is lost when a seed bank is destroyed? 

The threat to these efforts is not hypothetical. In November 2000, Israeli soldiers raided and damaged the Marda Sustainable Development Center near Salfit. A contemporary report by the MA’AN Development Center documented damage to nurseries, propagation trays, irrigation systems and equipment. [9] These losses undermined a site that had sought to connect sustainable agriculture with training and community production.

On 31 July 2025, Israeli authorities demolished a building serving a UAWC traditional seed-multiplication unit in the al-Simiya area near as-Samu’, south of Hebron. According to the Land Research Center, the unit occupied about ten dunums, of which four were planted with fifteen local summer vegetable varieties for seed multiplication. Damage to the facility and supporting infrastructure endangered the capacity to produce seed for the next season. The incident must be distinguished from destruction of UAWC’s entire seed collection: it was a multiplication facility that was hit. [10]

Gaza demonstrates the implications on a far wider scale. As of October 2026, approximately two-thirds of the Gaza Strip remained subject to Israeli-imposed access restrictions, including areas under direct Israeli military control. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), restrictions affected 65 percent of Gaza's territory, leaving the Palestinian population concentrated in the increasingly overcrowded remaining areas [11]. 

The implications for agricultural production are even more severe. A joint geospatial assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) found that, as of 24 June 2026, 73 percent of Gaza's cropland was inaccessible, while only three percent remained both accessible and undamaged [12]. Even the most resilient local seed cannot produce food without a farmer who has safe access to land, viable soil, water and the means to cultivate it. These figures demonstrate that the struggle for seed sovereignty in Palestine cannot be separated from the broader political question of territorial control. Preserving and multiplying indigenous seeds, however essential, cannot restore Palestinian food sovereignty without restoring farmers' access to land, water, and the means of agricultural production.

The recovery of Al-Qarara’s seeds therefore should not become a comforting narrative of resilience that eclipses destruction. What makes the story remarkable is precisely the scale of what farmers have lost. The initiative’s survival depended on seed kept outside its central store, informal solidarity and the possibility—however constrained—of cultivating plots again. It is evidence for decentralised conservation, not evidence that communities can compensate indefinitely for destroyed agricultural infrastructure.

From scattered initiatives to seed sovereignty

Palestinian Agricultural Law No. 2 of 2003 already treats agricultural genetic resources as subject to national sovereignty, assigning public authorities the responsibility to document, conserve, and manage them. It also recognises individual farmers’ property rights in locally circulated varieties. [13] The challenge is to translate these principles into arrangements that protect community stewardship rather than reducing seed sovereignty to state ownership or centralised storage.

The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture offers relevant guidance. Its Article 9 recognises farmers’ contributions, the importance of traditional knowledge and participation in decisions. It safeguards existing rights to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, subject to national law and as appropriate. [14] These principles suggest that effective governance must link research institutions to the people who continue to develop crop diversity in their fields.

A workable Palestinian approach would start by mapping existing seed collections and the farmers conserving traditional varieties, while recognising that documentation must protect sensitive knowledge and community interests. Seed samples should be backed up in several locations, with living stocks multiplied in fields and returned to communities. Laboratories and agricultural extension services can help test seed health and germination, while participatory breeding and local knowledge guide adaptation to drought, disease and changing climatic conditions.

Equally important is the economic side. Seeds conserved in a bank but unavailable in useful quantities will have little influence over dependence on external suppliers. Community seed lending, cooperatives, local marketing arrangements and support for products grown from baladi varieties can make conservation economically viable. Women farmers and rural knowledge holders must be involved in decisions and recognised for their expertise rather than treated simply as beneficiaries. None of this removes the need for public financing, clear rules, and access to markets.

In Gaza, rebuilding seed banks must be part of agricultural recovery, not an isolated heritage project. Farmers need safe access to their land, rehabilitated water infrastructure, functioning nurseries and the ability to move seed and equipment. Humanitarian seed distributions should, wherever feasible, strengthen locally adapted varieties and farmer-managed systems rather than create a fresh cycle of dependency.

Ultimately, the measure of seed sovereignty is not how many varieties sit on a shelf. It is whether farmers can decide what to plant, save seed for the following season, exchange it without losing their rights, and sustain livelihoods from the food they produce. Palestinian baladi seeds embody inherited knowledge, but their significance is oriented toward the future. Ultimately, their survival poses a much larger political question: who will control the next harvest?

items.title: Who Controls the Next Harvest? Palestine’s Seeds and the Politics of Food Sovereignty Article In Palestine, saving a seed is more than preserving an old crop variety. It is a struggle over who can produce food, retain agricultural knowledge, and decide what happens after the next harvest. From Gaza’s devastated seed banks to community initiatives in the West Bank, agroecology is exposing the economic and political stakes of a seemingly small resource. Abdalaziz Al-Salehi
items.summary:
In Deir al-Balah, in the Gaza Strip, displaced farmers have been rebuilding something that can fit inside a handful: the seeds of future harvests. Before Israel’s war on Gaza, the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Khan Younis, established by agronomist Salama Ayesh Muhanna in 2017, held an estimated 70 tonnes of seed covering 42 crops. Its premises were destroyed, in Al-Qarara town, during the Israeli war on Gaza Strip, in ​early 2024. Yet, the initiative survived in a different form. Muhanna, his daughter Hanadi and other farmers began recovering seeds kept by families, multiplying them and lending them to growers. By September 2026, they had recovered approximately 32 local varieties. [1]

The story reveals two things at once: the extraordinary vulnerability of agricultural systems under military destruction, and the profound resilience of the knowledge and genetic resources dispersed among farming communities. A destroyed building may be reconstructed; a lost local crop variety, selected over generations and adapted to particular soils and (micro) climates, may be impossible to recover. For Palestinians, the question is therefore not simply how to store seeds safely, but who holds the power to keep Cultivating them.

When seeds become instruments of power

A seed begins the agricultural production cycle, but it also defines relationships between farmers, markets, and institutions. Can farmers save part of their harvest for the following season? Must new seed be purchased every year? Who selects varieties, sets standards, controls access to genetic material, and benefits from improvements? These are questions of political economy, not merely agronomy.

Globally, the seed industry has become increasingly concentrated. According to a 2025 analysis by ETC Group and GRAIN, four corporations—Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta and BASF—controlled approximately 56 percent of the commercial seed market and 61 percent of the pesticides market. The figures concern commercial markets, not the entirety of farmers’ own seed systems. Nevertheless, they indicate the influence a handful of companies can exercise over the technologies, inputs and choices available to growers. [2]

This concentration does not make every commercial or hybrid variety inherently undesirable. Some varieties deliver valuable agronomic performance. The problem arises when farmers’ choices narrow, seed saving becomes economically or legally constrained, and agricultural production depends on purchasing a package of seed, pesticides and other inputs. Seed sovereignty, by contrast, is about keeping farmers’ capacity to conserve, select, improve, multiply, and exchange seed—as well as to participate in deciding how agricultural genetic resources are governed.

These concerns are acute in Palestine, where market dependence is layered onto occupation, restrictions on land and water, and fragmented geography. According to UN Comtrade data accessed through the World Bank’s WITS database, the occupied Palestinian territory imported US$9.18 million in seeds, fruits and spores for sowing under tariff heading HS 1209 in 2023. Imports recorded from Israel accounted for US$5.79 million, or approximately 63 percent of the total. The figures identify a recorded trading partner, not necessarily the genetic origin or corporate ownership of every seed. Still, they illuminate the weight of one route through which Palestinian agricultural inputs are supplied. [3]

The corporate landscape is interconnected as well. Hazera, with operations in Israel, is part of the French-based Limagrain Group, while Swiss agribusiness company Syngenta announced its acquisition of Israeli seed producer Zeraim Gedera in 2007. These links show how the local seed market is embedded in transnational networks of plant breeding, investment and distribution; they do not, by themselves, establish which branded varieties individual Palestinian farmers purchase. [4]

The 1994 Paris Economic Protocol adds a structural dimension. It established trade and customs arrangements under which Palestinian autonomy to import goods is subject to specified lists, procedures and restrictions. The agreement does not directly prohibit farmers from saving traditional seeds. Rather, it limits the space for an independent trade policy and influences the ability to diversify sources of agricultural inputs. [5] Dependency here is neither simply a consumer preference nor a purely technical outcome; it is also produced by the rules governing the economy.

Local seeds, living knowledge

Palestine’s varied ecological zones—from the humid highlands to the semi-arid eastern slopes and the Jordan Valley—have long supported diverse cropping practices. Traditional baladi seeds are not relics preserved unchanged in a museum. Farmers have selected and adapted them through repeated cultivation, observing germination, taste, seasonal performance and suitability for local conditions. Their value resides both in genetic diversity and in the knowledge of how to grow, save and use them.

This is why agroecology has political meaning beyond reducing chemical inputs. It combines ecological practices with cooperation, locally situated knowledge and stronger farmer agency. Saving seed can reduce some recurring purchases, but community-based production also entails costs, including labour, irrigation, testing, storage and distribution. Romanticising it as effortless or automatically cheaper would obscure the investment needed to sustain it.

Palestinian farmers and organisations have nevertheless developed practical alternatives. The Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC) established its local seed-bank programme in the Hebron area in 2003, collecting, conserving and multiplying traditional varieties. Its model encourages farmers to plant locally supplied seeds and return part of the resulting seed harvest, allowing stocks to circulate beyond a single growing season. [6]

A significant step came in October 2024, when UAWC deposited 23 seed samples representing 21 species of vegetables, legumes and herbs in Norway’s Svalbard Global Seed Vault. The deposit is a safeguard against the loss of collections, rather than a substitute for growing and exchanging seeds in Palestinian fields. [7] A seed preserved abroad remains only a potential harvest until land, water, agricultural expertise and farmers can bring it back into use.

Other initiatives pursue complementary approaches. The Palestine Heirloom Seed Library, founded by Vivien Sansour, reconnects traditional varieties with the stories, foods and relationships carried by them. [8] Om Sleiman Farm in Bil’in links agroecological production with community-supported agriculture. Research organisations and community seed banks in places such as Jenin, Nablus and Bethlehem have experimented with conservation, participatory multiplication and seed-lending schemes. Earlier research on Palestinian food sovereignty documented an emerging network of farms and initiatives whose common premise was that farmers should rely more on local resources and have greater control over production. [6]

These initiatives are not interchangeable: a research genebank, a community seed library, and a farm producing vegetables perform different functions. Nor can the existence of small projects alone transform the food economy. Yet, their combined experience provides the ingredients for a wider system—scientific conservation, local multiplication, cultural transmission, community management and farmer-to-farmer exchange.

War on seeds: What is lost when a seed bank is destroyed? 

The threat to these efforts is not hypothetical. In November 2000, Israeli soldiers raided and damaged the Marda Sustainable Development Center near Salfit. A contemporary report by the MA’AN Development Center documented damage to nurseries, propagation trays, irrigation systems and equipment. [9] These losses undermined a site that had sought to connect sustainable agriculture with training and community production.

On 31 July 2025, Israeli authorities demolished a building serving a UAWC traditional seed-multiplication unit in the al-Simiya area near as-Samu’, south of Hebron. According to the Land Research Center, the unit occupied about ten dunums, of which four were planted with fifteen local summer vegetable varieties for seed multiplication. Damage to the facility and supporting infrastructure endangered the capacity to produce seed for the next season. The incident must be distinguished from destruction of UAWC’s entire seed collection: it was a multiplication facility that was hit. [10]

Gaza demonstrates the implications on a far wider scale. As of October 2026, approximately two-thirds of the Gaza Strip remained subject to Israeli-imposed access restrictions, including areas under direct Israeli military control. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), restrictions affected 65 percent of Gaza's territory, leaving the Palestinian population concentrated in the increasingly overcrowded remaining areas [11]. 

The implications for agricultural production are even more severe. A joint geospatial assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) found that, as of 24 June 2026, 73 percent of Gaza's cropland was inaccessible, while only three percent remained both accessible and undamaged [12]. Even the most resilient local seed cannot produce food without a farmer who has safe access to land, viable soil, water and the means to cultivate it. These figures demonstrate that the struggle for seed sovereignty in Palestine cannot be separated from the broader political question of territorial control. Preserving and multiplying indigenous seeds, however essential, cannot restore Palestinian food sovereignty without restoring farmers' access to land, water, and the means of agricultural production.

The recovery of Al-Qarara’s seeds therefore should not become a comforting narrative of resilience that eclipses destruction. What makes the story remarkable is precisely the scale of what farmers have lost.
