items.content_html:
Full circle

Aleksandar Vučić gave a telling concession speech on the evening of October 25. Hours earlier, while voting was still under way, riot police in armored vehicles had sealed off part of central Belgrade, ostensibly to guard the Republic Electoral Commission – from whom, remains unclear. At the same time, masked thugs were again swarming around Pionirski Park, the para-state camp that had become the regime’s last refuge.

Instead of the refusal to recognize the result and the violent escalation many had feared, Vučić – no longer president, having resigned weeks earlier to run for prime minister – conceded. But true to form after almost 15 years of absolute rule, he said nothing about popular sentiment, political accountability or the need for change. No “we have heard the people, we will do better and come back stronger.”

Rather, he went full circle, traveling back to 2008, when he broke with his political alma mater, the extreme-right Serbian Radical Party, to found the populist, seemingly pro-EU Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). In a cynical display, he openly taunted citizens for the terrible choice they had made. As his scarecrow he picked Nataša Kandić, a human rights activist who played no role in this election: “I congratulate Nataša Kandić, her policy has won,” he said, adding that she had won with enormous foreign support. 

He went on to claim that his opponents had lied about everything – from predictions that he would flee or go into hiding to the “sound cannon,” the acoustic weapon allegedly used against protesters in Belgrade on March 15, 2025. Behind those lies, he suggested, stood various European countries and the “American deep state” opposed to President Trump. 

Since then, he has been rebranding himself as “leader of the opposition” – the hate-spreading tabloids still loyal to him need a title for him, after all. Free of institutional restraints, he promises to fight more fiercely against the “color revolution” supposedly orchestrated from abroad against the country and himself as its supreme protector. In practice, this means a full return to the ideological roots of a far-right politician: stoking the most nationalist sentiments in parts of the population, using them for his interest group’s benefit, and obstructing the incoming government, which he already accuses of “revolutionary terror.”

In that world, even the collapse of the station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, could have been sabotage meant to trigger the color revolution – a possibility Vučić himself said a year ago he “did not exclude.” The irony is hard to miss: had his own institutions held those responsible to account, none of what followed would have happened.

The new leader of the opposition also leaves a legacy from his days in office: a string of pardons.

The new leader of the opposition also leaves a legacy from his days in office: a string of pardons. On September 27, the day he resigned, he pardoned 49 people, whose names were kept from the public until a week after the election. He claimed that these were persons unknown to the public. According to names now published by the courts, however, they include Dijana Hrkalović, the former interior ministry state secretary who stood trial for influence peddling and whom investigative journalists have linked to organized crime; a man accused of running over a student and causing her serious bodily harm; and several people accused of attacking protesters, publicly known and SNS-affiliated. Vučić framed the decree as even-handed, since it also covered twelve Novi Sad activists the regime had branded a “terrorist group.” Pardoning people before any verdict is abolition, not mercy – legal experts described it as the president stepping outside the bounds of the Constitution – and a clear misuse of the institution of pardon. 

In addition, on November 2, Vučić declared that he never signs anything to do with money, so nothing can be found against him – hardly what an innocent man would choose to say.

The clock is ticking 

Since November 1 the count has been complete. After the vote was rerun at 53 polling stations, the Republic Electoral Commission puts the Student List at 53.01 percent and the SNS-led “United Serbia” at 38.98 percent. Once the commission formally proclaims the final result – expected within days – parliament must convene within 30 days, and a government must then be formed within 90 days.

The upcoming presidential election follows its own clock. Ana Brnabić, acting president since Vučić resigned – and for years his prime minister, a wannabe Medvedev to Vučić’s Putin, of sorts – must call it by November 27; the vote has to take place 30 to 60 days after it is called, and no later than December 27. If no candidate wins an absolute majority, a runoff between the top two follows two weeks later. Brnabić may serve as acting president for three months at most; once the new parliament elects its speaker, that person takes over the role until a new president is sworn in.

Vučić has already announced that the SNS will not take part in the presidential election, calling it a “farce.” A more plausible explanation: after years of building a personality cult around one man, the elite around him has no other candidate who could remotely threaten whoever the Student List puts forward.

Costly inheritance

The para-state does not disappear with an election result. In power or in opposition makes little difference to an elite that regards the country – above all its economy – as its property. But even before the actual transfer of power, the first days have shown panic-stricken behavior across the police, the judiciary and business.

Tellingly, Alta Bank, which amassed wealth and influence as a preferred address under SNS rule, has lost its license, and its owner Davor Macura was detained on November 2. He is suspected of removing 45 billion dinars – more than 380 million euros – from the bank’s vault. There are indications that this is only the tip of the iceberg, both in financial terms and in the depth of the ties between state and crime.

Alta is only the most visible part of the inheritance. EXPO 2027 is due to open in Belgrade on May 15. Its contracts, like those for other flagship projects, were concluded under a special law without regular public procurement rules, and the Fiscal Council has warned of cost increases of almost 100 billion dinars across EXPO and other major projects whose causes remain unknown. Add opaque long-term contracts and rising public debt, and the new government’s room for maneuvering is narrow.

Transitional accountability

Shredders have been busy ever since the results came in. The staff union at the Pension and Disability Insurance Fund (PIO) says documents that could incriminate its management have been shredded behind locked doors, day and night. The Student List has called on whistleblowers to report the destruction of records during the transition.

Supreme Public Prosecutor Zagorka Dolovac, notorious for her professional invisibility during SNS rule, has instructed prosecutors nationwide to request urgent police action to protect official records. The arrests have begun: on November 1, police detained Marko Kričak, head of the Criminal Investigation Directorate. Students accused him of abusing protesters in custody; one testified that he slapped her and threatened her with rape in the government building’s garage. Their complaints went nowhere for over a year – he was finally arrested over his handling of an unrelated murder investigation.

The students are watching all this with caution rather than triumph.

The students are watching all this with caution rather than triumph. The group from the Faculty of Organizational Sciences in Belgrade pointed out that the old government is still in office as a caretaker: the arrests are either institutions finally doing their job, or score-settling within the former regime. “Full accountability is still to come. No one untouchable. No matter who is in power.”

Serbia, its neighbors and the EU

Then there is the incoming government’s international and regional standing. Doubters point out that a list of experts backed by a student movement is not a conventional political actor. Just as Vučić – a conventional actor in his own right, backed by international counterparts and shared interests – did not know how to defeat it at the ballot box, conventional actors in EU capitals, fixated on their own backyards, will have trouble knowing how to deal with it. 

There are signs that the EU will suddenly become more inclined to pursue value-based policies towards candidate country Serbia, impatiently asking the new government about its stance on Kosovo, the war crimes of the 1990s and relations with Russia. This comes after many key member states long tolerated an increasingly autocratic regime – one that in 2024 tried to persuade its citizens that the international community regards Serbs as a “genocidal people,” and that only recently buried Ratko Mladić, convicted of genocide, with state honors and senior officials in attendance. Many will be suspicious at best; the harshest critics will call it hypocrisy.

What gives reason for optimism is that the first statements by Ilija Srdanović, the cardiologist who headed the Student List, have been among the most reasonable to come out of Belgrade in many years. He told the Croatian news agency Hina that the new government will not exploit open issues with Croatia the way Vučić, his associates and some media did, and that good relations with neighbors come first – without them, one cannot expect good relations with major powers either. Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković called him the morning after the vote – even though he, too, complained a few days later about a “lack of European flags at the student rallies.”

On the EU, Srdanović has promised to continue accession and to bring domestic policy fully in line with chapters 23 and 24 on the judiciary and fundamental rights, noting that the previous government lost 20 percent of public support for EU integration over 15 years. On Russia, he says such questions must be settled through open public dialogue, not by one man; during the campaign the list ruled out sanctions. For Brussels, that should be an uncomfortable but honest starting point – after all, it patiently tolerated the same no-sanctions policy throughout Vučić’s stabilitocracy. 

Between plenum and parliament

The student plenums vetted every candidate – non-partisan experts mostly from the ranks of academia – and their list ran as a citizens’ group, not a party. No student will take a seat in the new parliament, yet the plenums expect a say in what happens there. Students and MPs are due to pick the cabinet together; Srdanović, despite heading the list, is not its prime minister by default.

Serbia has seen nothing like this before, and the arrangement is fragile. A leaderless movement built on direct democracy must now carry a government of majorities, hierarchies, a tight budget and the economic burdens left behind by the previous regime. If the plenums grip their MPs too tightly, they become an unelected shadow government – an easy target for the new opposition. If they take a more lenient approach, the government loses the base that won it the election.

The students’ safeguard is a signed pledge. Each candidate confirms they never profited from the old regime and will not vote against the list’s program, and any breach counts as resignation.

The movement’s next tests

The movement has built its own expiry date into its structures. The citizens’ association “Student List,” registered in spring 2026, has a fixed lifespan that ends on May 1, 2028 – a signal that the list is meant as a transitional instrument, not a new permanent party.

Through their plenums, the students face three tasks in the coming weeks: helping to shape the cabinet, positioning themselves for the presidential election due by December 27, and redefining their own role. 

The presidential race is a particular test. The movement has signaled it will field its own candidate. With the SNS boycotting, it must avoid a low-turnout contest without real competition, which the SNS would use to question the new president’s legitimacy from day one.

The citizens’ assemblies (zborovi) that sprang up across the country in 2025 may matter even more. Whenever the next local elections come, they will be the natural vehicle for change – and a recruiting pool for a new generation of local politicians.

Leader of what opposition?

The new parliament will be an unusual place – two blocs and a few minority MPs. The parties that stood aside for the Student List will be sitting this term out, hoping their support has earned them credibility they can cash in at the next local, provincial or parliamentary election. A genuine parliamentary life, with ideological debate and a pluralist opposition, will have to be rebuilt almost from scratch.

Vučić wants back in through the opposition benches. In his bid to return to power, he will undoubtedly count on the Student List’s ideological diversity turning into division. And he will be waiting on the right, where he started, to welcome the defectors he hopes for, this time with no need to keep up appearances abroad.

More likely, though, the SNS will fall apart. Stripped of its aura of invincibility and of the hitherto absolute control over the state apparatus, it is an empty shell. Its 39 percent was won in its own world – with state resources harnessed to the campaign and the overwhelming and omnipresent narrative of “the party is the state is the party” that it built so devotedly. That amounts to much less in the real world. And the real world seems to have finally caught up with Serbian politics.

The myth of Vučić as a brilliant strategist, always several moves ahead of his opponents – self-created and self-perpetuated, but sometimes absorbed even by his staunchest critics – is evaporating in real time. He was but an unscrupulous politician who waited patiently for his turn, and the ride is over. That does not make the bill he leaves behind any smaller. It is enormous.

This article first appeared here: rs.boell.org
items.title: Serbia After the Election: A Heavy Legacy for the New Government Analysis Barely an hour and a half after the polls closed, Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat. Ten days later it is clear that losing power and letting go of the state are two different things. Milan Bogdanović

Vučić has already announced that the SNS will not take part in the presidential election, calling it a “farce.” A more plausible explanation: after years of building a personality cult around one man, the elite around him has no other candidate who could remotely threaten whoever the Student List puts forward.

The para-state does not disappear with an election result. In power or in opposition makes little difference to an elite that regards the country – above all its economy – as its property. But even before the actual transfer of power, the first days have shown panic-stricken behavior across the police, the judiciary and business.

Tellingly, Alta Bank, which amassed wealth and influence as a preferred address under SNS rule, has lost its license, and its owner Davor Macura was detained on November 2. He is suspected of removing 45 billion dinars – more than 380 million euros – from the bank’s vault. Alta is only the most visible part of the inheritance. EXPO 2027 is due to open in Belgrade on May 15. items.title: Serbia after the vote: the old regime goes back to its roots, the new one faces the state it inherits Barely an hour and a half after the polls closed, Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat. Ten days later it is clear that losing power and letting go of the state are two different things – and that the new government will be judged by how efficiently it starts restoring the rule of law. items.content_html:
Ahmed Mohamed Jama knows that lived experience can change minds. As a person with a disability, he draws on his own perspective to encourage communities to reflect on the true cost of violence and the importance of choosing peace.

As Executive Director of the Galmudug Disability Organization (GALDO), Ahmed speaks with communities about the lasting consequences of conflict and the limited support available to people whose lives are permanently affected. He challenges young men to consider whether they want to contribute to more violence or become part of the solution.

After joining the Insider Peacebuilders Network in Galmudug state in central Somalia in 2018, Ahmed participated in conflict transformation and dialogue facilitation training supported by the Berghof Foundation. The training strengthened his ability to facilitate conversations across communities and contribute more actively to local peacebuilding initiatives.

A person who is fuelling or participating in conflict today cannot know what consequences may follow tomorrow. Conflict can affect anyone. Therefore, peace is a shared responsibility, and the costs of conflict are shared by everyone.Ahmed Mohamed Jama, insider peacebuilder

One of the most significant examples of this took place during a peace awareness campaign in Bidhaan Dheere, a community on the outskirts of Dhusamareb, the capital of Galmudug. A land dispute had fuelled growing tensions within the community, with the situation escalating to the point where violence appeared increasingly likely.

In response, the district administration brought together local leaders and community representatives to engage directly with residents, including young men who had been involved in the conflict. Through these discussions, they sought to raise awareness of the devastating consequences of violence, while encouraging residents to consider its impact on their families, their community, and their future.

Drawing on both his training and personal experience, Ahmed delivered a message that resonated deeply with the audience by reminding them that the only lasting outcomes of conflict are destruction, displacement, loss of property and disability.

The impact was immediate. Six young men who had been associated with the conflict publicly committed to refraining from violence and supporting peacebuilding efforts.

The engagement continued beyond the public meeting. Ahmed held follow-up conversations with the young men who had previously known little about solving conflicts without violence, encouraging them to look for alternatives and to being peacefully involved in their communities. Over time, they began rebuilding their lives through education, vocational training and employment opportunities. Two enrolled in masonry training, one returned to education through an adult learning programme, and others secured employment in Dhusamareb.

When Ahmed later met one of the participants, the young man reflected on the lasting effect of the intervention.

You cannot imagine how much your speech changed me. Today I live with peace of mind and stability. Following your advice was the best decision I ever made.Participant from the public meeting

Ahmed’s experience demonstrates how insider peacebuilders can use trusted local relationships and dialogue skills to influence behaviour, reduce support for violence and create pathways towards more constructive livelihoods. It also highlights the importance of ensuring people with disabilities are recognised not only as those affected by conflict, but as active contributors to peacebuilding.

By equipping local peacebuilders with practical mediation and dialogue skills, Berghof Foundation’s support to the Insider Peacebuilders Network has helped strengthen community-led efforts to prevent violence and build more resilient local peace infrastructures in Somalia.

Your support helps us do more

So much money is spent on war. It’s time to invest in peace. Your donation enables us to sustain and expand our work.

After joining the Insider Peacebuilders Network in Galmudug state in central Somalia in 2018, Ahmed participated in conflict transformation and dialogue facilitation training supported by the Berghof Foundation. The training strengthened his ability to facilitate conversations across communities and contribute more actively to local peacebuilding initiatives.

A person who is fuelling or participating in conflict today cannot know what consequences may follow tomorrow. Conflict can affect anyone. Therefore, peace is a shared responsibility, and the costs of conflict are shared by everyone.Ahmed Mohamed Jama, insider peacebuilder

One of the most significant examples of this took place during a peace awareness campaign in Bidhaan Dheere, a community on the outskirts of Dhusamareb, the capital of Galmudug. A land dispute had fuelled growing tensions within the community, with the situation escalating to the point where violence appeared increasingly likely.

In response, the district administration brought together local leaders and community representatives to engage directly with residents, including young men who had been involved in the conflict. Through these discussions, they sought to raise awareness of the devastating consequences of violence, while encouraging residents to consider its impact on their families, their community, and their future.

Drawing on both his training and personal experience, Ahmed delivered a message that resonated deeply with the audience by reminding them that the only lasting outcomes of conflict are destruction, displacement, loss of property and disability.

The impact was immediate. Six young men who had been associated with the conflict publicly committed to refraining from violence and supporting peacebuilding efforts.

The engagement continued beyond the public meeting. Ahmed held follow-up conversations with the young men who had previously known little about solving conflicts without violence, encouraging them to look for alternatives and to being peacefully involved in their communities. Over time, they began rebuilding their lives through education, vocational training and employment opportunities. Two enrolled in masonry training, one returned to education through an adult learning programme, and others secured employment in Dhusamareb.

When Ahmed later met one of the participants, the young man reflected on the lasting effect of the intervention.

You cannot imagine how much your speech changed me. Today I live with peace of mind and stability. Following your advice was the best decision I ever made.Participant from the public meeting

Ahmed’s experience demonstrates how insider peacebuilders can use trusted local relationships and dialogue skills to influence behaviour, reduce support for violence and create pathways towards more constructive livelihoods. It also highlights the importance of ensuring people with disabilities are recognised not only as those affected by conflict, but as active contributors to peacebuilding.

By equipping local peacebuilders with practical mediation and dialogue skills, Berghof Foundation’s support to the Insider Peacebuilders Network has helped strengthen community-led efforts to prevent violence and build more resilient local peace infrastructures in Somalia.

Managing diversity constructively is essential to tackling the root causes and structural drivers of conflict and strengthening resilience within societies. This toolkit builds on Berghof’s work in Syria and touches on illustrative examples from other contexts. It provides a human-rights informed, good-governance approach to managing cultural diversity. The toolkit offers reality-tested and practical guidance for relevant stakeholders and practitioners to support developing more inclusive institutions and more cohesive societies.

items.content_html:
In Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region, two communities, whose relationship had been marked by recurring violent conflict for nearly 20 years, are once again sharing grazing land and trading in a revived weekly market. When a recent dispute turned violent, members of both communities stepped in to de-escalate tensions and prevent a cycle of inter-communal violence and revenge killings.

These changes were made possible by a Sustained Dialogue (SD) process involving key community members and the district administrations, facilitated by the Berghof Foundation. By focusing on shared environmental pressures as an entry point, the process helped rebuild trust after decades of conflict.

How climate stress intensifies conflict

Climate stress and armed conflict shape everyday life in the areas. Between 2022 and early 2025 alone, more than 140 violent incidents and 1,200 fatalities were recorded. At the same time, recurring droughts, erratic rainfall, desertification and wider environmental degradation are putting fishing, pastoralism and rain-fed agriculture under increasing pressure.

As grazing land and water become scarcer, competition between communities has intensified, particularly where clear land ownership is unclear. Periods of relative calm can give way to sharp escalation of violence as control of the land and other resources shifts among state forces, militias and non-state armed groups. Climate stress therefore compounds existing insecurity and inter-communal tensions.

Building dialogue from the ground up

In response, the Berghof Foundation and local administrations supported the creation of two committees, each made up of 30 representatives from the respective communities. The committees embarked on a SD process, a structured, locally led, long-term approach to dialogue that brings together elders, youth, women and religious leaders to rebuild trust and develop joint solutions to deep-rooted conflicts.

During the first six months, the two committees met separately to strengthen the members’ dialogue skills and prepare to jointly engage with the neighbouring community. In these sessions, they examined links between environmental pressures and conflict and identified possible responses.

Both committees identified drought, water scarcity and shrinking grazing land as shared challenges affecting everyone. Their similar analysis provided common ground for joint sessions and shifted the focus away from divisive, politically charged topics.

The committees then began meeting across community lines. In two sessions, each committee hosted the other in their location, while ensuring everyone’s safety. Committee members later described seeing each other as “one big family” whose members support and care for one another. 

Throughout the dialogue process, participants also rediscovered family ties and renewed longstanding relationships, gradually developing a shared commitment to reunite their broader communities and address the issues that had divided them.

Preventing retaliation through collective action

Even when renewed violence made in-person sessions difficult, SD committee members continued engaging across conflict lines to build bridges between the communities. This proved critical after an incident that could have triggered the familiar pattern of retaliation and wider inter-community violence.

Committee members helped calm tensions and reframe the incident as an individual legal matter rather than a collective grievance. At the same time, young committee members used their communication networks to encourage restraint and respect for both formal and traditional justice processes. By doing so, the SD committee members managed to prevent another cycle of revenge killings between the communities. For many, the experience demonstrated for the first time how dialogue and collective action could break a cycle of violence that had endured for generations.

For many, the experience demonstrated for the first time how dialogue and collective action could break a cycle of violence that had endured for generations.

Sharing grazing land again

Years of hostility had turned the land between the communities into a “no-go zone”, preventing communal grazing and deepening hardships for pastoralists and farmers on both sides.

The committees identified shared grazing access as a practical first step towards cooperation. They established communication networks among pastoralists, key community stakeholders and decision makers, and advocated for safe, coordinated access. Gradually, cautious coordination developed into renewed cooperation, allowing both communities to safely let their livestock graze across previously contested areas.

Reviving trade

The reopening of a weekly market is one of the clearest signs of renewed trust. Insecurity and mistrust had brought trade between the communities to a halt, but the market now serves again as an economic hub for the wider area.

Every Friday, people exchange livestock, crops and other goods in a space both communities consider safe. These regular interactions create practical interdependence and make the benefits of cooperation visible.

Sustaining the momentum

The changed relationship between these two communities shows how sustained, locally led dialogue can shift even entrenched conflicts. Shared environmental pressures offered an entry point, while repeated engagement gave trust and cooperation time to develop.

Protecting and building on these gains will require continued engagement and adaptive support. But the two communities’ experience demonstrates what patient, community-led peacebuilding can achieve.

This impact story was adapted from a version originally published on the Weathering Risk initiative website by adelphi.

items.content_html:
Read Margaret Chaikosa's story!

More than 40 years after Zimbabwe gained independence, land ownership and control remains a huge challenge for local farmers trying to make ends meet.

Read on to find out how the Berghof Foundation and Africa University’s Insider Mediation Training is helping farmers secure irrigation schemes to water their crops throughout the dry season.

Without official documents for land tenure – a type of law that determines the control farmers can have over land they don’t own – it’s impossible for farmers to secure irrigation infrastructure from local authorities to water their crops. In the Chiwundura Area, Vungu District of Zimbabwe – livelihoods are now at risk.

Margaret Chaikosa works at the Centre for Conflict Management and Transformation (CCMT). After taking part in the Berghof Foundation and Africa University’s Insider Mediator Training, she decided to bring parties together to try to find a solution.

Margaret's goal was to assist farmers in getting boreholes, a type of irrigation infrastructure that pumps water from deep underground to the surface. For this, farmers needed local authorities to grant them the right to make decisions on issues affecting crop output. Such a right would help secure crop yields year on year – supporting entire communities.

The Insider Mediation Training helped me to enhance my capacity and confidenceMargaret Chaikosa

“The Insider Mediation Training helped me to identify networks that the CCMT can leverage to escalate the issue of land rights at the national and policy level. It also enhanced my capacity and confidence. The training approach – focused on negotiation and dialogue to reach a compromise – greatly enhanced our advocacy efforts and impact. As more parties are heard, I sense a greater openness towards finding a solution”, says Margaret about the training.

The parties involved in the dialogue process include the local authority, irrigation service providers, and the irrigation management committee representing farmers.

While conversations are still ongoing, Berghof and Africa University’s Insider Mediation Training is giving local actors the tools to navigate a historical and ever-present disparity: who controls land and livelihoods in Zimbabwe.

This project is made possible through the generous support of the European Union.

Since 2015, we have been working with the Hirshabelle Insider Peacebuilders Network (IPN) in Hirshabelle State, Somalia. The IPN is comprised of a group of 61 individuals from different societal, clan, and age groups, including youth and women, across the state of Hirshabelle. The network is active in the four districts of Balad, Jowhar, Bulla Burte and Beledweyne, where the members organise and lead peacebuilding and reconciliation activities across Hirshabelle State.

We support the independent mediation and reconciliation activities of the IPN members by providing capacity-building on relevant topics, including trauma healing, community policing, and climate security. We also offer crucial safe spaces for the members to meet and exchange on their experiences across the districts on a regular basis so they can learn from each other.

Why we work with insider peacebuilders in Somalia

The Hirshabelle Insider Peacebuilders Network (IPN) directly addresses the need for locally-owned mechanisms for conflict transformation. Building the capacity of and motivating Somali citizens to act as “insider mediators” or “insider peacebuilders” has great potential in Somalia, as many of the conflicts that are happening in the country are extremely difficult for external actors to address. Thus, empowering insiders to work more actively for peace allows international actors, like the Berghof Foundation, to sustainably support conflict transformation in the country.

As the network has expanded over the years, there has been an increasing need to monitor and track their many activities. Travel within Hirshabelle State can be immensely difficult due to a fluctuating security situation; at times, network members cannot meet, and opportunities for them to connect, engage and learn from each other are disrupted. In order to connect the local peacebuilders across the different districts and foster peer exchange, we have added a digital approach to our support for the network by incorporating GiS mapping software to create a “peace map” of their activities.

This “peace map” functions as a virtual and immersive space for IPN members to track where and how they engage in conflict transformation activities, exchange on their experiences, and network virtually across Hirshabelle State – while narrating their stories in their own voice.

The software captures local peacebuilding processes in an interactive and “living” map, connecting each peacebuilding story with its direct location in Hirshabelle State, allowing us to showcase the network’s activities with the goal of creating and fostering a culture of peace on the community level.

Incorporating technology-focused solutions into ongoing peacebuilding support presents new challenges and risks but also great opportunities. On the one hand, both data protection and security need to be key priorities when selecting virtual tools, and our team carefully monitors risks and adopts additional measures to ensure the IPN members can connect safely with each other. On the other hand, the GIS mapping software allows our team to enhance monitoring and evaluation of the manifold activities that the network members implement independently across Hirshabelle State. The tool has improved our ability to assess the impact of the IPN activities within communities. It also allows us to better identify the network members' needs so that we can adapt our support accordingly and provide them with tailored capacity-building.

In addition, the “peace map” enables the IPN members to share their stories and experiences with a wider audience in their own words, through audio and video clips, or in written form. Being able to share the impact of their work encourages the IPN members to connect with each other digitally and to exchange across district borders. By strengthening their peer exchange, the “peace map” helps us foster a culture of learning and support within the network.

Overall, creating a digital means of storytelling and mapping peacebuilding efforts not only offers new opportunities for our peace support to local insider peacebuilders, but also allows us to rethink and better adapt existing peacebuilding and reconciliation efforts to the evolving needs in Hirshabelle State.

The Berghof Foundation has worked with people from Abkhazia, Georgia and South Ossetia since 2012, focusing on their personal memories and identity.

This approach aims to overcome victim-hero narratives, start dialogue about the shared history and allow for an acknowledgement of grievances caused by violence and injustice on all sides of the conflict.

Together with our local partners, we organised workshops, so-called Biographical Salons, where participants exchanged biographical stories and thereby their take on the conflicts’ history. Listening to different voices, sharing experiences and voicing grievances made the workshop participants appreciate the other side’s losses. This is a first step towards forgiveness.

These Biographical Salons have become regular events and were broadcast by Abkhaz television so the new narratives and mutual understanding created during the events could reach a broader audience in the region.

items.content_html:
Our radio programme in Somalia fosters community dialogue around climate change and conflict.

Somalia has been experiencing an increase in extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods, both in frequency and intensity over the past decade. As Somali society and economy largely depend on pastoralism and agriculture, the changing weather has had massive negative consequences for the livelihoods of the people. As an alternative income source, many Somalis have entered the charcoal trade, further exacerbating environmental degradation. Moreover, the changing weather patterns have led to a notable decrease in the availability of natural resources, such as potable water. This in turn has significantly escalated competition among Somalis for these scarce resources, thus increasing the likelihood of violence.

In 2021, we began streaming the radio programme “Garasho-wadaag”, which translates to “sharing of knowledge”, in the central Somali state of Galmudug to address the issues rising from the complex interaction of climate change, environment degradation and conflict.

Radio shows are very popular in rural and remote areas of Somalia. So, our team decided to utilise this medium to increase awareness and bring local peacebuilders together with experts and community members to discuss how environmental degradation exacerbates conflict, and what adaptation measures or coping mechanisms could look like.

Please click on the box of the bottom right corner of the video to enable subtitles.

This programme has done a lot in raising public awareness. Many people who used to fight over grazing lands and over water wells now let their animals graze and drink water together. They formed peacebuilding committees.Abdifatah Abdullahi Hussein, radio programme listener

The episodes address topics ranging from climate, dialogue and religious responsibilities. Graphic © Odile Stabon, adelphi

Each episode begins with a short drama sketch followed by a live discussion with guests, typically community peacebuilders and representatives from local authorities. The drama titled “Geedi and Gobaad” is about two protagonists, a young man and his grandmother, who engage with their communities to address current issues and raise awareness about the conflict-climate nexus.

Moderated by Burhan Abdullahi, a prominent young journalist from Galkayo who also plays the character of Geedi in the drama, the subsequent discussions explore topics such as the merits of inclusive and collaborative peacebuilding, the religious and traditional responsibilities to protect the environment, clan conflicts and revenge killings, climate change-induced conflicts, deforestation and other forms of environmental degradation, and the myriad of sociopolitical and economic implication.

When you listen to the drama story of "Geedi and Gobaad", you will realise that conflicts could be best resolved through dialogue. I can confidently say that Garasho-wadaag is a very important programme for the community.Maymun Ali Nur, Chairperson of Women’s Association in Galkayo, radio programme listener

The guests chosen reflect the diversity of the actors involved in peacebuilding in Galmudug. Graphic © Odile Stabon, adelphi

The radio programme is aired live from a station in Galkayo and broadcasted on three further stations in Galmudug. To reach a broader audience inside and outside of Somalia, the programme is streamed live on facebook and the audio is later made available as a podcast. On Facebook alone, the programme has already reached 75,000 people.

Our efforts are limited in the sense that we can only gather four to five people to discuss issues, whereas the programme uses mass media to convey the message.Nabadon Abdulqadir Ali Hashi, radio programme listener

Due to the popularity of the programme and extensive positive feedback from guests, listeners, and followers on social media, the radio programme has been extended from airing once a month to twice a month in Galmudug. Inspired by its success, we started a second radio programme in Hirshabelle State and we are planning to further expand the radio programmes in order to reach as many Somalis as possible who are interested in environmental peacebuilding.

The radio programme is part of our work within the Weathering Risk consortium led by adelphi.

Read more on adelphi's website.

The episodes address topics ranging from climate, dialogue and religious responsibilities. Graphic © Odile Stabon, adelphi

Each episode begins with a short drama sketch followed by a live discussion with guests, typically community peacebuilders and representatives from local authorities. The drama titled “Geedi and Gobaad” is about two protagonists, a young man and his grandmother, who engage with their communities to address current issues and raise awareness about the conflict-climate nexus.

Moderated by Burhan Abdullahi, a prominent young journalist from Galkayo who also plays the character of Geedi in the drama, the subsequent discussions explore topics such as the merits of inclusive and collaborative peacebuilding, the religious and traditional responsibilities to protect the environment, clan conflicts and revenge killings, climate change-induced conflicts, deforestation and other forms of environmental degradation, and the myriad of sociopolitical and economic implication.

When you listen to the drama story of "Geedi and Gobaad", you will realise that conflicts could be best resolved through dialogue. I can confidently say that Garasho-wadaag is a very important programme for the community.Maymun Ali Nur, Chairperson of Women’s Association in Galkayo, radio programme listener

The guests chosen reflect the diversity of the actors involved in peacebuilding in Galmudug. Graphic © Odile Stabon, adelphi

The radio programme is aired live from a station in Galkayo and broadcasted on three further stations in Galmudug. To reach a broader audience inside and outside of Somalia, the programme is streamed live on facebook and the audio is later made available as a podcast. On Facebook alone, the programme has already reached 75,000 people.

Our efforts are limited in the sense that we can only gather four to five people to discuss issues, whereas the programme uses mass media to convey the message.Nabadon Abdulqadir Ali Hashi, radio programme listener

Due to the popularity of the programme and extensive positive feedback from guests, listeners, and followers on social media, the radio programme has been extended from airing once a month to twice a month in Galmudug. Inspired by its success, we started a second radio programme in Hirshabelle State and we are planning to further expand the radio programmes in order to reach as many Somalis as possible who are interested in environmental peacebuilding.

The radio programme is part of our work within the Weathering Risk consortium led by adelphi.

items.content_html:
Read Owen Dhliwayo’s story!

Communities in the Chipinge district of Zimbabwe are facing dispossession. Nearly 1,800 households have already been forcibly displaced to clear land for the establishment of an ethanol plant. In addition, nearly 1,000 households have been served eviction notices by the government. In Zimbabwe, evictions have been flooding the nation. People have been forced from their homes to make room for new businesses. Conflicting interpretations of the Zimbabwean constitution that prioritise the land rights of religious leaders have prolonged this issue.

To solve this conflict and bring more clarity to the situation, our local insider mediator Owen Dhliwayo started a mediation process. In a series of mediation meetings, he brought together relevant conflict stakeholders, including people who had been evicted as well as institutional leaders, to showcase the different perspectives and work towards the various parties understanding each other’s positions. Through this dialogue process, he managed to facilitate an agreement between the conflicting parties that settled the issues that caused land-based disputes.

Parallel to Owen’s mediation efforts, civil society organisations of the Chipinge district went to the local courts and demanded the current eviction policybe altered. Since the courts and other parties to the conflict saw the success of Owen‘s efforts, they proposed another dialogue session with him and other insider mediators in order for all conflict stakeholders to reach an agreement peacefully. This proved to be a shift in culture in understanding the value of mediation in the Chipinge district.

The Insider Mediation Training helped me gain a better understanding of what conflict transformation could look like in Chipinge.Owen Dhliwayo

Owen had taken part in our training with Africa University where the participants learned about theoretical and practical foundations for the sustainable transformation of conflict. “The Berghof Foundation and Africa University’s Insider Mediation Training helped me gain a better understanding of what conflict transformation could look like in Chipinge. It imparted mediation skills that focused on reaching a solution via consensus and dialogue and stressed the importance of strategic coordination, flexible mandates, and appropriate timelines that fit all parties,” says Owen about his experience at the training.

Thanks to Owen’s groundwork, the Chipinge Rural District Council has acknowledged that arbitrary evictions increase the vulnerability of communal land and livelihoods and undermine the local economy. The Council has halted arbitrary evictions and traditional leaders are now in the process of implementing a law that will protect and secure access to land in the district.

This project is made possible through the generous support of the European Union.

items.content_html:
On 5 October 2026, The Guardian published an article based on an analysis by UCLA researchers using Carbon Mapper satellite data, which identified the 10 landfill sites in Turkey with the highest methane emissions. According to the report, the Silivri landfill site in Istanbul emits an average of 7.4 tonnes of methane per hour, whilst the landfill site in Şile emits approximately 4 tonnes. The timing of the report is particularly noteworthy for Turkey, which is set to host the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) from 9 to 20 November 2026. 

This is because Turkey has placed zero waste and methane reduction among the priority items on the action agenda for the summit. Although it supported the Declaration on the Reduction of Methane from Organic Waste at COP29 in Baku, it has not yet joined the Global Methane Pledge (GMP), which currently includes 159 countries and the European Commission and aims to reduce global anthropogenic methane emissions by at least 30 per cent by 2030 compared to 2020 levels. Consequently, three questions come to the fore ahead of the summit to be held in Antalya in November. How prominent is zero waste on the COP31 agenda? What is the current situation regarding waste management in Turkey and globally? What can realistically be expected from the COP31 summit?

Zero Waste: Strong Rhetoric, Unclear Framework

The key question regarding the zero-waste agenda is to what extent this rhetoric will translate into concrete and measurable policies.

The COP31 Presidency identified zero-waste as one of its priorities from the outset. The role of High-Level Climate Champion was assigned to the President of the Zero Waste Foundation, one of the leading figures behind Turkey’s official ‘Zero Waste’ narrative. The Global Zero Waste Forum, organised by the Foundation in June 2026 and attended by participants from various regions of the world, was also presented as part of the preparations for COP31. Furthermore, on 9 June, COP31 President Murat Kurum announced a target to halve the growth in global waste generation by 2035. However, the details of this target – in terms of the base year, scope and implementation tools – remain unclear. It is also uncertain how the announced target addresses issues such as reducing plastic production, ensuring a just transition for waste collectors, and dealing with waste incineration and pyrolysis.

Whilst ‘zero waste’ has been one of the prominent themes on the COP31 agenda from the outset, electrification appears to be taking centre stage as the summit approaches. However, the key question regarding the zero-waste agenda is to what extent this rhetoric will translate into concrete and measurable policies; in other words, whether this rhetoric will translate into measurable policies and tangible changes on the ground. Turkey’s current waste management practices, methane emissions and recycling figures also make this question all the more important.

The Situation in Turkey: Methane, Landfill, Recycling

In Turkey, local authorities collect approximately 33 million tonnes of waste annually; 50.3 per cent of this – that is, half – consists of organic waste. With approximately 70 per cent of waste going to landfill, landfilling remains Turkey’s main waste management method. Whilst 16.5 million tonnes of compostable waste is generated annually, the amount of waste recovered at composting facilities is just 124,000 tonnes. In other words, a significant amount of organic waste is being sent to landfill sites.

Methane emissions from solid waste could be reduced by 95 per cent by 2030.

However, as The Guardian report illustrates, significant amounts of methane can escape into the atmosphere from landfill sites. Whilst the proportion of methane that can be captured depends on the site’s design, the system’s efficiency, and maintenance and operational conditions, even a well-equipped site can capture no more than 60 per cent of the methane produced. Due to the lack of an adequate and effective waste management infrastructure in the country, most waste ends up in landfill sites in a mixed state. However, when waste prevention, separate collection at source and bio-stabilisation methods are applied together, methane emissions from solid waste could be reduced by 95 per cent by 2030. Even separating organic waste – one of the most sustainable ways to reduce methane emissions – would cut landfill methane by 62 per cent.

It remains unclear what policies and financing mechanisms will underpin Murat Kurum’s statements on reducing methane emissions from waste. Viewed on a global scale, funding priorities also present a contentious picture. According to Climate Policy Initiative’s tracking of methane-abatement finance for 2021-2022, 94 per cent of global climate finance allocated to methane reduction in the solid waste sector (approximately 3.86 billion dollars) went to incineration plants, whilst the share allocated to organic waste management stood at just 1 per cent. This distribution of funding also contributes to a situation in which global waste management approaches are trapped in a choice between incineration and landfilling, pushing waste reduction at source further down the agenda. Landfilling and incineration generate different greenhouse gas emissions. While organic waste decomposing in landfill sites releases methane, burning waste produces CO₂ emissions, particularly from fossil-derived materials such as plastics. Although incineration may be considered more climate-friendly than landfilling under certain conditions, reports suggest that waste incineration plants can produce more greenhouse gas emissions than many other forms of power generation, including coal-fired power plants.

Whilst waste incineration reduces the volume of waste and is presented as a method of energy production, it does nothing to address the current shortfall. The high investment costs of incineration plants mean they require a steady supply of waste over the long term, creating pressure on municipalities to maintain a steady flow of waste to these facilities. Consequently, approaches that would genuinely contribute to the circular economy – such as prevention, recovery and reuse – are sidelined or not prioritised.

The discrepancies in waste recovery performance data in Turkey are also striking: whilst the Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, headed by COP31 President Kurum, has announced a municipal waste recovery rate of 36.08 per cent for 2024, independent estimates suggest this rate is around 10–12 per cent and therefore well below the EU average (48 per cent). In this context, the legal framework in Turkey is also rather inadequate. The Single-Use Plastics Regulation, announced in March 2026, was due to come into force on 1 September; however, as of October, when this article was written, the regulation had still not come into force. It has been claimed that one of the reasons for this delay is the dominant role played by the industry in decision-making processes.

Meanwhile, Turkey’s plastics sector ranks second in Europe and sixth in the world in terms of production capacity. Moreover, the construction of a 27-billion-dollar petrochemical complex in Yumurtalık and Ceyhan in Adana is planned to push this ranking even higher.

Waste Trade and the Mediterranean

Turkey’s leading position in the plastics sector is not limited to production. Turkey is the top destination for plastic waste exports from the EU. The volume of plastic waste sent from the EU to Turkey reached a record level of approximately 510,000 tonnes in 2025. Under the new Waste Shipment Regulation adopted by the EU in 2024, the export of plastic waste to third countries has been subject to a prior notification and authorisation procedure since May 2026; the export of plastic waste to non-OECD countries, meanwhile, will be banned from 21 November 2026. As Turkey is an OECD member, it is not covered by this ban. The fact that the country is currently the EU’s largest OECD recipient of plastic waste is raising concerns about the potential impact of the ban on the volume of waste directed towards Turkey; indeed, it is forecast that, unless further measures are taken, imports could exceed 1 million tonnes in 2026.

Turkey is currently the EU’s largest OECD recipient of plastic waste.

The environmental consequences of the plastic waste trade are becoming particularly evident around the Mediterranean. Microplastic pollution, which came to the fore along the Adana and Mediterranean coasts throughout 2026, also highlighted the environmental impacts of plastic recycling activities. A 2026 study conducted in the irrigation canals surrounding recycling facilities in Adana revealed that microplastic concentrations in the canals downstream of the facilities were up to 132 times higher than in the upstream sections. Given the canals’ connection to rivers and the sea, the possibility that the Seyhan River could carry 5.3 billion microplastic particles into the Mediterranean Sea every hour is a cause for concern. Furthermore, the presence of certain plastic pellets and industrial copolymers – detected exclusively in the lower reaches of the facilities – clearly demonstrates that this pollution is directly linked to recycling activities.

The sector’s environmental impact is not limited to microplastics or plastic pollution. In Turkey, more than 600 fires have occurred at recycling facilities over the past five years. INTERPOL’s assessment of the global plastic waste trade notes an increase in illegal waste fires in Europe and Asia, whilst highlighting strong indications that deliberate fires are being set in some countries to dispose of non-recyclable stockpiles.

Despite the fate of some of the waste – much of which originates from the EU – as described above, the assessment published by the European Commission in September 2026 is striking in that it highlights the EU’s contradictory stance. The report highlights deficiencies in data and oversight regarding the management of exported plastic waste, as well as incidents of open burning and dumping, and issues such as uncontrolled microplastic emissions and air, water and soil pollution. Despite these findings, and without providing any concrete indicators, the Commission states that exports will continue to be monitored and that shipments to Turkey will be reassessed by the end of 2028, whilst making specific reference to Turkey’s efforts to bring its legislation up to EU standards. This approach has also drawn criticism that the EU prioritises the monitoring of shipments through data collection rather than making a genuine effort to reduce plastic waste exports.

The Global Picture: Fragmented Commitments

The waste sector is a significant source of pollution and emissions, driven not only by local waste management practices but also by the global circulation of waste. Current estimates indicate that the waste sector is responsible for approximately one-fifth of global anthropogenic methane emissions. However, disposal methods requiring significant investment – particularly waste incineration – are criticised for their high financial costs, their potential to lock in waste, and their contribution not only to CO₂ emissions but also to chemical pollutants.

A report published in October 2026 by the global anti-incineration network GAIA, which examined 20 operational or planned incineration plants worldwide, also highlights certain aspects of this debate. According to the report, the 11 plants with publicly available emissions data release at least 5.5 million tonnes of CO₂e annually. It appears that the Runcorn plant in the UK alone was responsible for over 1.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions in 2025. To date, approximately 7 billion dollars have been invested in the 20 plants examined. The report also emphasises that long-term contracts oblige local authorities to send a specific amount of waste to the plants, which is in conflict with waste reduction policies.

These plants emit mercury, dioxins, furans and heavy metals from their chimneys. The remaining ash poses a separate problem. Publicly available data from the plants under review indicates that they produce at least 1.7 million tonnes of incineration ash annually. At this point, the lack of publicly available, transparent and comparable data regarding the emissions from incineration plants in Turkey, the volume of ash produced and how it is managed is striking. Given that the COP31 Presidency has presented the ‘zero-waste’ agenda as one of its priority topics, transparency in this aspect of waste management is also crucial for the credibility of the agenda.

Despite all these impacts, capacity figures in Europe are reigniting the debate on new incineration investments. According to a 2026 study prepared for Zero Waste Europe using Eurostat data, the total capacity of incineration plants in the EU reached 198.4 million tonnes in 2022, whilst approximately 133.6 million tonnes of waste were incinerated in the same year. The difference of approximately 65 million tonnes between these two figures implies that around one-third of Europe’s current incineration capacity remains unused. Whilst incineration capacity increased by an average of approximately 8 million tonnes per year between 2004 and 2012, the rate of increase has since 2012 been observed to be approximately 2 million tonnes per year. Based on these figures, it is argued that there is no need for new incineration capacity in the EU and that new investments could conflict with waste prevention and recycling targets. 

Plastic production is also a direct climate issue.

A similar divide is evident in the negotiations on the Global Plastics Treaty. The negotiations, held in Geneva in August 2025, concluded without agreement on the text of the treaty. One of the key points of contention was whether the agreement would cover the entire life cycle of plastics and include restrictions on primary plastic production. Whilst a group of countries called for global and binding measures, including production limits, some countries argued that the scope of the agreement should be limited primarily to product design, recycling and waste management. Fossil fuel-producing countries, which are among the main opponents of production limits, have been criticised for attempting to reduce the agreement essentially to waste management.

Yet plastic production is also a direct climate issue. Approximately 99 per cent of plastics are produced from fossil fuel-derived raw materials. According to a study, primary plastic production alone accounted for 5.3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2019, with 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon emissions. However, this calculation does not include emissions from plastics after the end of their useful life.

What Can Be Expected From COP31?

The current situation suggests that it is more likely that COP31 will result in voluntary commitments rather than a binding international regulation on zero waste. Although the host country, Turkey, may call for a new declaration or alliance, the summit’s success should be assessed by the extent to which this rhetoric is translated into concrete targets, timetables, funding and implementation mechanisms. In this context, the steps listed below could serve as key indicators for evaluating the extent to which COP31’s zero-waste agenda has been realised:

  • The introduction of sector-specific quantitative methane reduction targets, interim targets and measurement, reporting and verification mechanisms for the waste sector;
  • Turkey’s accession to the Global Methane Pledge and the setting of time-bound targets to end the disposal of organic waste in landfill sites within the next five years;
  • The COP31 Presidency issuing an international call to ban the import of plastic waste and to end the international waste trade;
  • The implementation of legislation on single-use plastics in Turkey, including a production ban, and the signing of a global declaration of intent in this context;
  • The explicit inclusion of targets for the separate collection of organic waste at source in national climate plans and NDCs, and the setting of short-, medium- and long-term targets for composting;
  • A commitment that, within the framework of climate finance, no funds will be channelled towards high-cost disposal technologies such as waste incineration and chemical conversion;
  • The official recognition of waste collectors, their inclusion in the social security system, and ensuring their participation in decision-making processes regarding waste policies.

The question to be asked at the end of the summit is a simple one: Will “zero waste” become a measurable policy that genuinely reduces emissions and waste generation, or will it remain largely a matter of rhetoric?
items.title: Will COP31’s Zero-Waste Agenda Move Beyond Rhetoric? Analysis Turkey heads into COP31 prioritising zero waste and methane reduction. Yet much of its waste still ends up in landfills emitting methane visible from space, while plastic waste imports continue. What can realistically be expected from COP31? Prof. Dr. Sedat Gündoğdu

Despite all these impacts, capacity figures in Europe are reigniting the debate on new incineration investments. According to a 2026 study prepared for Zero Waste Europe using Eurostat data, the total capacity of incineration plants in the EU reached 198.4 million tonnes in 2022, whilst approximately 133.6 million tonnes of waste were incinerated in the same year. The difference of approximately 65 million tonnes between these two figures implies that around one-third of Europe’s current incineration capacity remains unused. Whilst incineration capacity increased by an average of approximately 8 million tonnes per year between 2004 and 2012, the rate of increase has since 2012 been observed to be approximately 2 million tonnes per year. Based on these figures, it is argued that there is no need for new incineration capacity in the EU and that new investments could conflict with waste prevention and recycling targets. 

Plastic production is also a direct climate issue.

A similar divide is evident in the negotiations on the Global Plastics Treaty. The negotiations, held in Geneva in August 2025, concluded without agreement on the text of the treaty. One of the key points of contention was whether the agreement would cover the entire life cycle of plastics and include restrictions on primary plastic production. Whilst a group of countries called for global and binding measures, including production limits, some countries argued that the scope of the agreement should be limited primarily to product design, recycling and waste management. Fossil fuel-producing countries, which are among the main opponents of production limits, have been criticised for attempting to reduce the agreement essentially to waste management.

Yet plastic production is also a direct climate issue. Approximately 99 per cent of plastics are produced from fossil fuel-derived raw materials. According to a study, primary plastic production alone accounted for 5.3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2019, with 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon emissions. However, this calculation does not include emissions from plastics after the end of their useful life.

What Can Be Expected From COP31?

The current situation suggests that it is more likely that COP31 will result in voluntary commitments rather than a binding international regulation on zero waste. Although the host country, Turkey, may call for a new declaration or alliance, the summit’s success should be assessed by the extent to which this rhetoric is translated into concrete targets, timetables, funding and implementation mechanisms. In this context, the steps listed below could serve as key indicators for evaluating the extent to which COP31’s zero-waste agenda has been realised:

  • The introduction of sector-specific quantitative methane reduction targets, interim targets and measurement, reporting and verification mechanisms for the waste sector;
  • Turkey’s accession to the Global Methane Pledge and the setting of time-bound targets to end the disposal of organic waste in landfill sites within the next five years;
  • The COP31 Presidency issuing an international call to ban the import of plastic waste and to end the international waste trade;
  • The implementation of legislation on single-use plastics in Turkey, including a production ban, and the signing of a global declaration of intent in this context;
  • The explicit inclusion of targets for the separate collection of organic waste at source in national climate plans and NDCs, and the setting of short-, medium- and long-term targets for composting;
  • A commitment that, within the framework of climate finance, no funds will be channelled towards high-cost disposal technologies such as waste incineration and chemical conversion;
  • The official recognition of waste collectors, their inclusion in the social security system, and ensuring their participation in decision-making processes regarding waste policies.

The question to be asked at the end of the summit is a simple one: Will “zero waste” become a measurable policy that genuinely reduces emissions and waste generation, or will it remain largely a matter of rhetoric?

Somalia has suffered from ongoing violent conflict for close to three decades, leaving 12 million people in need of humanitarian assistance. So far, the many international attempts at brokering peace have failed.

The Berghof Foundation supported community representatives in the federal member state of Hirshabelle in central Somalia in their efforts to build peace by creating a network of insider peacebuilders who have the skills and experience to encourage dialogue and reconciliation in their communities.

These trained peacebuilders jointly facilitated a series of Shirarka in Hirshabelle State in 2018. Shirarka are six-day traditional Somali assemblies that bring together individuals from various clans and subclans. They involve representatives from all segments of society, including women, young people, professionals, elders, poets and religious leaders. These assemblies provide an inclusive space for all to express their views on conflict with the goal of motivating people to work together towards transforming the violent conflicts that affect them as well as preventing new conflicts from occurring.

Your support helps us do more

So much money is spent on war. It’s time to invest in peace. Your donation enables us to sustain and expand our work.

Donate

We aim to strengthen people’s capacity to solve their own conflicts and help them realise that they themselves have the ability to shape the outcomes on the ground and become peacemakers.

For example, one of the members of the peacebuilders network, Abdikarim Omar Maalim, a local journalist, resolved a conflict between two football teams that had become violent. Not only did he mediate between the teams in order to resolve their issues peacefully, but he approached the local business community to fund the reconstruction of the football field. The inauguration game attracted hundreds of spectators, including Vice President Ali Abdullahi Guudlawe, showing how significant this initiative was.

When asked why he did this, Abdikarim said: “When I returned from our training in Djibouti, I asked myself, why don’t I try and do something about this conflict. The training really motivated me and gave me the required skills. I would have never even thought about it before the training.”

The Shir has an effect on me, because the discussions are on contentious issues, the problems we have and on things which caused the destruction of our country... all of this has effects on me and will have effects on the people who are connected to me.Participant at the Jowhar Shir

Based on the information and experience gained during the project, the Berghof Foundation communicates the perspectives of the communities in Hirshabelle State to the local, state and federal authorities in Somalia as well as to the international community through events and reports. We also provide advice and recommendations on reconciliation and conflict transformation in Somalia.

Elisabeth Meyer
Senior Strategic Partnerships Manager

Watch Tatuli Beraia's story

The Berghof Foundation has been organising dialogues with people from Georgia and Abkhazia since 2014 aimed at fostering empathy between them and breaking the cycle of intergenerational trauma. Tatuli Beraia, a participant in our programme, highlights the crucial role of dialogue in addressing the deep psychological scars left by conflict.

Read her story or watch the video below.

Born in 1990, in Gulripshi, Abkhazia, Tatuli’s early life was deeply affected by the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict. After Georgia gained independence from the Soviet Union, many Abkhazians pursued their own state. The war that ensued in the summer of 1992 was fought entirely in Abkhazia and claimed around 10,000 lives, including numerous civilians on both sides. Nearly all Georgians and other ethnic groups fled Abkhazia, and also Tatuli and her family, who are ethnically Georgians, had to leave her childhood home. "I was so small—two, two and a half. My father fought in Sukhumi [on the Georgian side]. We left him there. Mama, her cousin, and I escaped on a steamer”, Tatuli tells us.

They relocated to a hostel originally built for Olympic reservists in Georgia where she lived until she was 20. "It was a building with [many] rooms along a [long] corridor; we all lived like one big family. But I developed a complex. I didn’t want to invite my friends, so as to stop them knowing the conditions in which I lived."

After conflicts end, transgenerational trauma often hinders meaningful dialogue about rebuilding relationships within a society or establishing lasting peace. The challenge of confronting a violent past spans generations and is filled with obstacles. In many countries or regions, the enduring state of conflicts is preserved within family histories, marked by deep wounds and a persistent mistrust of the “other side”. As a result, younger generations, who have not directly experienced the conflict, frequently inherit the traumas of their parents.

At school, for example, Tatuli’s best friend was Abkhazian and they became friends right away. But many were surprised about their friendship since Tatuli was Georgian while her friend was from the ethnic group blamed for the conflict that forced her family to leave their home. “My mother wasn’t happy about it and didn’t want to sit next to my friend’s mother on excursions.", says Tatuli.

Her father, an ex-combatant, carried deep psychological trauma from the war: "Every night before going to sleep, he walks himself in his mind through the streets of Sukhumi so as not to forget. If he can’t remember which alley comes after this or that street, he gets stressed and upset." With her family’s background and the grievances they carry, Tatuli was at danger of inheriting biases and trauma from her parents and elders.

In families who had lived through the war, there’s a great danger that because of the conversations taking place, children can grow up in hatred and enmity, with stereotypes. I’m very happy that I was able to overcome that danger, but it wasn’t easy.Tatuli Beraia

Tatuli took part in our History Dialogue process, in which Abkhaz and Georgian people listened to and discussed stories of the war from both sides. The goal of the dialogue was to develop empathy for each other to build a peaceful future together. Among the many stories Tatuli heard, one that particularly resonated with her was that of Guli, an Abkhazian mother who lost her son in the conflict. Despite her profound loss, she demonstrated the strength to sit down with another person who has also suffered and lost loved ones, serving as a powerful example of reconciliation.

Tatuli realised that true heroism lies in the strength to embrace humanity after the horrors of war. "I [think] that Guli’s son would be very proud of what his mother is doing,” she said after the workshop.

Over the past five years alone, our team organised over 4,000 workshops with participants from all walks of life in Georgia and Abkhazia. We reached over 49,000 people who were open to exchange about the country's past and deal with their trauma.

The transformative stories shared at these workshops by the facilitators, the participants, and many supporters who were involved in the process, played a crucial role in helping young people like Tatuli to break the cycle of transgenerational trauma. Their stories of personal transformation reveal how mutual understanding and healing grievances can pave the way for a future where dialogue and peace are not merely aspirations but lived realities.

This article was updated on 12 September 2024 to fix some typos.
