After eight years of war, tens of thousands of civilian casualties, and over 4 million displaced people – among which almost 80 per cent are women and children – the situation in Yemen remains bleak. The UN-brokered truce between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthi movement, signed in April 2022 and renewed in June is a welcome relief. Even though this was an important step, it is only the first of many that need to be taken in order to reach a comprehensive and lasting solution to end the war.

In the absence of a sustainable peace plan that would stabilise the entire country, the Berghof Foundation has taken concrete steps toward improving the lives of Yemeni people at the local level.

Funded by the European Union and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, we work to enhance community safety in five Yemeni cities: Aden, Al-Mukalla, Dhamar, Sana’a, and Taiz. We seek to enhance both the communities’ capacities to provide a safe environment for their citizens and people’s perception of safety in these cities.

Your support helps us do more

So much money is spent on war. It’s time to invest in peace. Your donation enables us to sustain and expand our work.

Donate

Our community safety initiatives are set up in an inclusive manner, so people from all parts of the local community are involved in the effort to achieve local security for all. This approach is central to our work as we believe that if communication channels for regular exchange between community members and the police are established, then the perceived and real safety within the communities will improve. Ultimately, this will help restore basic state functions and improve the stability of governance structures in Yemen.

We partnered with the Political Development Forum in Yemen (PDF Yemen) and the team worked relentlessly to map and to implement activities on the ground. Together, we established community safety committees (CSCs) and worked closely with local authorities and police institutions to build trust and confidence between the members of the respective community and the security and judiciary providers. After four years, with the pilot phase of this project coming to an end, our initiatives have impacted many communities in the five cities.

Community safety describes a concept in which local police and government authorities work together with members of local communities to jointly enhance the citizens’ day-to-day safety.

In the port city of Aden, for example, the project’s impact has been twofold: The community safety committee in the district of Crater identified the need for increased fire safety. The committee members collaborated with a host of local authorities, such as the Security Director and the civil defense in Aden, in order to raise awareness and render firefighting kits accessible to everyone. The CSC-Crater also organised an awareness-raising campaign among Crater’s citizens. They distributed brochures to guide people on how to use the firefighting kits, they conducted training sessions in schools and communal institutions that taught people basic knowledge of first response in case of fires, and they supplied 14 mosques around Crater with firefighting equipment. The kits were placed so they are easily accessible to all visitors, including women in their part of the mosque.

To this day, the equipment that was provided has been used successfully in a number of cases, saving lives and properties all over Crater. Influential actors in Aden – such as the Southern Transitional Council, representatives of the internationally recognised government, or the governor of Aden – have expressed their continued support to the committee, which enjoys a considerable political backing.

Thank you Berghof and PDF for what you are doing here in Crater. Without the firefighting equipment my property would now be in ashes.A pastry shop owner in the district of Crater in the city of Aden, Yemen

In summer 2021, the CSC also helped solving the bread crisis that had broken out due to a 10 per cent price increase in Aden. Bakery owners had seen the prices of raw materials go up, which in turn had led them to increase the price of their product. Members of the committee successfully supported the mediating efforts of the local police to reach an agreement between the bakery owners and the raw material suppliers. The outcome of the mediation was a deal on affordable fixed prices for both the raw materials and the bread. This successful mediation process is a great example of the quality of the training that the local police and the committee members had received, so they were equipped to help the parties negotiate a solution that can only be described as a win-win situation.

The initiatives working in Aden, as well as in the other four cities have had a profound impact on the lives of Yemeni people. Building trust among all the different stakeholders at community level as well as improving people’s everyday lives are concrete steps toward mitigating the consequences of the humanitarian crisis in Yemen and, eventually, toward an overall national reconciliation in the country.

We support communities facing climate-related challenges by facilitating dialogues to address shared concerns and collaboratively develop solutions. In Southern Iraq, these efforts culminated in a social pact signed by local leaders, authorities, and residents, aiming to reduce conflicts and foster stability. This participatory process has strengthened resilience and social cohesion in the region.

Iraq is facing severe climate change impacts that are reshaping its social and economic landscape. Among those most acutely affected are the farmers in the Dhi Qar and Missan governorates. Heat waves and water shortages are becoming more frequent, leading to increasing levels of crop failures and livestock losses. With their livelihoods at risk, many young farmers abandon their farms and migrate to urban centres like Basra (detailed view of the governorate map). There, they often find themselves in informal settlements without water, electricity, or job opportunities, and at risk of being driven to illicit economies or violent activities.

This urbanisation and the resulting competition over scarce resources strain local services and exacerbate tensions between new arrivals and host communities. Local governments, with low levels of trust and limited conflict management mechanisms, are often unequipped to deal with these challenges. At times, these tensions escalate into incidents of violence between and within communities.

Integrating climate and environmental security into dialogues to transform tensions

Over the past two years, the Berghof Foundation and its Iraqi partner Peace Paradigms Organisation (PPO) have been integrating climate and environmental security into dialogues to address this complex problem – among others in Al-Fidha neighbourhood in the Al-Zubair district, located in the Basra governorate.

Through the dialogues [implemented by Berghof and PPO], we are currently trying to counter these incidents which are caused by these big community changes. That’s why we have chosen Al-Fidha neighbourhood as a model for a diverse society. Understanding and accepting others is the fundamental element in confronting tensions and conflicts.Participant at our dialogue in Al-Zubair

Our work began by listening to the needs of the new arrivals and the host communities. Separate sessions were held where members of both groups were able to express their experiences, needs and grievances. It quickly became clear that each group had their fears and concerns. Host communities accused new arrivals of bringing tribal conflicts and crime to their city, while new arrivals reported facing discrimination and violence.

As a next step, we organised dialogues between various communities about several topics, foremost individual and collective fears and concerns. Additionally, the dialogues addressed the effects of climate change and how to develop a common approach to these issues. Underlying this approach is the empirically tested assumption that dialogue can help to overcome these feelings of aversion, foster understanding of diverse perspectives and encourage learning from others' experiences. Through dialogue, participants are given the space to work towards a common understanding, break down stereotypes, and build meaningful relationships.

This dynamic could also be observed with the participants of the dialogue in Al-Zubair. During the dialogue, both groups began to identify shared needs and risks to their livelihoods, such as lack of services, unemployment, and school kidnappings. Participants also recognised climate change as a shared challenge that exacerbates crop failure, water scarcity, and the increased need for electricity, especially in hotter months for air conditioning. Lastly, women from both communities reported an increased threat of gender-based violence, suggesting that this rise in violence is related to the climate-induced loss of livelihoods and lack of future prospects.

The communities signed a social pact to address climate-related security risks

The communities then took their shared concerns to the mayor, a member of the Iraqi Parliament representing Zubair, local authorities, community police, and tribal and religious leaders, with the aim of collaboratively tackling the most pressing issues and mitigating climate-related risks. The process and mechanism to jointly design and implement solutions were formalised in a social pact that was signed by all dialogue participants. This represents the first-ever pact in Al-Fidha neighbourhood addressing conflicts and tensions between both communities.

The pact outlines a set of principles which can translate into a comprehensive set of measures aimed at reducing conflict and fostering stability in the area. The participants agreed that they should reduce mutual accusations between new arrivals and the host communities to enhance the sense of belonging for all communities living in Al-Fidha neighbourhood. Simultaneously, leaders began emphasising the importance of collaboration to address the shared challenges posed by climate-related security risks. Furthermore, the police have increased patrols around schools to reduce crime and enhance security, ensuring that children can pursue education as one viable pathway to alternative livelihoods.

Promoting communal peace and harmony among all the members of Al-Fidha neighbourhood is a shared responsibility between all community, security, administrative and religious actors.Participant at our dialogues in Al-Zubair

Through this participatory process, the dialogue managed to instil a sense of ownership and responsibility in both the communities and authorities to address climate-related security risks. Dialogue participants have highlighted how the joint assessment of the cascading effects of climate change and a shared commitment to developing practical solutions have helped strengthen both resilience and social cohesion in Al-Fidha neighbourhood.

The overwhelmingly positive feedback from dialogue participants led to the adoption of a larger-scale approach to cover more neighbourhoods in Al-Zubair. The Berghof Foundation and PPO plan to further expand this dialogue initiative to enable even more people to participate in efforts toward peace and climate security.

Heat waves and water shortages are becoming more frequent, leading to increasing levels of crop failures and livestock losses. With their livelihoods at risk, many young farmers abandon their farms and migrate to urban centres like Basra (detailed view of the governorate map). There, they often find themselves in informal settlements without water, electricity, or job opportunities, and at risk of being driven to illicit economies or violent activities.

This urbanisation and the resulting competition over scarce resources strain local services and exacerbate tensions between new arrivals and host communities. Local governments, with low levels of trust and limited conflict management mechanisms, are often unequipped to deal with these challenges. At times, these tensions escalate into incidents of violence between and within communities.

Integrating climate and environmental security into dialogues to transform tensions

Over the past two years, the Berghof Foundation and its Iraqi partner Peace Paradigms Organisation (PPO) have been integrating climate and environmental security into dialogues to address this complex problem – among others in Al-Fidha neighbourhood in the Al-Zubair district, located in the Basra governorate.

Through the dialogues [implemented by Berghof and PPO], we are currently trying to counter these incidents which are caused by these big community changes. That’s why we have chosen Al-Fidha neighbourhood as a model for a diverse society. Understanding and accepting others is the fundamental element in confronting tensions and conflicts.Participant at our dialogue in Al-Zubair

Our work began by listening to the needs of the new arrivals and the host communities. Separate sessions were held where members of both groups were able to express their experiences, needs and grievances. It quickly became clear that each group had their fears and concerns. Host communities accused new arrivals of bringing tribal conflicts and crime to their city, while new arrivals reported facing discrimination and violence.

As a next step, we organised dialogues between various communities about several topics, foremost individual and collective fears and concerns. Additionally, the dialogues addressed the effects of climate change and how to develop a common approach to these issues. Underlying this approach is the empirically tested assumption that dialogue can help to overcome these feelings of aversion, foster understanding of diverse perspectives and encourage learning from others' experiences. Through dialogue, participants are given the space to work towards a common understanding, break down stereotypes, and build meaningful relationships.

This dynamic could also be observed with the participants of the dialogue in Al-Zubair. During the dialogue, both groups began to identify shared needs and risks to their livelihoods, such as lack of services, unemployment, and school kidnappings. Participants also recognised climate change as a shared challenge that exacerbates crop failure, water scarcity, and the increased need for electricity, especially in hotter months for air conditioning. Lastly, women from both communities reported an increased threat of gender-based violence, suggesting that this rise in violence is related to the climate-induced loss of livelihoods and lack of future prospects.

The communities signed a social pact to address climate-related security risks

The communities then took their shared concerns to the mayor, a member of the Iraqi Parliament representing Zubair, local authorities, community police, and tribal and religious leaders, with the aim of collaboratively tackling the most pressing issues and mitigating climate-related risks. The process and mechanism to jointly design and implement solutions were formalised in a social pact that was signed by all dialogue participants. This represents the first-ever pact in Al-Fidha neighbourhood addressing conflicts and tensions between both communities.

The pact outlines a set of principles which can translate into a comprehensive set of measures aimed at reducing conflict and fostering stability in the area. The participants agreed that they should reduce mutual accusations between new arrivals and the host communities to enhance the sense of belonging for all communities living in Al-Fidha neighbourhood. Simultaneously, leaders began emphasising the importance of collaboration to address the shared challenges posed by climate-related security risks. Furthermore, the police have increased patrols around schools to reduce crime and enhance security, ensuring that children can pursue education as one viable pathway to alternative livelihoods.

Promoting communal peace and harmony among all the members of Al-Fidha neighbourhood is a shared responsibility between all community, security, administrative and religious actors.Participant at our dialogues in Al-Zubair

Through this participatory process, the dialogue managed to instil a sense of ownership and responsibility in both the communities and authorities to address climate-related security risks. Dialogue participants have highlighted how the joint assessment of the cascading effects of climate change and a shared commitment to developing practical solutions have helped strengthen both resilience and social cohesion in Al-Fidha neighbourhood.

The overwhelmingly positive feedback from dialogue participants led to the adoption of a larger-scale approach to cover more neighbourhoods in Al-Zubair. The Berghof Foundation and PPO plan to further expand this dialogue initiative to enable even more people to participate in efforts toward peace and climate security.

So much money is spent on war. It’s time to invest in peace. Your donation enables us to sustain and expand our work.

items.content_html:
The stakes for COP31 could not be higher. This year governments head to the annual summit in Antalya, Türkiye, facing the impacts of the largest energy supply crisis in history and ever worsening climate crisis. The economic and security risks of relying on fossil fuels exposed following the US/Israel war on Iran, compounding climate impacts from this year’s Super El Niño, and the reality that the world is now expected to overshoot the 1.5°C temperature goal, reinforce the urgency for COP31 to live up to the Presidencies’ promise of an “implementation COP.”

The flagship initiative of the COP31 Presidency presented by Türkiye to address the twin crises is a new global target on electrification. The proposed “35 by 35” target aims to increase global electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, up from around 20 percent today. This ambition is welcome – electrification is one of the strongest tools we have available to accelerate the global energy transition, but only if that electrification is powered by renewables and accelerates the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF). This is one of the seven essential guardrails civil society are calling on to anchor the electrification target.

IRENA modelling points to the scale of the challenge: to align with 1.5°C, increasing the global electrification rate to 35% by 2035 must be achieved with at least 78 percent of the electricity coming from renewables. At the same time, the IEA finds for electrification to deliver benefits and align with 1.5°C, coal-fired power must fall by around 70 percent, and gas-fired power by around 60 percent by 2035.

As it stands, the proposed global electrification target that governments are being encouraged to sign up to via a pledge at COP31, does not commit or encourage governments to deliver electrification with renewables and simultaneously displace fossil fuels. Without specifying the energy sources that will underpin the additional energy demand created by increased electrification, the global target risks becoming a trojan horse for governments and industry, including Big Tech, to justify their continued dependency on fossil fuels, locking us into increased emissions and worsening climate and energy insecurity. 

Renewables-Based Electrification Is a Critical Driver of the Energy Transition Away From Fossil Fuels

Delivering on the 35-by-35 target with renewable energy (wind, solar, grids and storage) would be transformative for the energy transition, as well as bring wider economic and energy security benefits.

The electrification of “end-use sectors” e.g. vehicles, heating and cooling of buildings, and industrial processes, is recognised as a crucial step to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. When the electricity comes from solar and wind, not gas and coal, it reduces emissions, increases efficiency at the point of use compared to fossil-fuelled technologies, and expands the share of energy demand that can be met with renewable power, thus helping to accelerate economy-wide decarbonisation. Relying on new nuclear power, which takes more than ten years and massive public subsidies to be built, is incompatible with the 2035 target.

Electrification using renewable energy can also significantly expand energy access.

Electrification using renewable energy can also significantly expand energy access. With 730 million people still lacking access to electricity globally, electrification with renewables can deliver more affordable and reliable electricity systems, and strengthen the investment case for grids, mini-grids and distributed energy solutions.

The IEA has confirmed that getting the world to 35 percent electricity by 2035 is cost-effective, can cut household energy bills by 15 percent, reduce fuel import bills by over $400 billion a year, and slash CO₂ emissions from transport, buildings and industry by up to 40 percent. Crucially, they found that electrification delivers maximum economic and climate benefits when powered by clean energy, not fossil fuels. 

COP31’s Call to Action on Electrification Is Missing the Words That Matter

The COP31 Presidency's proposed 35-by-35 global electrification pledge is too vague. The pledge calls for the target to be met with “diverse and sustainable energy sources.” In practice, this means that governments could pursue national electrification policies and plans, and be technically contributing to achieving the target, by shifting their reliance on fossil fuels from one part of the energy system to the other, and adding new energy demand from coal or gas-fired electricity. 

This language has been significantly watered down since Türkiye first launched the initiative at Bonn in June. COP31 President-Designate, Murat Kurum, initially called for “a major acceleration in the shift from direct fossil fuel use to clean electricity across buildings, transport and industry.” Since then, neither Türkiye or Australia have shown leadership to ensure the proposed global target defines electrification to be delivered with renewables or clean electricity, nor have they made any efforts to ensure electrification must go hand in hand with TAFF.  Without these crucial guardrails, the 35-by-35 target will not deliver on its promised economic, security and climate benefits, and risks accelerating rather than limiting climate change. 

Electrification for Big Tech and Data Centres

Unchecked data centre expansion significantly increases the risk that the 35-by-35 target will be met with coal and gas-fired electricity, rather than renewables. Today, new data centres, propelled by Big Tech’s AI race, are one of the main drivers of the global expansion of fossil gas power generation in countries such as the UK, where more than 100 data centres plan to burn gas to generate electricity, and the US, where over 40% of electricity for datacentres is currently powered by gas. In the other largest data centre market, China, around 70% of data centre electricity today comes from coal. The IEA estimates fossil fuel-based electricity will be used to power around 40% of all datacentres globally by 2035.

Data centre expansion is only adding new demand and risks.

Even if powered by renewables, data centre expansion is only adding new demand and risks eating into the renewable electricity supply to critical industries, buildings and transport which should be on top of the decarbonisation agenda. Without robust regulation such as requiring data centres to bring their own new additional renewable energy, prioritising electrification of other sectors (e.g. households, transport, heavy industry), as well as requiring data centres to bear the whole cost of new power grid infrastructure, the data centre boom risks cannibalising energy from critical societal needs and fueling ever-increasing demand cycles.

We are already seeing datacentre expansion in Europe threaten electrification progress. In Denmark for example, Lidl could not electrify its fleet due to a lengthy grid queue with data centres making up the majority of requests. Denmark has introduced measures to deprioritise data centres for grid access. In Ireland and the Netherlands, both heavily congested data centre hubs, electrification of transportation has been stalled. In Spain, industries are asking the government to deprioritise data centres to ensure affordable clean energy for other key sectors like steel and chemicals. Meanwhile, shares of renewable energy in data centre-heavy regions like Ireland are stagnating, and electricity growth is putting pressure on even regions like Aragon in Spain with abundant wind and solar energy. 

Translating Türkiye’s Global Ambition Into National Action

Global ambition surrounding the 35-by-35 target will also need to move beyond the COP stage and be translated by governments into tailored national roadmaps to deliver  electrification with renewables, accelerate supporting infrastructure such as grids and storage, and support TAFF. 

As the key champion of the global electrification target, Türkiye is expected to soon unveil a revision of its own National Energy Plan ahead of COP31. Türkiye currently has no plans to phase out fossil fuels, and is looking for new ways to diversify its imports and increase local exploration for oil and gas, while continuing to support local coal production, planning for new coal plants, and avoiding any discussion on a national coal phaseout plan. 

This is therefore a key opportunity for Türkiye to show credible leadership on how to deliver electrification at home in the right way - with renewables, not fossil fuels. A critical first step to advance electrification in Türkiye would be to announce a just coal phase-out plan, as currently coal remains the leading source of electricity generation in Türkiye, and more than 60 percent of coal-fired electricity is produced using imported coal. At the same time, strengthening the grid and unlocking Türkiye’s untapped wind and solar potential must also be prioritised. Without a clear roadmap to exit coal, efforts to raise the electrification rate in Türkiye to 35 percent by 2035 will result in fossil fuel emissions and energy imports increasing to meet the rising electricity demand. 

Action on Electrification Must Be Accompanied by Finance

Electrifying the world with renewables will also require an unprecedented investment in renewable energy generation, transmission networks, modernised grids, battery storage, and energy access. Governments, development banks, investors, utilities, philanthropies, and businesses must work together to turn COP31’s electrification ambitions and growing political support into finance partnerships that truly address country priorities and just transition needs. 

Electrifying the world with renewables will also require an unprecedented investment.

The COP31 Presidency’s Climate Implementation Bridge offers to play this connecting role by linking country priorities and project pipelines with finance and on the ground implementation partners. Given its expected focus to be on advancing electrification in pilot countries, the Climate Implementation Bridge should prioritise unlocking financing for renewable energy, grids, storage and electricity infrastructure. Without enough finance to turn ambition into action, electrification risks becoming a target on paper rather than real change on the ground.

COP31’s Electrification Legacy

The choice to be made at COP31 is clear. Governments could leave Antalya having committed to implementing a 35 percent global electrification target powered with renewables, backed by credible finance, and recognised as part of an overall package to transition away from fossil fuels. This would meet the crisis moment we find ourselves in, support delivery of the existing COP28 energy goals, and accelerate wider global momentum for the clean energy transition. 

Or, governments could use the 35-by-35 target to steer the global energy transition off course, legitimising the current and future actions of governments and Big Tech to electrify with fossil fuels, and locking in countries’ fossil-fuel dependence. The world is entering the “Age of Electricity”, so governments must seize the opportunity COP31 provides to ensure an electrified world delivers for people, communities and the climate, rather than the fossil fuel industry and Big Tech.
items.title: Electrification at COP31: An Accelerator for Climate Action or Trojan Horse for Fossil Fuel Lock-In? Analysis Türkiye and Australia are asking governments at COP31 to commit to a new global electrification target of 35 percent by 2035. Can this target accelerate the renewable energy transition, or will it only serve to lock-in more fossil fuels? Claire Smith, Duygu Kutluay et al.

items.content_html:
Aden and Abyan in southern Yemen share deep economic, social and infrastructure ties, yet conflict and fragmented governance have weakened cooperation between them. This report examines these interdependencies and identifies practical opportunities to strengthen coordination and mediation. Drawing on local interviews and expert consultations, it explores how shared water resources, infrastructure and existing community mediation networks can help rebuild trust and support cooperation between the two governorates.

Raiman Al-Hamdani

items.content_html:
Compte tenu du rétrécissement de l’espace civique dans la région, il reste essentiel de protéger le travail et le bien-être des acteurs progressistes de la société civile pour garantir la résilience et la cohésion sociales. En 2025, les attaques ont considérablement augmenté, tandis que de sévères coupes budgétaires ont réduit les ressources disponibles pour y faire face. Notre rapport de 2024, qui a recensé les types d’aide d’urgence les plus courants dans les Balkans occidentaux, a servi de base à une analyse et à une action collectives.

En 2025, un petit groupe de bailleurs de fonds s’est associé pour donner suite à l’une des principales recommandations du rapport d’analyse : la création d’un fonds d’urgence. Ces efforts ont abouti à la mise en place du Civic Emergency Fund pour les Balkans occidentaux, lancé de manière informelle à la fin de l’année 2025. Ce fonds commun constitue un mécanisme de financement rapide et flexible, piloté par la Fondation de la société civile du Kosovo (KCSF) et la Fondation Trag.

Le fonds est accessible tant aux initiatives et aux militants enregistrés qu’à ceux qui ne le sont pas, et offre un soutien flexible pour diverses situations d’urgence. Il s’agit d’une ressource collective importante, qui permet de répondre aux atteintes aux libertés civiques dans toute la région.

At the closing plenary of the 30th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30), held in Belém in 2025, COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago announced the development of two Presidency-led roadmaps: one on transitioning away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly, and equitable manner (TAFF) and another on enhancing efforts towards halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation by 2030.

The announcement from do Lago followed the failure of countries to reach consensus on including roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation in the summit’s headline political outcome, the “Global Mutirão”. The Brazilian Presidency nevertheless decided to take both initiatives forward, seeking to mobilise political support and cooperation beyond the formal negotiating process.

Both Roadmaps were launched on 3 November 2026, following an extensive multi-stakeholder consultation process.

Their publication marks an important moment in the international effort to advance existing climate, biodiversity and sustainable development commitments. But it also raises a more fundamental question: what happens now that the Roadmaps have been launched?

While the just energy transition agenda and TAFF Roadmap have gained unprecedented political visibility, notably through the Santa Marta Conference that took place in April 2026, the Forest Roadmap has maintained a comparatively lower political profile.

Yet its publication provides an important opening to reinvigorate international cooperation on forests and bring renewed political momentum to the 2030 forest goals.

Bringing Forests Back Into the Political Spotlight

Protecting and restoring forests’ ecological integrity is critical for climate stability and resilience, and has direct implications for biodiversity, the rights and territories of Indigenous Peoples, local livelihoods, food sovereignty and security, water cycling and many other ecosystem services underpinning human well-being and macroeconomic stability.

Over the past decades, governments and non-state actors have pursued a succession of initiatives and commitments on forests and land use, as well as a range of financial instruments and incentives to incentivise forest protection.

In 2014, nearly 40 governments, over 55 major companies and other actors signed the New York Declaration on Forests, pledging to eliminate deforestation from agricultural supply chains, halve deforestation by 2020 and end global natural forest loss by 2030. Most recently in 2021, the Glasgow Leaders Declaration on Forests and Land Use was launched and later endorsed by over 140 countries committing to “halting and reversing forest loss and land degradation by 2030”.

These 2030 forest goals - to halt and reverse deforestation and forest degradation by 2030 - were later formally cemented in the outcome of the Paris Agreement’s First Global Stocktake (GST 1), a periodic process to assess collective progress towards achieving its long-term goals.

However, many of these pledges and initiatives have fallen short of their intended outcomes.

While deforestation has slowed globally in the last decade, at the current rate of nearly 10.9 million hectares per year - roughly the size of South Korea -, the world remains seriously off track to meet these 2030 ambitions. Even more alarming is forest degradation, a largely “hidden crisis” that has been estimated to occur on a much greater scale than deforestation, yet remains chronically underreported and unmonitored.

These trends highlight the scale of the challenge facing global forest protection, and the persistent gap between political commitments and implementation on the ground.

What Does the COP30 Presidency Forest Roadmap Bring to the Table?

The decision to develop Roadmaps outside the formal negotiating process reflects the Brazilian COP30 Presidency’s broader vision of a “two-tier” approach to climate multilateralism. An approach that seeks to preserve consensus-based negotiations as the foundation of the international climate regime, while complementing them with an implementation-focused track mobilising coalitions of state and non-state actors around the delivery of already agreed upon commitments.

The Forest Roadmap aims to support progress towards the 2030 forest goals agreed under GST 1, by identifying priority pathways for action and providing a more coordinated framework for international cooperation and domestic efforts.

Acknowledging different national contexts, the first part of the Roadmap sets out a menu of recommendations for domestic actions across five areas: deforestation; forest degradation; restoration, reforestation and afforestation; sustainable forest management, bioeconomy and agroforestry; and forest conservation.

The second part addresses the international architecture and “enabling conditions” for domestic implementation, including on technical cooperation and capacity building, forest monitoring and international regulatory frameworks on trade and transnational environmental crime.

The third part examines the forest finance gap, and the range of national and international sources and instruments available to support forest action, including results-based payments, carbon markets, jurisdictional REDD+ and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). It also identifies opportunities to scale up resources and to better align existing instruments with the needs of countries and Indigenous Peoples, and local communities.

However, an important question is how far these proposals address the wider political-economic ‘rules of the game’ and structural drivers that continue to drive forest loss. While the Roadmap recognises issues such as debt and subsidies, it gives greater prominence to mobilising investment and developing forest-related financial instruments than to reforming the rules and incentives that direct capital flows towards activities driving deforestation, and ultimately reinforce countries' dependence on extractive development pathways. 

Ensuring coherence between the TAFF and Forest Roadmaps will also be critical to avoid that efforts to accelerate the energy transition do not undermine forest protection. This is particularly relevant to the promotion of bioenergy and forest-based bioeconomy pathways, whose expansion risks creating competing pressures on land that threaten forest ecosystem integrity and undermine the rights and livelihoods of forest-dependent communities.

While reactions to its recommendations will continue to emerge in the coming weeks, the publication of the Roadmap should not become an endpoint in efforts to accelerate progress towards the 2030 forest goals.

Beyond the Launch: Delivering a Step Change in Implementation Ambition

With only four years remaining until 2030, and the Brazilian COP30 Presidency's mandate coming to an end, the priority now is to sustain political leadership and strengthen cooperation to advance domestic and international action on forests.

COP31 offers an early opportunity to reaffirm the international community’s commitment to the 2030 forest goals, including through a planned high-level event on forests and the second Global Stocktake (GST 2), beginning at COP31 and concluding at COP33 in 2028. The COP30 Presidency has expressed its intention to bring the Forest Roadmap into this process as an input.

But political momentum alone will not deliver the 2030 forest goals. A step change in cooperation is needed to overcome fragmentation and bring collective efforts to the scale and impact required, while building on existing initiatives.

Achieving such a step change in cooperation requires more equitable participation in decision-making by Indigenous Peoples, peasants, Afro-descendant communities, local communities and other rights-holders, who play a critical role in forest stewardship. As highlighted by the Roadmap, one way forward could be to explore the co-design of a multi-stakeholder process: a sustained platform for collaboration bringing together diverse actors and existing initiatives that could focus on addressing critical implementation gaps by facilitating opportunities for learning and collaboration.

The question is whether governments and other actors are prepared to take this forward, and change the way they work together to turn the political opportunity presented by the COP30 Presidency into a break with business as usual in cooperation on forests.
items.title: The COP30 Presidency Forest Roadmap Is Out. So, What Happens Next? Analysis The just-published COP30 Presidency's Forest Roadmap offers a timely opportunity to reinvigorate international cooperation on forests and build momentum towards the 2030 forest goals. The challenge now is to build on this opportunity to better align and connect existing efforts, bring underrepresented voices into decision-making, and tackle the implementation barriers. Catalina Gonda

At the closing plenary of the 30th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30), held in Belém in 2025, COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago announced the development of two Presidency-led roadmaps: one on transitioning away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly, and equitable manner (TAFF) and another on enhancing efforts towards halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation by 2030.

The announcement from do Lago followed the failure of countries to reach consensus on including roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation in the summit’s headline political outcome, the “Global Mutirão”. The Brazilian Presidency nevertheless decided to take both initiatives forward, seeking to mobilise political support and cooperation beyond the formal negotiating process.

Both Roadmaps were launched on 3 November 2026, following an extensive multi-stakeholder consultation process.

Their publication marks an important moment in the international effort to advance existing climate, biodiversity and sustainable development commitments. But it also raises a more fundamental question: what happens now that the Roadmaps have been launched?

While the just energy transition agenda and TAFF Roadmap have gained unprecedented political visibility, notably through the Santa Marta Conference that took place in April 2026, the Forest Roadmap has maintained a comparatively lower political profile.

Yet its publication provides an important opening to reinvigorate international cooperation on forests and bring renewed political momentum to the 2030 forest goals.

Bringing Forests Back Into the Political Spotlight

Protecting and restoring forests’ ecological integrity is critical for climate stability and resilience, and has direct implications for biodiversity, the rights and territories of Indigenous Peoples, local livelihoods, food sovereignty and security, water cycling and many other ecosystem services underpinning human well-being and macroeconomic stability.

Over the past decades, governments and non-state actors have pursued a succession of initiatives and commitments on forests and land use, as well as a range of financial instruments and incentives to incentivise forest protection.

In 2014, nearly 40 governments, over 55 major companies and other actors signed the New York Declaration on Forests, pledging to eliminate deforestation from agricultural supply chains, halve deforestation by 2020 and end global natural forest loss by 2030. Most recently in 2021, the Glasgow Leaders Declaration on Forests and Land Use was launched and later endorsed by over 140 countries committing to “halting and reversing forest loss and land degradation by 2030”.

These 2030 forest goals - to halt and reverse deforestation and forest degradation by 2030 - were later formally cemented in the outcome of the Paris Agreement’s First Global Stocktake (GST 1), a periodic process to assess collective progress towards achieving its long-term goals.

However, many of these pledges and initiatives have fallen short of their intended outcomes.

While deforestation has slowed globally in the last decade, at the current rate of nearly 10.9 million hectares per year - roughly the size of South Korea -, the world remains seriously off track to meet these 2030 ambitions. Even more alarming is forest degradation, a largely “hidden crisis” that has been estimated to occur on a much greater scale than deforestation, yet remains chronically underreported and unmonitored.

The climate crisis is accelerating and its effects are felt around the globe. The decarbonization and electrification of the European Union is long overdue. European industry must shift from fossil fuel consumption to renewable powered-electrification and achieve climate neutrality in Europe - just as the EU intends.

Unfortunately, Europe itself is currently dependent on two super powers in the energy sector:

  1. The USA for fossil energy, predominantly Liquified Natural Gas (LNG), which has replaced the former dependency on Russian Natural Gas for the most part. 
  2. China for Green Technology to produce renewable energy: such as solar panels, lithium-ion batteries, magnets and raw materials. 


It is clear that Europe needs to quickly reduce its dependency on US-LNG and phase it out eventually. At the same time, Europe should avoid becoming fully dependent on China for Green Technologies, as this would introduce economic and eventually geopolitical dependencies, along with cybersecurity threats.

Race to Net-Zero Emissions Development in the Global South - A benefit for Europe

Every ton of CO₂ matters. To avoid the worst of the unfolding climate catastrophe, Europe should not only shift its own industries to carbon neutrality but also use its influence to accelerate decarbonization in the Global South. This would not be charity, but self-interest. Accelerating decarbonization could lead to the Global South leapfrogging the fossil phase altogether and using cheap, efficient renewables as soon as possible. This has already been the case for telecommunication - instead of using landlines, the developing world has gone fully mobile. Apart from the obvious benefits of lowering CO2-emissions and improving air quality, the benefits of switching to renewables are manyfold: Electrification creates stable jobs, sustainable growth in the community, more equality and social mobility. 

The Global South has ideal conditions for large-scale renewable energy infrastructure: abundant access to sun, wind and critical minerals, great potential for economic growth, as well as a growing work force. Still, it has yet to adopt it at scale. The problems with installing large-scale renewable energy facilities differ among countries and are complex, but can be summarized roughly to lacking the capacity for large infrastructure development and overwhelming debt burdens limiting space for investments. Still today, large-scale solar farms in the developing world often are not financially viable because the cost still is too high, despite decreasing massively over the past years. Therefore, the Global South would benefit from support in their Net-Zero Emissions transition.

For the EU, supporting Net-Zero Emissions Development worldwide, would not only be beneficial in terms of its climate policy, but also for maintaining its economic competitiveness and securing its geoeconomic independence. However, the EU by itself lacks the means to do so. This begs the question: Who else has interest in decarbonization? The USA has bid farewell to the fight against the climate crisis, as well as on development cooperation. Even worse, they are pushing aggressive fossil fuel overreach. 

Europe and China Interaction in the Global South

China, while remaining in the German view a systematic rival, a competitor or at the very least a difficult partner, remains a reliable resource in the fight against climate change. It single-handedly drove down the costs of numerous green technologies, making renewable energy affordable for many developing countries. Through its Belt and Road Initiative - which in 2021 shifted to Small but Beautiful - it also actively cooperates with them.

Europe should define its China policy as part of its broader effort to advance electrification across the Global South. In order to keep some of its influence, Europe needs to engage meaningfully in the energy transition in the Developing World.

The EU and China are the major actors in the field of net-zero development. For both EU and China clean tech leadership signifies energy security and an economic advantage, leading to strategic sovereignty and diplomatic influence. This has been amplified by the recent US attack on Iran. Our recent study examined how the EU and China interact in Global South countries in support of net-zero development. 

Three patterns were observed:  

  • Complementarity: Parallel, synergetic involvement by EU and China, without deliberate coordination between the two governments. Complementarity is orchestrated by the host country, which requires a critical amount of institutional capacity and bargaining power on its side. 
     
  • Cooperation: Intentional, coordinated joint efforts by European and Chinese actors in third countries in form of bilateral or trilateral partnership agreements. This has become quite rare, since there is a lack of political will in Brussels and in some EU capitals to sign official agreements with Chinese partners for three-way cooperation at the state level. Cooperation mostly is confined to narrow technical exchanges or multilateral institutions. 
     
  • Competition: This represents the most common mode of EU-China engagement in the global South. It revolves around market share, political influence, and standard-setting. While Chinese firms primarily compete among themselves, European firms focus on defending technological quality in niche markets. Beyond commercial interests, both sides vie for strategic influence. In theory, this rivalry could benefit third countries, but with declining concessional finance, such benefits may not materialize.

EU and China mostly interact in competition or complementarity with each other. Competition proves unavoidable in sectors of strategic dependency and probably will continue to do so in the foreseeable future. Complementarity is possible whenever the host country has got a critical amount of institutional capacity and bargaining power. Yet, the lack of cooperation in these areas signals a major opportunity, particularly in underdeveloped markets.

How should the EU move forward in Global Net-Zero Development? 

So far, the EU is not fully capitalizing on its assets, including development finance expertise, regulatory influence, technical knowledge, and diplomatic capital, thereby putting itself at a disadvantage. Meanwhile, China has a more flexible approach and seizes opportunities where they present themselves and serve China’s strategic interest. 

The EU cannot compete with Chinas enormous industrial capacity. But the study shows that Europe has a role to play if it utilizes its expertise and capital in development finance. Therefore, to foster net-zero development in developing countries, Europe should employ its development finance and enable renewable energy projects by de-risking them with concessional lending. In order to do so, it must stop cutting Official Development Assistance (ODA) and extend it to industrial cooperation. 

Furthermore, while the EU most likely cannot outperform China’s enormous production capacity anymore, it should identify those net-zero technologies it wants to be competitive in and pursue production, involving third countries. For this, it has to keep in mind at what cost it is willing to avoid technological dependence on China. Also, it should focus European industrial policy on defensible niches: for example, offshore wind, complex systems integration, climate adaptation, project development and the combination of adaptation technologies with emerging technologies. These are technologies in which China has not yet established dominance. 

Regarding raw materials, the EU should pursue supply chain security and governance and foster the establishment of a predictable and transparent framework for critical mineral mining, including ecological and social criteria as well as processing and trade. The strategy for raw materials should also include supply diversification, partnering with upcoming clean tech powers.

Lastly, as a major market for net-zero technology from China, Europe can use its leverage and set standards regarding quality, access, sustainability, circularity, workers’ rights and cybersecurity risks. Setting social and environmental standards will amplify the positive effects of green technology even further. 

The global expansion of Chinese Green Technology presents a historic opportunity for humankind to combat climate change. However, if it is not sustained by increasing manufacturing capacity, growth and employment all around the globe, it may come to a halt. Europe, in particular, has a critical role to play in driving global decarbonization. If it continues to reduce Official Development Assistance (ODA) and concessional finance, it risks undermining its own influence and the collective progress toward a sustainable future.
items.title: Decarbonisation for Development: How Europe and China can engage in the Global South Analysis To avert the worst of the climate crisis, renewable energy and electrification around the globe are essential. In order to do so, Europe and China must join efforts and foster the clean technology expansion in developing countries. A more cooperative approach between them is needed. Christina Rode
