items.content_html:
The re-election of Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential race is a huge victory for progressive politics in Latin America, narrowly avoiding descent once more into the chaos of the far-right Bolsonaro dynasty. Lula’s decisive win is also a victory against U.S. interventionism, and the Trump Administration’s efforts to impose its political, neocolonial and military dominance across the region. 

However, one consequence of the result is that a lifeline has been thrown to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new and highly controversial forest finance scheme championed by the Brazilian government. A Bolsonaro victory would undoubtedly have been the final nail in the coffin for TFFF, a silver lining to an otherwise very big, dark cloud. 

The TFFF is still on life support though—it has until the end of the year to secure USD 10 billion in initial funding, which it has so far failed to do, or face key investors such as the Norwegian government pulling out, regardless of whether Lula or Bolsonaro sit in the presidential chair. 
This makes COP31 make or break for TFFF. Although not on the formal agenda of the UN climate negotiations, the scheme's backers will be desperately seeking additional pledges in the corridors of the Antalya conference centre. 

What Went Wrong in Belém?

Alongside the failure of COP30 in Belém, Brazil, to establish a binding roadmap to end deforestation, the TFFF also fell short of its promise to secure the “future of tropical forests”. Brazil’s flagship financing scheme had attracted only USD 6.7 billion in sponsor capital, well below the USD 25 billion initially required to operate at a full scale. 

What it did attract was widespread opposition from civil society and Indigenous Peoples’ organisations. Messaging against TFFF featured prominently in demonstrations in Belém, and a statement rejecting TFFF and defending forest rights was signed by 205 organisations, many of which were participating in counter-mobilisations.1 

The plan had been to use the USD 25 billion in sponsor capital to issue up to USD 100 billion of “senior market debt” (low interest rate, high repayment priority loans and bonds), at a one to four leverage, to build a total investment fund of USD 125 billion. 

This sum would then be invested by the fund at a higher rate of return in order to generate an anticipated revenue of USD four billion per year, which would be paid to tropical forest countries in exchange for conserving one billion hectares of standing tropical forests. 

In Belém, sponsor capital pledges from the Global North included Norway’s USD 3 billion, Germany’s €1 billion (USD 1.15 billion), and France’s €500 million (USD 577 million), totalling USD 4.7 billion, all with specific conditions and strings attached. 

So far, more than a quarter of TFFF funds come from countries that are supposed to be its main beneficiaries

Brazil and Indonesia, which are two of the three largest tropical forest countries, committed USD one billion each in sponsor capital. That means that so far, more than a quarter of TFFF funds come from countries that are supposed to be its main beneficiaries. 

In addition to these five countries, very small pledges from the Netherlands (USD 5 million), Portugal (USD 1 million), and the Minderoo Foundation (USD 10 million) brought the total to USD 6.7 billion, although this sum isn’t available immediately due to several of the conditions imposed.2

Since then, other pledges have trickled in, such as the UK's £400 million (approximately USD 534 million), and another USD 500 million from the Netherlands post-election, taking the total to USD 7.8 billion. At the same time though, Europe's steady march to the right and cooling of climate commitments has put some pledges in doubt. A member of the German Chancellor’s CDU budget committee has argued that Germany’s €1bn investment is hard to justify and should be removed from the 2027 national budget. 

A “once-in-a-generation initiative (…) via an innovative financing mechanism” was promised, but what is the financial logic behind the TFFF and will it tackle the underlying drivers of deforestation? Let’s start at the beginning.

Whose Proposal Is It?

The Brazilian government claims that the TFFF is led by Global South tropical forest countries. In reality, it is a proposal written by bankers for bankers, and was conceived of in the Global North under the leadership of the World Bank.

One of its earliest iterations was a set of four papers published in 2018 by the Center for Global Development (CGD) under the title “Creating a Multilateral Wealth Fund for a Global Public Good: A Proposal for a Tropical Forest Finance Facility”. Among the authors is Kenneth Lay, former vice president and treasurer of the World Bank from 2006 to 2010. Other Global North contributors are cited, as well as officials from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. 

However, there is no mention of Brazil, Indonesia or the Democratic Republic of the Congo in this initial documentation, and the participation of these tropical forest countries and the subsequent leadership of the Brazilian government have come later, giving legitimacy to the scheme.

A Neo-Colonial Economic Model Underlies the TFFF

According to the 2018 version of the scheme, 

“TFFF is a proposal to mobilise significant low-cost resources which can be invested in private markets to generate a financial return for rewarding successful actions that contribute to achieving a global goal, reduced deforestation. (…) Utilising primarily public funds to generate investment profits from the private sector that in turn provide international finance for public goods could serve to move beyond the finite borders of overseas development aid.” 

From its inception, the intention was clear: the TFFF was designed to use limited public funds to leverage much larger private investments in order to generate profit for wealthy investors and claim to contribute to “halting deforestation”. A convenient formula for limiting public contributions and maximising private returns, while claiming deforestation benefits in the Global South.

This original 2018 financial logic has been revived in the three concept notes subsequently presented by the Brazilian government3, which hinge on: 1) converting money borrowed from wealthy investor countries and companies into profit that can be used to “drive change in developing countries”; and 2) distributing these funds using a results-based aid approach once pre-agreed measurable outcomes are achieved. 

In essence, it reproduces a neo-colonial and technocratic dynamic.

In essence, it reproduces a neo-colonial and technocratic dynamic that privileges “measurable outcomes” over lived realities, reducing complex social, cultural, and ecological factors to narrow metrics. What is easy to measure tends to be prioritised over what matters most, sidelining gender justice, Indigenous governance systems, collective rights, structural drivers of inequality and other forms of environmental harm beyond deforestation. 

TFFF is presented as a “country-led” approach, but reinforces a paternalistic mindset in which donors and Global North actors “drive change” in the Global South, rather than addressing historical responsibility for climate breakdown, ecological harm, colonial crimes, and debt injustices. 

The TFFF is seen by its proponents as a unique opportunity to kill two birds with one stone, allowing private investors to make money and secure corporate greenwashing by reporting their alleged “contributions” to ‘Net Zero commitments’ and ‘nature positive finance’, such as the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)4. All of which have been denounced by civil society as controversial schemes to perpetuate corporate abuses, human rights violations and environmental crimes. 

Who is Really Funding the Fund? 

One of the most concerning aspects of the scheme is its heavy reliance on bond markets for Global South debt. In essence, the money used to “protect” tropical forests will be largely paid for by countries in the Global South, through debt servicing and payments to wealthy international investors. As the Third World Network has warned, the real financing will come from “developing countries themselves, disguised by the international capital markets as ‘natural’ return on investments”.

This reflects a perverse money-machine logic: the TFFF will borrow billions of dollars from sponsors and wealthy investors at a lower interest rate, and then invest those resources heavily in emerging market bonds, issued, for example, by highly indebted Global South countries or companies driving deforestation that need immediate liquidity, at a higher rate of return. These emerging market bonds are issued at higher interest rates as they are judged to involve higher risk for the lender (in this case, the TFFF), as it is assumed, for example, that Global South borrowers are more likely to default.

The TFIF will make its money through deepening the debt crisis and insolvency in the Global South.

The profit generated through this difference in interest rates (and often unjust assessment of risk) will then be used primarily to repay lenders, cover World Bank fees, and service interest on sponsor capital. Only if there are profits left over following these transactions would any funds actually be transferred to tropical forest countries. Therefore, the TFIF will make its money through deepening the debt crisis and insolvency in the Global South, at a time when debt levels are already unprecedented. 

Merel van der Mark, Forests and Finance Coalition Coordinator and an expert on financial mechanisms, has made the link between a failure of the Global North to pay what is owed when it comes to climate and biodiversity finance, and the shift towards private finance to make up the shortfall. 

In an interview given for this article, she explains how 

“for years and years, tropical forest countries have asked for support from richer countries, for the protection of their forests. But rich countries have failed to mobilise the amounts that are needed to achieve real forest protection.” 

“So the TFFF seems to me a sad acknowledgement that rich countries are not doing their part, and that the only way to mobilise them to allocate money to forest protection is if they get their money back, with interest. So in that sense, I think that TFFF does not mobilise finance in an equitable way.” 

Deforestation as a Market Failure

The TFFF’s rationale is that by valuing standing tropical forests, the fund will address a “market failure” by assigning a value to, and paying for, the “ecosystem services” provided by tropical forests, thereby incentivising their protection over their destruction or degradation. The financialisation of nature is therefore the proposal’s driving force, where forests are turned into a market value that can generate returns, prioritising capital accumulation above human rights, ecosystem integrity, and all other considerations. 

This poses a profound contradiction: the dominant economic system that turns nature into a financial asset is destroying the cultures, practices, rights and relationships to territories of Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women, and youth—the commodification of nature is therefore not compatible with respecting the interdependent complexities that make up an ecosystem.5 

The structural drivers of deforestation are precisely the same commodity supply chains and industrial processes that fuel the current economic system.

Aligning an economic and financial system designed to extract wealth from nature and forest-dependent peoples with the protection of tropical forests is a paradox in itself. The structural drivers of deforestation are precisely the same commodity supply chains and industrial processes that fuel the current economic system: agribusiness, intensive livestock farming, mining, fossil fuel extraction, infrastructure development, logging for pulp and paper and biomass energy, among other economic sectors. 

The same financial system that will sustain the TFFF generates vast profits from companies driving deforestation. It's like deliberately fighting a losing battle, just to ensure profits for wealthy investors. 

The Propaganda Trap: IPLC “Advice” Is Not the Same as Decision-Making Power

A key pillar of the TFFF is that tropical forest countries will allocate a minimum of 20% of payments they receive to supporting Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs). This means that if a tropical forest country receives USD four per hectare of standing forest, 80 cents would have to be allocated to IPLCs. 

Subsequently, the most recent TFFF proposal (Concept Note 3.1) developed “Guiding Principles for the Allocation to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities”, and established a “Technical and Scientific Advisory Panel” and an “IPLCs Advisory Council”. Primarily composed of 10 IPLC representatives, the IPLCs Advisory Council will only advise the TFFF Board, and will have no access to decision-making over mobilising and managing the fund’s overall resources. Moreover, the members of the IPLCs Advisory Council will need to be approved by the TFFF Board. 

The really important decisions will be taken by the Board of the Tropical Forest Investment Fund (TFIF), which is the “financial heart” of the fund and responsible for managing the capital (discussed in more detail below). As the World Rainforest Movement (WRM) points out in its analysis of the scheme, it is a mechanism steeped in colonial rationale. Giving IPLCs an advisory role and the power to decide how a fraction of the leftover resources are spent is not the same as giving them full access to decision-making and participation in the fund’s governance structure. 

Chief Ninawa Huni Kui, an Indigenous leader from the Brazilian Amazon and president of the Federation of the Huni Kui Indigenous People in Acre, Brazil, is highly skeptical of the scheme. In an interview given for this article, he said:

“I don’t believe we will have positive results with those actions. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility is just another propaganda trap that will generate huge profits [for wealthy investors]. From a critical perspective, it is a form of co-optation: involving Indigenous Peoples without letting them make the decisions. It's another deception. The fund's decisions will not respond to the real desires and needs of all peoples. This ends up weakening the Indigenous movement, rather than strengthening it”.

In addition to concerns about decision-making, the Huni Kui leader also sees the TFFF’s speculative nature as a contradiction to the cosmovision of Indigenous Peoples. “A capitalist fund is very contrary to the spiritual worldviews of Indigenous Peoples, to the relationship between bem viver6 and territories. Financial resources cannot be confused with bem viver. ‘I'll give them some money and they'll have a better relationship with nature.’ It’s not about that. We're talking about a deeper notion; it’s about reverence and recognition of nature,” he said. 

On top of this, the fund’s stated commitment to equity, rights and inclusion—expressed through the introduction of “funding access modalities” for IPLCs and tropical forest countries—is not guaranteed in the event of market stress, liquidity pressure, drawdowns or default. Even if the financial architecture of the fund remains intact, tropical forest countries, and therefore IPLCs, may receive no payments, as priority would be given to repaying investors. 

TFIF: the Real Decision-Making Player 

The governance structure of the TFFF involves two independent entities: the Tropical Forest Investment Fund (TFIF) and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (“the Facility” or TFFF).

The TFIF will be responsible for mobilising and managing financial resources, and will take important decisions through the TFIF Board, a central institution in the scheme. The TFIF will have its own governance structure and the freedom to make “market-driven decisions”, which will inevitably mean prioritising economic interests over rights. The TFFF will be limited to "oversee[ing] the forest cover rewards system, including eligibility criteria, monitoring methodologies, and disbursement rules”.

The TFFF Board will include eighteen member countries: nine sponsor countries and nine non-sponsor tropical forest countries that meet the criteria set out in the Facility Charter, the fund’s institutional governance framework, which will guide implementation arrangements, eligibility criteria, and other foundational considerations. All sponsor countries contributing at least USD one billion to the TFFF will be granted a seat on the TFFF Board, until the total number reaches nine. 

The Technical and Scientific Advisory Panel and the IPLCs Advisory Council will function under the supervision of the TFFF Board, which limits their decision-making power in key areas such as conflict resolution, enforcement action, defining indicators, and setting baselines. This contradicts principles of Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) and weakens democratic control.

On the other hand, the TFIF Board will consist of “professionals” with the required “expertise”, and will be nominated and appointed by the “Sovereign Sponsors” (national governments providing sponsor capital) from an “independent committee’s recommendation”.

The Role of the World Bank 

The World Bank will be the scheme’s trustee and host the TFFF Secretariat, and may also “provide certain Treasury Management services to TFIF”. Its reputation has been discredited in the Global South as it has been widely recognised for sinking countries in debt, imposing unjust conditions on loans, shaping economies to benefit big corporations instead of people, and even backing military dictatorships. 

The TFFF will therefore be hosted by and benefit an organisation responsible for promoting policies that exacerbate inequalities and ecological impacts in the Global South7, which could prove even more problematic in times of global crisis and financial instability. 

The payment hierarchy that the World Bank will oversee will be determined according to the revenues of the TFIF, and will be prioritised in the following way: 

  1. Bond-holders, including “debt service and fees payments” to those who lent their money to the TFFF and World Bank fees;
  2. Other Private investors; 
  3. Sovereign sponsors, which are mainly state loans; 
  4. In last place, eligible tropical forest countries that have a deforestation rate lower than 0,5 percent. 

If revenues decline, payments to tropical forest countries will be the first to be postponed, and if things get even worse, the TFIF will “commence an orderly liquidation”.

This payment hierarchy matters: in years when returns are low, forest-based payments would be reduced before investor returns are affected. In extreme market downturns, forest-related payments might pause altogether. Next in line would be reductions in payments to sovereign sponsors, further protecting the interests of private investors. 

Payments to IPLCs will therefore be the lowest priority, while the interests of sponsors and wealthy private investors will be protected through the fund’s investment strategy. Trying to align profit-making with environmental outcomes in this way could therefore put more pressure on forest-dependent communities, as it is ultimately they that will bear the greatest risk burden from market volatility, potential liquidation, and penalties. 

Will the TFFF Incentivise Investments that Harm Forests?

Although the TFFF’s concept note 3.1 states that investments in deforestation, coal, peat, oil, and gas will be excluded, the fund’s unclear investment exclusion criteria are a serious concern. Questions remain unanswered about whether and how the criteria would effectively prohibit investments in sectors that cause deforestation, and ensure that companies that are linked to harmful biodiversity impacts would not benefit from the scheme. 

Van der Mark points out that there are many more industrial sectors that have “impacts on biodiversity, like the use of agrotoxics and intensive water use, that are for now not excluded. And here lies a tension, because if the exclusion criteria are too strict, they will exclude too many activities and the fund won’t be able to generate the returns it needs to make the payments to forest countries.” 

Generating profits from speculative financial markets while relying on exclusion criteria to avoid investing in biodiversity-destroying activities reveals a fundamental contradiction at the fund’s core. What’s the point in creating a scheme that could lead to social and environmental harms if safeguards are not developed and strictly enforced? 

The TFFF also claims that it will have strict criteria to ensure that payments to tropical forest countries will be reduced significantly if their deforestation rates increase. However, as van der Mark explains, there is a risk of leakage to other biomes if TFFF-related payments mean that commodity production just expands into areas not covered by the scheme. 

Furthermore, “there is also the risk that intensification of production on already converted areas, through the use of more fertilisers and pesticides, will harm nature in other ways than through deforestation.” The TFFF’s criteria are not able to mitigate either of these risks. 

The TFFF may become another tool to instrumentalise finance for destruction

Civil society organisations have long warned about the urgent need to halt destructive finance that is directed towards activities that harm forests and biodiversity. Ironically, by its design, the TFFF may become another tool to instrumentalise finance for destruction, displace forest loss into other biomes within eligible tropical forest countries, and detract from efforts to fundamentally change how international finance flows. 

The current climate and biodiversity finance architecture—designed to support the goals of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)—is subservient to the extractive economic model. The barriers to accessing funding by Global South countries, such as power asymmetries, debt injustices and challenges in resource mobilisation are not going to be overcome with debt-driven conservation schemes like the TFFF. 

“As much as it's important to mobilise finance for nature protection, as TFFF is trying to do, it is even far more important to regulate harmful finance. If destructive finance is not halted, it's like mopping the floor with the tap still open,” 

explains van der Mark. 

“To really halt destructive finance, we must address the core problem: our economic system built on extractivism and a structural dependence on perpetual growth. This growth imperative drives ecological overshoot, social inequity, and financial practices that externalise harm while privatising gains. We need to shift to an economic system that operates within planetary boundaries, that restores ecosystems, and prioritises sufficiency over accumulation.”

Real Solutions: Addressing the Root Causes of Deforestation and Biodiversity Loss

Market-based approaches to climate change and biodiversity loss are constantly embroiled in scandals and facing serious questions over integrity.8 Concerns over human rights violations and poor performance records demand alternative approaches rooted in human rights, traditional knowledge, and gender justice.

An effective funding mechanism must aim to address the root causes of deforestation, climate change and biodiversity loss, as well as transform dominant economic and financial structures to prioritise nature and social equity over private interests. While common but differentiated responsibilities among countries are a crucial foundation to build strong finance architecture around, the TFFF design has major flaws and won’t be able to mobilise resources in a sustained, gender-responsive, equitable and predictable manner for tropical forest countries. Instead, the TFFF is a speculative financial mechanism that will feed off Global South debt and gamble on volatile financial markets amid geopolitical instability. 

The much-lauded 20 percent direct access to funds for IPLCs is a trap designed to buy support from Indigenous groups: having a say over the leftovers is not the same as having full governance power over the fund. Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth must have full access to decision-making in the entire governance structure of any fund that truly wants to be effective. 

An effective fund must ensure continuous capacity-building, legal protection, and strong regulations to protect land rights, alongside a robust grievance mechanism. It must also actively support efforts to dismantle the financial incentives that drive deforestation, while strengthening legal systems to address the high levels of risk faced by environmental defenders when protecting their territories.9 

An effective fund must ensure continuous capacity-building, legal protection, and strong regulations to protect land rights

Moreover, institutional arrangements and policy decisions that genuinely aim to enable transformative change must address underlying structural constraints, including:

Debt restructuring and cancellation10, and tax justice: priority must be given to relieving the fiscal pressures on Global South countries to expand commodity production and dependence on destructive activities. Public sources of funding must be increased to fund social and environmental priorities, rather than perpetuating the debt crisis. In this context, taxing the super-rich and extractive sectors is an urgent conversation to design an efficient fund capable of addressing the root causes of deforestation and biodiversity loss.

Recognition of ecological debt: Global North countries are historically responsible for the majority of biodiversity destruction and ecological degradation, but they continue to evade their responsibilities. Only two countries have contributed their share of USD 20 billion per year agreed under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF)11. An effective fund must ensure not only human rights-based and gender-responsive approaches, but also recognise the colonial legacies of nature depletion and its implications for societies, economies, traditional cultures, and ecosystems. 

Increasing public finance for biodiversity and climate action while lessening the fiscal pressures that push Global South countries toward biodiversity-harming activities is essential to achieving meaningful and lasting outcomes. 

In Conclusion: The Ecological Collapse Caused by Capitalism will not be Solved with More Capitalism

Genuine efforts to curb deforestation demand moving away from market-based approaches that perpetuate wealth accumulation and greenwashing, and instead support inclusive decision-making while confronting the structural drivers of forest loss. The TFFF cannot meaningfully challenge agribusiness, extractive industries, illegal logging, false solutions, and perverse incentives that sustain destructive activities. 

Forest protection requires robust, rights-based public financing mechanisms.

At its core, the TFFF is a leveraged bet on risky emerging market debt12 that embodies contradictory approaches to forest conservation and diverts attention from the urgent need to halt the expansion of extractive sectors. It also obscures the role of state policies—often shaped by pressures from the international financial system—that render extractivism a perceived necessity for maintaining financial stability. 

Forest protection requires robust, rights-based public financing mechanisms that place ecosystem integrity and the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities at the center, rather than market-driven schemes that demand regulation, investment screening, and social and environmental safeguards. 

Real solutions are already being built on the ground, and we must work towards ensuring that the right financial resources, as well as political, social and economic conditions, are in place to allow them to flourish. These alternatives need to be strengthened, policies must be coherent, and key conditions such as land rights must be guaranteed. 

Recognising that forests and biodiversity cannot be treated as commodities or financial assets is essential. Fundamentally, the ecological collapse caused by capitalism will not be solved with more capitalism.

  • 2See “Investment Tracker,” TFFF Watch, https://tfffwatch.org/investment-tracker/Norway.

items.title: The Clock is Ticking for TFFF: Will COP31 Deliver Where COP30 Failed? Analysis Lula’s victory has saved the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) for now, but its reliance on private investment, Global South debt, and dubious governance means that it is still a false solution for forests, regardless of who is in power in Brazil. Valentina Figuera Martínez, Oli Munnion
items.summary:
The re-election of Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential race is a huge victory for progressive politics in Latin America, narrowly avoiding descent once more into the chaos of the far-right Bolsonaro dynasty. Lula’s decisive win is also a victory against U.S. interventionism, and the Trump Administration’s efforts to impose its political, neocolonial and military dominance across the region. 

However, one consequence of the result is that a lifeline has been thrown to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new and highly controversial forest finance scheme championed by the Brazilian government. A Bolsonaro victory would undoubtedly have been the final nail in the coffin for TFFF, a silver lining to an otherwise very big, dark cloud. 

The TFFF is still on life support though—it has until the end of the year to secure USD 10 billion in initial funding, which it has so far failed to do, or face key investors such as the Norwegian government pulling out, regardless of whether Lula or Bolsonaro sit in the presidential chair. 
This makes COP31 make or break for TFFF. Although not on the formal agenda of the UN climate negotiations, the scheme's backers will be desperately seeking additional pledges in the corridors of the Antalya conference centre. 

What Went Wrong in Belém?

Alongside the failure of COP30 in Belém, Brazil, to establish a binding roadmap to end deforestation, the TFFF also fell short of its promise to secure the “future of tropical forests”. Brazil’s flagship financing scheme had attracted only USD 6.7 billion in sponsor capital, well below the USD 25 billion initially required to operate at a full scale. 

What it did attract was widespread opposition from civil society and Indigenous Peoples’ organisations. Messaging against TFFF featured prominently in demonstrations in Belém, and a statement rejecting TFFF and defending forest rights was signed by 205 organisations, many of which were participating in counter-mobilisations.1 

The plan had been to use the USD 25 billion in sponsor capital to issue up to USD 100 billion of “senior market debt” (low interest rate, high repayment priority loans and bonds), at a one to four leverage, to build a total investment fund of USD 125 billion. 

This sum would then be invested by the fund at a higher rate of return in order to generate an anticipated revenue of USD four billion per year, which would be paid to tropical forest countries in exchange for conserving one billion hectares of standing tropical forests. 

In Belém, sponsor capital pledges from the Global North included Norway’s USD 3 billion, Germany’s €1 billion (USD 1.15 billion), and France’s €500 million (USD 577 million), totalling USD 4.7 billion, all with specific conditions and strings attached. 

So far, more than a quarter of TFFF funds come from countries that are supposed to be its main beneficiaries

Brazil and Indonesia, which are two of the three largest tropical forest countries, committed USD one billion each in sponsor capital. That means that so far, more than a quarter of TFFF funds come from countries that are supposed to be its main beneficiaries. 

In addition to these five countries, very small pledges from the Netherlands (USD 5 million), Portugal (USD 1 million), and the Minderoo Foundation (USD 10 million) brought the total to USD 6.7 billion, although this sum isn’t available immediately due to several of the conditions imposed.2

Since then, other pledges have trickled in, such as the UK's £400 million (approximately USD 534 million), and another USD 500 million from the Netherlands post-election, taking the total to USD 7.8 billion. At the same time though, Europe's steady march to the right and cooling of climate commitments has put some pledges in doubt. A member of the German Chancellor’s CDU budget committee has argued that Germany’s €1bn investment is hard to justify and should be removed from the 2027 national budget. 

A “once-in-a-generation initiative (…) via an innovative financing mechanism” was promised, but what is the financial logic behind the TFFF and will it tackle the underlying drivers of deforestation? Let’s start at the beginning.

Whose Proposal Is It?

The Brazilian government claims that the TFFF is led by Global South tropical forest countries. In reality, it is a proposal written by bankers for bankers, and was conceived of in the Global North under the leadership of the World Bank.

One of its earliest iterations was a set of four papers published in 2018 by the Center for Global Development (CGD) under the title “Creating a Multilateral Wealth Fund for a Global Public Good: A Proposal for a Tropical Forest Finance Facility”. Among the authors is Kenneth Lay, former vice president and treasurer of the World Bank from 2006 to 2010. Other Global North contributors are cited, as well as officials from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. 

However, there is no mention of Brazil, Indonesia or the Democratic Republic of the Congo in this initial documentation, and the participation of these tropical forest countries and the subsequent leadership of the Brazilian government have come later, giving legitimacy to the scheme.

A Neo-Colonial Economic Model Underlies the TFFF

According to the 2018 version of the scheme, 

“TFFF is a proposal to mobilise significant low-cost resources which can be invested in private markets to generate a financial return for rewarding successful actions that contribute to achieving a global goal, reduced deforestation. (…) Utilising primarily public funds to generate investment profits from the private sector that in turn provide international finance for public goods could serve to move beyond the finite borders of overseas development aid.” 

From its inception, the intention was clear: the TFFF was designed to use limited public funds to leverage much larger private investments in order to generate profit for wealthy investors and claim to contribute to “halting deforestation”. A convenient formula for limiting public contributions and maximising private returns, while claiming deforestation benefits in the Global South.

This original 2018 financial logic has been revived in the three concept notes subsequently presented by the Brazilian government3, which hinge on: 1) converting money borrowed from wealthy investor countries and companies into profit that can be used to “drive change in developing countries”; and 2) distributing these funds using a results-based aid approach once pre-agreed measurable outcomes are achieved. 

In essence, it reproduces a neo-colonial and technocratic dynamic.

In essence, it reproduces a neo-colonial and technocratic dynamic that privileges “measurable outcomes” over lived realities, reducing complex social, cultural, and ecological factors to narrow metrics. What is easy to measure tends to be prioritised over what matters most, sidelining gender justice, Indigenous governance systems, collective rights, structural drivers of inequality and other forms of environmental harm beyond deforestation. 

TFFF is presented as a “country-led” approach, but reinforces a paternalistic mindset in which donors and Global North actors “drive change” in the Global South, rather than addressing historical responsibility for climate breakdown, ecological harm, colonial crimes, and debt injustices. 

The TFFF is seen by its proponents as a unique opportunity to kill two birds with one stone, allowing private investors to make money and secure corporate greenwashing by reporting their alleged “contributions” to ‘Net Zero commitments’ and ‘nature positive finance’, such as the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)4. All of which have been denounced by civil society as controversial schemes to perpetuate corporate abuses, human rights violations and environmental crimes. 

Who is Really Funding the Fund? 

One of the most concerning aspects of the scheme is its heavy reliance on bond markets for Global South debt. In essence, the money used to “protect” tropical forests will be largely paid for by countries in the Global South, through debt servicing and payments to wealthy international investors. As the Third World Network has warned, the real financing will come from “developing countries themselves, disguised by the international capital markets as ‘natural’ return on investments”.

This reflects a perverse money-machine logic: the TFFF will borrow billions of dollars from sponsors and wealthy investors at a lower interest rate, and then invest those resources heavily in emerging market bonds, issued, for example, by highly indebted Global South countries or companies driving deforestation that need immediate liquidity, at a higher rate of return. These emerging market bonds are issued at higher interest rates as they are judged to involve higher risk for the lender (in this case, the TFFF), as it is assumed, for example, that Global South borrowers are more likely to default.

The TFIF will make its money through deepening the debt crisis and insolvency in the Global South.

The profit generated through this difference in interest rates (and often unjust assessment of risk) will then be used primarily to repay lenders, cover World Bank fees, and service interest on sponsor capital. Only if there are profits left over following these transactions would any funds actually be transferred to tropical forest countries. Therefore, the TFIF will make its money through deepening the debt crisis and insolvency in the Global South, at a time when debt levels are already unprecedented. 

Merel van der Mark, Forests and Finance Coalition Coordinator and an expert on financial mechanisms, has made the link between a failure of the Global North to pay what is owed when it comes to climate and biodiversity finance, and the shift towards private finance to make up the shortfall. 

In an interview given for this article, she explains how 

“for years and years, tropical forest countries have asked for support from richer countries, for the protection of their forests. But rich countries have failed to mobilise the amounts that are needed to achieve real forest protection.” 

“So the TFFF seems to me a sad acknowledgement that rich countries are not doing their part, and that the only way to mobilise them to allocate money to forest protection is if they get their money back, with interest. So in that sense, I think that TFFF does not mobilise finance in an equitable way.”

Aligning an economic and financial system designed to extract wealth from nature and forest-dependent peoples with the protection of tropical forests is a paradox in itself. The structural drivers of deforestation are precisely the same commodity supply chains and industrial processes that fuel the current economic system: agribusiness, intensive livestock farming, mining, fossil fuel extraction, infrastructure development, logging for pulp and paper and biomass energy, among other economic sectors. 

The same financial system that will sustain the TFFF generates vast profits from companies driving deforestation. It's like deliberately fighting a losing battle, just to ensure profits for wealthy investors.

Moreover, the members of the IPLCs Advisory Council will need to be approved by the TFFF Board. 

The really important decisions will be taken by the Board of the Tropical Forest Investment Fund (TFIF), which is the “financial heart” of the fund and responsible for managing the capital (discussed in more detail below). Chief Ninawa Huni Kui, an Indigenous leader from the Brazilian Amazon and president of the Federation of the Huni Kui Indigenous People in Acre, Brazil, is highly skeptical of the scheme. In an interview given for this article, he said:

“I don’t believe we will have positive results with those actions. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility is just another propaganda trap that will generate huge profits [for wealthy investors]. From a critical perspective, it is a form of co-optation: involving Indigenous Peoples without letting them make the decisions. It's another deception. The fund's decisions will not respond to the real desires and needs of all peoples. This ends up weakening the Indigenous movement, rather than strengthening it”.

In addition to concerns about decision-making, the Huni Kui leader also sees the TFFF’s speculative nature as a contradiction to the cosmovision of Indigenous Peoples. “A capitalist fund is very contrary to the spiritual worldviews of Indigenous Peoples, to the relationship between bem viver6 and territories. Financial resources cannot be confused with bem viver. ‘I'll give them some money and they'll have a better relationship with nature.’ It’s not about that. We're talking about a deeper notion; it’s about reverence and recognition of nature,” he said. 

On top of this, the fund’s stated commitment to equity, rights and inclusion—expressed through the introduction of “funding access modalities” for IPLCs and tropical forest countries—is not guaranteed in the event of market stress, liquidity pressure, drawdowns or default. Even if the financial architecture of the fund remains intact, tropical forest countries, and therefore IPLCs, may receive no payments, as priority would be given to repaying investors. 

TFIF: the Real Decision-Making Player 

The governance structure of the TFFF involves two independent entities: the Tropical Forest Investment Fund (TFIF) and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (“the Facility” or TFFF).

The TFIF will be responsible for mobilising and managing financial resources, and will take important decisions through the TFIF Board, a central institution in the scheme. The TFIF will have its own governance structure and the freedom to make “market-driven decisions”, which will inevitably mean prioritising economic interests over rights. The TFFF will be limited to "oversee[ing] the forest cover rewards system, including eligibility criteria, monitoring methodologies, and disbursement rules”.

The TFFF Board will include eighteen member countries: nine sponsor countries and nine non-sponsor tropical forest countries that meet the criteria set out in the Facility Charter, the fund’s institutional governance framework, which will guide implementation arrangements, eligibility criteria, and other foundational considerations. All sponsor countries contributing at least USD one billion to the TFFF will be granted a seat on the TFFF Board, until the total number reaches nine. 

The Technical and Scientific Advisory Panel and the IPLCs Advisory Council will function under the supervision of the TFFF Board, which limits their decision-making power in key areas such as conflict resolution, enforcement action, defining indicators, and setting baselines. This contradicts principles of Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) and weakens democratic control.

On the other hand, the TFIF Board will consist of “professionals” with the required “expertise”, and will be nominated and appointed by the “Sovereign Sponsors” (national governments providing sponsor capital) from an “independent committee’s recommendation”.

The Role of the World Bank 

The World Bank will be the scheme’s trustee and host the TFFF Secretariat, and may also “provide certain Treasury Management services to TFIF”. Its reputation has been discredited in the Global South as it has been widely recognised for sinking countries in debt, imposing unjust conditions on loans, shaping economies to benefit big corporations instead of people, and even backing military dictatorships. 

The TFFF will therefore be hosted by and benefit an organisation responsible for promoting policies that exacerbate inequalities and ecological impacts in the Global South7, which could prove even more problematic in times of global crisis and financial instability. 

The payment hierarchy that the World Bank will oversee will be determined according to the revenues of the TFIF, and will be prioritised in the following way: 

  1. Bond-holders, including “debt service and fees payments” to those who lent their money to the TFFF and World Bank fees;
  2. Other Private investors; 
  3. Sovereign sponsors, which are mainly state loans; 
  4. In last place, eligible tropical forest countries that have a deforestation rate lower than 0,5 percent. 

If revenues decline, payments to tropical forest countries will be the first to be postponed, and if things get even worse, the TFIF will “commence an orderly liquidation”.

This payment hierarchy matters: in years when returns are low, forest-based payments would be reduced before investor returns are affected. In extreme market downturns, forest-related payments might pause altogether. Next in line would be reductions in payments to sovereign sponsors, further protecting the interests of private investors. 

Payments to IPLCs will therefore be the lowest priority, while the interests of sponsors and wealthy private investors will be protected through the fund’s investment strategy. Trying to align profit-making with environmental outcomes in this way could therefore put more pressure on forest-dependent communities, as it is ultimately they that will bear the greatest risk burden from market volatility, potential liquidation, and penalties. 

Will the TFFF Incentivise Investments that Harm Forests?

Although the TFFF’s concept note 3.1 states that investments in deforestation, coal, peat, oil, and gas will be excluded, the fund’s unclear investment exclusion criteria are a serious concern. Questions remain unanswered about whether and how the criteria would effectively prohibit investments in sectors that cause deforestation, and ensure that companies that are linked to harmful biodiversity impacts would not benefit from the scheme. 

Van der Mark points out that there are many more industrial sectors that have “impacts on biodiversity, like the use of agrotoxics and intensive water use, that are for now not excluded. And here lies a tension, because if the exclusion criteria are too strict, they will exclude too many activities and the fund won’t be able to generate the returns it needs to make the payments to forest countries.” 

Generating profits from speculative financial markets while relying on exclusion criteria to avoid investing in biodiversity-destroying activities reveals a fundamental contradiction at the fund’s core. What’s the point in creating a scheme that could lead to social and environmental harms if safeguards are not developed and strictly enforced? 

The TFFF also claims that it will have strict criteria to ensure that payments to tropical forest countries will be reduced significantly if their deforestation rates increase. However, as van der Mark explains, there is a risk of leakage to other biomes if TFFF-related payments mean that commodity production just expands into areas not covered by the scheme. 

Furthermore, “there is also the risk that intensification of production on already converted areas, through the use of more fertilisers and pesticides, will harm nature in other ways than through deforestation.” The TFFF’s criteria are not able to mitigate either of these risks. 

The TFFF may become another tool to instrumentalise finance for destruction

Civil society organisations have long warned about the urgent need to halt destructive finance that is directed towards activities that harm forests and biodiversity. Ironically, by its design, the TFFF may become another tool to instrumentalise finance for destruction, displace forest loss into other biomes within eligible tropical forest countries, and detract from efforts to fundamentally change how international finance flows. 

The current climate and biodiversity finance architecture—designed to support the goals of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)—is subservient to the extractive economic model. The barriers to accessing funding by Global South countries, such as power asymmetries, debt injustices and challenges in resource mobilisation are not going to be overcome with debt-driven conservation schemes like the TFFF. 

“As much as it's important to mobilise finance for nature protection, as TFFF is trying to do, it is even far more important to regulate harmful finance. If destructive finance is not halted, it's like mopping the floor with the tap still open,” 

explains van der Mark. 

“To really halt destructive finance, we must address the core problem: our economic system built on extractivism and a structural dependence on perpetual growth. This growth imperative drives ecological overshoot, social inequity, and financial practices that externalise harm while privatising gains. We need to shift to an economic system that operates within planetary boundaries, that restores ecosystems, and prioritises sufficiency over accumulation.”

Real Solutions: Addressing the Root Causes of Deforestation and Biodiversity Loss

Market-based approaches to climate change and biodiversity loss are constantly embroiled in scandals and facing serious questions over integrity.8 Concerns over human rights violations and poor performance records demand alternative approaches rooted in human rights, traditional knowledge, and gender justice.

An effective funding mechanism must aim to address the root causes of deforestation, climate change and biodiversity loss, as well as transform dominant economic and financial structures to prioritise nature and social equity over private interests. While common but differentiated responsibilities among countries are a crucial foundation to build strong finance architecture around, the TFFF design has major flaws and won’t be able to mobilise resources in a sustained, gender-responsive, equitable and predictable manner for tropical forest countries. Instead, the TFFF is a speculative financial mechanism that will feed off Global South debt and gamble on volatile financial markets amid geopolitical instability. 

The much-lauded 20 percent direct access to funds for IPLCs is a trap designed to buy support from Indigenous groups: having a say over the leftovers is not the same as having full governance power over the fund. Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth must have full access to decision-making in the entire governance structure of any fund that truly wants to be effective. 

An effective fund must ensure continuous capacity-building, legal protection, and strong regulations to protect land rights, alongside a robust grievance mechanism. It must also actively support efforts to dismantle the financial incentives that drive deforestation, while strengthening legal systems to address the high levels of risk faced by environmental defenders when protecting their territories.9 

An effective fund must ensure continuous capacity-building, legal protection, and strong regulations to protect land rights

Moreover, institutional arrangements and policy decisions that genuinely aim to enable transformative change must address underlying structural constraints, including:

Debt restructuring and cancellation10, and tax justice: priority must be given to relieving the fiscal pressures on Global South countries to expand commodity production and dependence on destructive activities. Public sources of funding must be increased to fund social and environmental priorities, rather than perpetuating the debt crisis. In this context, taxing the super-rich and extractive sectors is an urgent conversation to design an efficient fund capable of addressing the root causes of deforestation and biodiversity loss.

Recognition of ecological debt: Global North countries are historically responsible for the majority of biodiversity destruction and ecological degradation, but they continue to evade their responsibilities. Only two countries have contributed their share of USD 20 billion per year agreed under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF)11. An effective fund must ensure not only human rights-based and gender-responsive approaches, but also recognise the colonial legacies of nature depletion and its implications for societies, economies, traditional cultures, and ecosystems. 

Increasing public finance for biodiversity and climate action while lessening the fiscal pressures that push Global South countries toward biodiversity-harming activities is essential to achieving meaningful and lasting outcomes. 

In Conclusion: The Ecological Collapse Caused by Capitalism will not be Solved with More Capitalism

Genuine efforts to curb deforestation demand moving away from market-based approaches that perpetuate wealth accumulation and greenwashing, and instead support inclusive decision-making while confronting the structural drivers of forest loss. The TFFF cannot meaningfully challenge agribusiness, extractive industries, illegal logging, false solutions, and perverse incentives that sustain destructive activities. 

Forest protection requires robust, rights-based public financing mechanisms.

At its core, the TFFF is a leveraged bet on risky emerging market debt12 that embodies contradictory approaches to forest conservation and diverts attention from the urgent need to halt the expansion of extractive sectors. It also obscures the role of state policies—often shaped by pressures from the international financial system—that render extractivism a perceived necessity for maintaining financial stability. 

Forest protection requires robust, rights-based public financing mechanisms that place ecosystem integrity and the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities at the center, rather than market-driven schemes that demand regulation, investment screening, and social and environmental safeguards. 

Real solutions are already being built on the ground, and we must work towards ensuring that the right financial resources, as well as political, social and economic conditions, are in place to allow them to flourish. These alternatives need to be strengthened, policies must be coherent, and key conditions such as land rights must be guaranteed. 

Recognising that forests and biodiversity cannot be treated as commodities or financial assets is essential. Fundamentally, the ecological collapse caused by capitalism will not be solved with more capitalism.

  • 1“NO to TFFF, YES to Forest Rights. Statement from Civil Society Organisations on the Launch of the Tropical Forests Forever Fund (TFFF)”, Global Forest Coalition (GFC), November 2025, https://globalforestcoalition.org/no-to-tfff-yes-to-forest-rights/. 
  • 2See “Investment Tracker,” TFFF Watch, https://tfffwatch.org/investment-tracker/Norway.
  • 3The first Concept Note was published by the Brazilian government in July 2024, the second one in February 2025, the third one in August 2025, and the fourth one (Version 3.1) was released in October 2025. 
  • 4The TNFD is a voluntary initiative for corporate greenwashing made up of a group of large corporations–including many with a terrible track record in environmental issues. It is based on the core claim that more self-reporting by corporations on their nature-related impacts is key to solving the biodiversity crisis. This taskforce has been developing a framework on what a business should report on. To learn more see “The TNFD: What it is, who’s behind it and why it’s a major greenwashing risk,” Global Forest Coalition (GFC), December 2022. The TFFF will allow corporations profiting off environmental abuse to report “compliance”with the TNFD, and apply “financial products” that supposedly “support nature” to greenwash their polluting activities. 
  • 5For an analysis on commodifying nature and avoiding a real change see “Marketing the planet: The financialization of nature”, by Helena Paul, Radical Ecological Democracy, January 2022, https://www.cbd.int/cms/ui/forums/attachment.aspx?id=417&exp=639052793791354386&uid=1&key=07baea2208edfad639fb5530f97da407.
  • 6South American Indigenous philosophy that favors deep relationships between humans and nature over individualistic material and consumerist development.   • 7See also The World Bank: A Critical History (2023), by Éric Toussaint, https://www.plutobooks.com/product/the-world-bank-a-critical-history/.
  • 8“Rise in legal challenges over carbon credit schemes”, The Guardian, June 25, 2025, https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/jun/25/courts-corporate-carbon-offsetting-claims-lse-report; Souparna Lahiri and Valentina Figuera Martínez, Biodiversity Offsetting: A corporate social license to perpetuate biodiversity destruction and gender inequality, Global Forest Coalition (GFC), October 2024, https://globalforestcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/EN_Biodiversity-Offsetting-Briefer.pdf.

U.S. voters are sharply focused on technology this year. Trust in Silicon Valley companies is low and communities have reacted viscerally to the physical realities-especially data centers-of the AI era. Candidates from both parties have run campaigns around limiting data center development and restricting police use of Flock cameras that can use AI to track cars around the U.S. It is not yet clear that the electoral attention will mean a significant shift toward firmer digital governance, though some changes are already underway. The recent settlement between Meta and a bipartisan group of attorneys general from U.S. states was only possible with widespread political support for protecting young people online. But significant new federal U.S. technology rules, driven by policymakers, are still likely a ways away.

The Turn Against Data Centers

AI might be unpopular, but investment into AI is driving U.S. market growth and is a source of U.S. geopolitical leverage. Why, then, are election campaigns shifting against tech, and AI in particular? Not all are optimistic about the way it is shaping the future. The debate over existential AI risks has entered the mainstream. In the short term, there is evidence that AI is starting to impact the job market, especially for young people. The construction and operation of data centers to power AI is a factor in rising energy prices as the surge in demand outpaces supply. The ongoing war with Iran means prices are unlikely to come down anytime soon.

A broad group of communities and interests have sought to slow down the rapid data center buildout. Political observers were caught off-guard at how quickly the data center backlash arose. A bipartisan collection of governors have intervened in their states. New York and Texas are among a group of states that have limited new data centers. President Trump has continued supporting rapid AI development, citing competition with China and a concern that an AI slowdown would mean slow markets. The government is taking steps to keep the construction going. For example, the Environmental Protection Agency is seeking to make data center construction easier while limiting public engagement in the permitting process. 

A broad group of communities have sought to slow down the rapid data center buildout.

Congress may pass legislation aimed at reducing data center pressure on consumer energy rates and the House already passed a bill with broad bipartisan support, but many states are already enacting rules on their own and advocacy organizations are skeptical it will have much impact. For now, there is bipartisan support for some form of rules governing AI or data centers though that may change as party leaders work toward common positions. 

Controlling AI

There is rhetorical agreement among political and corporate leaders that humans should maintain control over AI and the benefits should be shared widely, but they do not agree on the mechanisms. Some of the ideas, like creating a U.S. sovereign wealth fund for AI, could lead to more international tension. Europe is prioritizing digital sovereignty over fears that the U.S. government will continue to cut off access to core digital services. The U.S. government directive to Anthropic earlier this year targeting foreign access to cutting edge models raised alarm bells in Europe. The European Commission quickly raised objections. Anthropic restored access to the models but the U.S. government remains on alert about security risks of frontier AI models and could very well unilaterally cut off access again in the future.

In the U.S., Americans are so far more concerned about the potential for mass unemployment from AI than the security and existential risks. If the Democrats win Congress, they plan to focus on AI, but they will have to decide how to address the range of issues competing for attention under the broad umbrella of AI governance. Some members of Congress are seeking a law that would regulate frontier AI models to ensure developers are managing security risks. California and New York have already passed such laws. As is often the case, there is tension between lawmakers as federal proposals threaten to preempt state rules just as those rules are being implemented. Meanwhile, progressive civil society is focused on issues like labor, climate, and surveillance that voters can feel more directly. Democrats have an opportunity to develop a uniform voice on AI governance that responds to the political energy, but it will not be easy.

Concerns about Cameras

For Americans, one technology company in particular has served as a focus of the resistance to surveillance and authoritarianism. Thousands of police departments in the U.S. have partnered with Flock, which operates a network of cameras called Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) that can track and locate cars across the country. There are worrying reports of abuse of the technology with reports of police officers using it to track their exes and, at least in one case, to track a woman seeking an abortion after they were made illegal in her home state. 

The anger is an extension of the protests in response to ICE raids and mass deportations

The outrage over Flock cameras has gone viral. The anger is an extension of the protests in response to ICE raids and mass deportations in U.S. cities in 2025 and 2026. ICE does not directly have access to Flock data, but police departments can and do share access to Flock data with ICE. A number of state governments, led by both Democrats and Republicans, have reduced the use of ALPR devices. Members of Congress opposed to widespread surveillance have introduced legislation to limit the use of Flock and similar devices, however, President Trump has supported their use. As with AI, any significant change in federal rules to limit surveillance is unlikely during the remainder of his term. 

Rules for Young People

With federal inaction, states have imposed their own rules to govern technology. Meta’s addictive design settlement was possible through collaboration and pressure from a broad coalition of states. Meta agreed to pay a settlement payment and to implement platform changes for young people, such as limiting infinite scroll on social media and the total time that can be spent on their platforms. Meta is hoping the changes become the industry standard. These are significant changes for users, but far from comprehensive. For example, the settlement does not directly address the potential dependency on AI chatbots, which some states are now seeking to address.

There is strong global pressure to protect young people online, and while the efforts are often disconnected, the same dependency anxieties driving EU digital sovereignty efforts are influencing European regulation. The European Commission is also targeting addictive design under the Digital Services Act and has proposed similar limits on social media for children that extends to AI chatbots. Those changes could lead to similar design changes in both the U.S. and EU. However, the unilateral national rules push platforms toward blanket age verification, which can harm the very users the rules are intended to protect. Critics have pointed out that many of the changes are already leading the platforms to block services or collect much more personal data. Despite some common ground, the growing interest in the U.S. for tech accountability stands in contrast with the EU’s desire to deregulate and slow enforcement of some tech rules in an effort to better compete with the U.S. and China.

The election this year already shows the potential for technology policy to become a mainstream political issue.

The opportunities for significant changes in technology policy in the U.S. are limited for now but the possibility is there. President Trump is prioritizing U.S. technology industry dominance over the populist demand for greater democratic control, but the election this year already shows the potential for technology policy to become a mainstream political issue. As AI reshapes our society, and landscapes, voters are likely to keep pushing for political leaders who offer a technology future they want.
items.title: AI, Data Centers, Flock Cameras: How Tech Is Shaping the 2026 Midterms Analysis Technology policy is a key issue for the American public. Questions about disruptive technologies such as AI, data centers, and Flock cameras are hotly debated. But what are the political implications? Drew Mitnick

items.content_html:
Despite the United States’ global standing, foreign policy has been understood to play a minor role in U.S. midterm and presidential elections. A growing body of literature, however, suggests that foreign policy plays a larger role than previously thought, particularly due to the interconnectedness of issues. Global events have local ramifications. Arguably, the ongoing war in Iran has lent further credence to this argument, with the conflict contributing to and exacerbating widespread domestic drivers in the United States–the feeling of a widening and insurmountable economic gap tied to the cost of living crisis, the dislike of entanglement in costly overseas wars, and the ongoing generational shift regarding U.S. policy towards Israel underway since the Israel-Hamas War. More so than in previous midterm elections, foreign policy has become emblematic of issues driving American voters. For some Americans, these foreign policy challenges can no longer be separated from their day-to-day lives, leading to a breaking point for many Americans that will impact how they vote. 

Looking back at the last midterms, held in November 2022, the world was in a very different state and foreign policy held a lesser importance in voters’ minds. The world was coming out of a global pandemic, travel and tourism were slowly resuming, and post-pandemic economic recovery was going well in the United States. Russia’s renewed aggression against Ukraine and February 2022 invasion–although a watershed moment for European security and with profound implications for NATO, the European Union, and Germany–did not factor heavily into the 2022 midterms. In part, this was due to broad bipartisan support for the conflict, with nearly two thirds of Americans supporting military assistance to Ukraine. This high and broadly bipartisan support for Ukraine meant that foreign policy did not serve as a determining factor between candidates in the minds of most American voters. 

That’s changed. Foreign policy is not the deciding factor for voters–instead it’s primarily the economy and the cost of living crisis–but foreign policy is contributing to these factors more than in the past. The war with Iran sent shockwaves across global energy markets, harkening back to similar crises of the 1970s, with a direct impact on U.S. consumers. Record-breaking prices at the gas pump have led to higher transportation costs causing prices to go up across the board. For Democrats and progressive politicians, tapping into the kitchen-table issues concerning most voters has yielded results–with most looking to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s playbook on affordability as one potential avenue. Midterms campaigns are seeing candidates focusing on these issues and possibly linking them to wider foreign policy developments. This has been most apparent with the Trump administration’s war of choice in Iran. 

The War of Choice in Iran: A breaking point for most Americans?

To understand the impact of the Iran conflict in the upcoming U.S. midterms, it is worth looking at the origins of the war and public sentiment surrounding the conflict. Relations between Iran and the United States have been antagonistic since the 1979 Iranian Revolution. The two sides have no formal diplomatic relationship, instead their relationship is defined by punctuated bilateral or multilateral negotiations. The United States leads a robust sanctions regime that has contributed to the isolation of the Iranian economy. Iran has been a recurring foreign policy focus for successive U.S. administrations seeking to respond to Iran’s missile and nuclear weapons program, support for regional terrorism, human rights violations, deepening coordination with Russia and China, and Iran’s frequent attacks on key U.S. allies in the region, particularly Israel. Trump in particular has focused on dealing with Iran as both a foreign policy imperative and a cornerstone of his ongoing legacy-building efforts. 

Iran has been a fixation of MAGA since Trump’s first administration. In his first term, despite being surrounded by pro-war advisors, the U.S. only narrowly avoided going to war with Iran. He has been far more willing to use military force in his second term. The June 2025 strike on Iranian nuclear sites, which ended after 12 days and eroded Iran’s nuclear capabilities, did not end the country’s nuclear ambitions. After the Venezuela operation in January 2026 that led to the capture of Maduro–which saw no U.S. casualties and accomplished its primary goal–Trump felt particularly emboldened to use force against Iran. With a strong push from the Israeli Prime Minister, reflecting the Israel government’s long-held view of Iran as a threat, the United States began a costly military conflict in February 2026. This war–which can be understood as a war of choice due to its questionable urgency–is costly in every sense: in terms of civilian lives, global economic disruptions, erosion of norms of conflict, and the dramatic draining of U.S. military stockpiles. Importantly, this conflict saw Trump break one of his most core ideals of not beginning another overseas “forever” war. 

Public approval for the conflict was low from the start, the lowest in Gallup’s history (since the 1980s) of tracking U.S. engagement overseas. Even the Iraq and Afghanistan wars started at a higher level before plummeting in approval as they went on. In part, the low approval rating for the Iran conflict can be understood as the result of a  lack of communication and imprecision about U.S. goals and long-term plans for the country and region, stories related to the mistreatment of servicemembers on U.S. aircraft carriers in the region over many months, and the loss of American troops’ lives. 

The Trump administration failed to clarify its messaging as the war progressed, leading to questions over whether this operation’s primary purpose is to benefit Iranian protesters, whether Congressional approval was needed, as well as the timeline for engagement. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz–which handles about one-fifth of global oil shipments, fertilizer, and LNG–has sent economic shockwaves across the world. Although the worst impact has been on east Asia, particularly Japan and South Korea which receive 80% of their oil via the Strait of Hormuz, the costs of the war are being felt at home. 

The considerable lack of public support for this war also reflects the economic realities facing most Americans in their day to day lives. This conflict has been immensely costly at a time when Americans are struggling to make ends meet. At the time of writing, the cost of the war for taxpayers is approximately $38 billion. A further $67 billion was requested from Congress by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, in part to cover the cost of restocking munitions. And this translates to American pocketbooks. While the impact has been comparatively muted in the United States given it is the largest oil producer and a net exporter of oil, U.S. consumers have largely borne the brunt of the economic fallout of the war. Gas prices have surged to record highs in the short-term. In the long-term, the economic effects of the conflict have barely begun to impact U.S. consumers. Fertilizer shortages will only be felt in 2027, the war is contributing to the recurring challenge of inflation, and the job market remains uneven.   

For Trump’s supporters, many (but not all) of whom are opposed to foreign conflicts, the decision to launch a war with long-term global and domestic economic consequences has proven costly. His base widely does not support the war, with many of his supporters breaking with the MAGA movement over it. From May to July, MAGA supporters who felt the war was worth the cost fell from half of respondents to a third. Trump’s handling of the economy is similarly facing low support, with only about 30% of adults holding a favorable view, in large part due to the war. As his base splinters over the war, Americans will have an opportunity to express their opinions via the ballot box this November. 

The Generational Shift on Israel

Foreign policy is also contributing to internal divisions within the Democratic Party. The party is split between the more progressive camp–often simplistically, associated with the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)–and the centrist establishment Democratic Party. Although bread and butter issues are top of mind, foreign policy has emerged as an unlikely test for candidates. Their foreign policy views have become a proxy for their willingness to stand up to establishment forces. This has further contributed to the breakdown in the distinction between foreign policy and domestic policy. This is most reflected in the dramatic shift in discourse around US-Israel relations in the last few years. 

Previously considered the third rail of foreign policy, support for the Israeli government has waned considerably. According to a Pew Research poll, more than half of American adults (53%) have an unfavorable view of Israel. Decades of broad bipartisan support for Israel is reaching a nadir. An entire generation of Americans, who have only known Israel as a dominant regional power and through its policies towards the West Bank, the treatment of Palestinians, and involvement in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, are now openly questioning the security guarantees and support by the U.S. government. For many American voters, U.S. military support for Israel has implicated the United States in the destruction and suffering of the Palestinian people. 

Some Republicans who favor an isolationist or more restrained U.S. foreign policy have also struggled with its relationship with Israel, particularly amid reports the Israeli government persuaded the United States to begin its unpopular war against Iran. American conservatives who view China as America’s primary geopolitical adversary in the near- and long-term feel the United States’ unconditional support for Israel has been at the cost of preparedness for a looming conflict with China.   

In part, this shift is also generational. The nationwide protests at U.S. universities in early 2024, especially in April and May, were the most visible signs of popular discontent with the current U.S.-Israel relationship. Surveys show that younger Americans are not only more supportive of the Palestinian people, but were also critical of the U.S. support for Israel and the Biden administration’s handling of unconditioned support. This critical stance also reflects a growing fatigue among younger voters for foreign policy more broadly. In a wide-ranging study of youth perspectives, a few interesting trends emerge that show younger generations are less interested in an active U.S. foreign policy role. They are not seeking a purely isolationist approach–while they are opposed to U.S. conflict intervention, they support U.S. humanitarian aid and international cooperation. As an example, newer generations feel less threatened by China and seek engagement rather than conflict. This trend crosses party lines, with those under 35 placing international issues near the bottom of their priority lists. Europeans need to prepare for a Democratic party that is more inward looking. 

Growing Discontent – How Bad Will it Be?

For the reasons outlined above, foreign policy plays a larger role in this year’s U.S. midterms compared to the previous midterms. The growing connectivity and intertwining of foreign and domestic policy adds a further layer to policymaking. Multiple global conflicts have resulted in knock-on effects, contributing to or exacerbating ongoing domestic crises that are more tangible to voters. This upcoming midterm will likely prove to be a breaking point for many Americans–however what remains to be seen is how this break will manifest and what the wider foreign policy implications will be as a result.
items.title: Breaking Point: U.S. Foreign Policy, the Iran War, and the Midterms Background Foreign policy has emerged as central in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Trump’s war against Iran and the rapidly rising cost of living are already dividing the MAGA base. In November, Americans will have their say at the ballot box. Jason C. Moyer
