Content
Approaching 1.5°C Overshoot: Fossil Fuel Phase-Out, Not Speculative Technology
COP31 Presidency Arrangement: Türkiye & Australia
Electrification Done Right: A Just, Renewable-Powered 35x35 Target 
Climate Finance Remains at the Centre of the Debate
Global Goal on Adaptation (Gga) Must Address Adaptation Finance Shortfall
Just Transition and Emissions Reductions
Loss and Damage: Renewed Focus After Himalaya Glacier Collapse?
Carbon Markets in an Era of Overshoot: The Risks of Article 6
Backlash Against Gender and Human Rights
Domestic Politics in Türkiye Ahead of COP31

At the heart of COP31 lies the growing contradiction between the escalating climate crisis and governments’ continued failure to deliver the decisive action needed to keep the 1.5°C limit within reach, including an immediate and equitable phase-out of fossil fuels rather than reliance on speculative technologies. Deeply unequal access to climate finance, the persistent failure to adequately fund adaptation and address loss and damage, and the continued burdening of the Global South with debt expose the structural injustices undermining global climate action. Meanwhile, the expansion of carbon markets risks entrenching false solutions and prolonging fossil fuel dependence.

Yet COP31 also presents opportunities to make tangible progress: a genuinely just electrification agenda, powered exclusively by renewables and backed by public climate finance, could reduce fossil fuel dependence, expand access to affordable energy and ensure that communities currently left behind benefit from the transition. Fully operationalising the Belém-Antalya Mechanism could likewise strengthen international cooperation and provide developing countries with the technical assistance, knowledge-sharing and support needed to advance inclusive and equitable transitions across their economies and societies. Whether these opportunities translate into meaningful progress will depend on confronting entrenched inequalities and fossil fuel interests, rather than allowing false solutions, inadequate finance and political resistance to undermine an inclusive and just transition.

Approaching 1.5°C Overshoot: Fossil Fuel Phase-Out, Not Speculative Technology

Overshoot of 1.5°C and its wider implications will likely loom large over COP31 – and possibly even find its way into a potential COP31 cover decision. The UNEP Limiting Overshoot Report, published in early September 2026, has shaped and shifted the debate on overshoot of 1.5°C by establishing a trajectory of “overshoot, peak and decline” as the best remaining option to address the climate crisis. The report is unequivocal that this is far from a benign scenario – overshoot of 1.5°C will mean excessive harm for communities, ecosystems and economies, and in part those impacts will be irreversible on human timescales.

However, the ‘decline’ part of the equation implies very large amounts of CO2 being removed from the atmosphere and stored away permanently. Even just reducing temperature by 0.1°C requires around 200 Gigatonnes of CO2 removals from the atmosphere – which is equivalent to 4-5 years of total global annual emissions. The technologies to implement such large-scale Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) do not exist at any meaningful scale; and it is highly uncertain if it will ever be possible to effectively remove CO2 from the atmosphere at the Gigatonne scale.

All of the proposed CDR technologies, if implemented at climate-relevant scales – in addition to doubts about their feasibility and effectiveness – would come with serious detrimental impacts on people and communities, land, ecosystems, water availability and resource extraction. Large-scale CDR would likely exacerbate other global ecological crises, like ecosystem and biodiversity loss. The impacts of such technologies would once more fall on those already hit hardest by the climate crisis, while allowing continued fossil fuel extraction and consumption decades into the future.

For many communities and ecosystems, 1.5°C is an existential limit. So what does approaching 1.5°C really mean? Scaling up support for adaptation actions, as well as paying up for loss and damage and climate reparations. It must also mean moving much faster on the known and tested solutions to the climate crisis – phasing out all fossil fuels (oil, gas, and coal) immediately in the rich producing and consuming countries across all sectors, and globally in an equitable, fair and funded way, shifting to renewables, agroecology and circular economy approaches as well as protecting and restoring our global ecosystems in a rights-based way.

In this context, the Santa Marta Conference on Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels (TAFF), co-convened by Colombia and the Netherlands in April 2026, provides a glimmer of hope. The second International Conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels, hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland, will take place in the Pacific in July 2027 – creating a space to make progress on a just and equitable decline of fossil fuels in line with the international legal obligation to limit warming to 1.5ºC. Importantly, the process also aims to tackle some of the structural barriers and challenges – like excessive debt burdens, high costs of capital, limited fiscal space, technological barriers and investment frameworks – facing the Global South in the transition away from fossil fuels.

COP31 also comes on the heels of another failed attempt to reach agreement on the schedule for the IPCC’s 7th Assessment Report (AR7) – a sustained negotiation deadlock that will likely cast another shadow over COP31, including in the discussions on the preparation of the second GST in 2028. Whichever final publication timeline will eventually be agreed upon by governments in the IPCC (hopefully when the suspended session is resumed in the very near future), it is crucial that IPCC scenarios centre climate justice and equity, show what an accelerated fossil fuel phase-out can contribute to keeping 1.5°C within reach, and stop overrelying on speculative and unproven technology like Carbon Capture (Use) and Storage (CC(U)S) and CDR.

COP31 Presidency Arrangement: Türkiye & Australia

For the first time, COP31 has a shared presidency split between Türkiye as the official and logistical host and Australia as the president of negotiations. This arrangement was agreed after a long and deadlocked standoff between the two countries vying for COP31 presidency.

The Action Agenda of the Turkish-Australian presidency revolves around a number of priorities, including electrification, zero waste, climate-resilient cities and oceans, while trying to sideline debates about fossil fuel phase-out, which risks turning not just the electrification agenda into a trojan horse for continued fossil fuel consumption.

According to the bilateral agreement between Türkiye and Australia, in case of difference, “consultations will take place until the difference is resolved to mutual satisfaction.” To what extent that complicates negotiation dynamics in practice remains to be seen. In order to keep front and centre the profound challenges faced by Pacific Island nations in Australia’s neighbourhood, the Pre-COP was held in Fiji, Tuvalu and Palau.

Whether this year’s split presidency arrangement sets a precedent for future COPs is also open. COP32, however, is scheduled to take place in Addis Ababa, under the solo presidency of Ethiopia.

A legacy from last year’s presidency - COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago – are two Presidency-led Roadmaps that were announced at the closing of COP30 in Belém and will have to report back at COP31 on progress made: one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly, and equitable manner” (TAFF Roadmap) and another on “halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation by 2030” (Deforestation Roadmap). For both Roadmaps, contributions and submissions by governments and non-government stakeholders were invited; the TAFF Roadmap also draws on deliberations and outcomes of the Santa Marta TAFF Conference, and the Deforestation Roadmap is accompanied by the Brazilian-led initiative for a Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF, for a critical assessment see here).

Electrification Done Right: A Just, Renewable-Powered 35x35 Target 

The COP31 Presidencies are proposing as a key element of COP31 – possibly as part of an anticipated cover decision – a global target of 35% electrification of final energy demand by 2035. Political momentum is picking up around electrification through initiatives like the COP31 35 by 35 Global Electrification Pledge and the Electrify Now campaign. Civil society has largely welcomed a focus on electrification as renewables-based electrification can be a powerful tool to address both the climate crisis and the fossil energy crisis that has led to price shocks and shortages around the world. Importantly, civil society has also drawn attention to crucial guardrails to ensure electrification serves the objective of climate justice: Electrification has to be built on renewables, reduce fossil fuel dependence, and deliver for people without energy access, without repeating the harms of extraction.

An open letter, signed by 90+ civil society networks and organisations, argues that electrification targets must be exclusively based on renewable energy, and exclude both fossil and nuclear power, as well as go hand in hand with the commitments of tripling renewable energy and doubling energy efficiency by 2030, and transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, as agreed under the first Global Stocktake (GST). In high-income countries in particular, energy efficiency and sufficiency should be prioritised, for instance by shifting to public transport rather than private electric vehicles. Also: People should come before data centres.

655 million people worldwide have no access to electricity, and many more remain without reliable or affordable supply. Electrification must also serve to close the energy access gap by supporting distributed and community-based renewable energy, including off-grid solar and mini-grids, to reach unserved communities faster and at lower cost than waiting for grid extension, and ensuring affordability. Electrification must be implemented in a just, equitable and rights-based way, and backed by public climate finance and means of implementation.

Finally, critical energy transition minerals must not create new technological dependence or reproduce the harms of fossil fuel extraction and existing mining: The transition must respect rights and due diligence, including the rights of Indigenous Peoples and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) and the rights of affected communities and workers, as well as protect ecosystems, water and biodiversity and exclude deep-sea mining. Primary demand for critical minerals has to be reduced through sufficiency, efficiency, reuse, recycling and circular design. Signatories also call for multilateral implementation of the principles of the UN Secretary-General's Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals.

Climate Finance Remains at the Centre of the Debate

In times of drastically sinking official development assistance and record military expenditure by developed countries, the focus in Antalya will remain on climate finance as a cross-cutting enabler of progress in other negotiation streams, such as for the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA), progress in operationalizing the Belém Antalya Mechanism (BAM) under the Just Transition Work Programme or preparing the second Global Stocktake (please see our detailed technical analysis on climate finance issues at COP31).

While the new collective quantified goal on climate finance (NCQG) agreed at COP29 with promises of delivering US$ 300 billion per year by 2035 to developing countries is now technically under implementation, there is still no clarity on a stepwise action plan to scale up climate finance, nor on how much would be public versus private finance and how the money would be allocated for mitigation, adaptation and to address loss and damage. An even more ambitious, ‘Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3 Trillion’ counting on massive private sector mobilizations and growing carbon revenues, which was presented in Belém, is pushed forward by the outgoing Brazilian COP30 Presidency, which will report back on its implementation progress in Antalya. However, the roadmap’s future is uncertain in times of competition for and increasing costs of capital for climate actions in developing countries.

Most finance controversy in Antalya will be likely around the two-year climate finance work programme (CFWP) approved at COP30. This was the imperfect consolation prize for developing countries unhappy with the NCQG and its fuzziness regarding who will contribute the lion’s share of the goal. While some discussions were already held in Bonn in June, countries in the Global South want to reset it as a separate agenda item to focus the work of the program exclusively on the obligation of developed countries to provide public climate finance to developing countries and opposed by developed countries. This commitment is enshrined in Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement. Placed on the initial agenda for COP31 by the outgoing Brazilian Presidency, in Antalya it could very well come to a repeat of the agenda fight from Belém on this item, which could delay the start of the negotiations.

The focus on the role of public climate finance provision looks beyond quantity also to the quality of climate finance in times of sinking finance delivery – grants instead of loans which would aggravate already unsustainable debt burden in developing countries, easier and more direct access to funds, including for local communities, as well as the integration of human rights and gender equality in climate finance flows. This discussion is even more important in light of the headwinds multilateral climate funds under the UNFCCC are facing in seeking their regular replenishment, including underwhelming outcomes for the Adaptation Fund and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) in 2026, and concerns for the upcoming mobilization efforts of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD).

Antalya will also see discussions under the Veredas Dialogue on making all financial flows consistent with low-emission and climate-resilient development under Article 2.1.c of the Paris Agreement. Developing countries successfully pushed for safeguards to ensure that recommendations such as on green taxonomies or domestic mobilization efforts are non-prescriptive and respect national circumstances. Initial talks have seen a focus on ‘practical solutions’, including at a High Level Roundtable bringing climate negotiators together with finance ministers, central banks and regulators during the recent IMF-World Bank annual meetings, such as debt-for-climate swaps or guarantee instruments to give developing countries a bit of breathing room. Yet to be meaningful, the dialogue must go beyond temporary fixes to address some of the structural inequities and imbalances in the global financial system that makes access to capital for developing countries onerous and costly.

Global Goal on Adaptation (Gga) Must Address Adaptation Finance Shortfall

Climate adaptation, and in particular addressing the adaptation finance shortfall of some US$387 billion annually by some accounts, remains a priority in Antalya and will also likely be at the heart of the African COP32 in Addis Ababa. COP30 advanced the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) by agreeing on a set of 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators (BAI). However, technical negotiations crashed in Bonn following the refusal of developed countries to establish a clear link in the GGA implementation to provision of financing. Countries of the Global South want a clear reference included to the Belém promise to triple adaptation finance by 2035 to roughly US$120 billion from 2025. This builds on the old target from COP26 in Glasgow to double adaptation finance from 2019 levels by 2025 – which is likely to be missed. According to the OECD, in 2024 only US$31.7 billion was provided for adaptation, most of it in the form of loans, many even at market rates. This adds insult to injury as the most climate-vulnerable developing countries are already heavily indebted and spend more on debt service annually than on education or health – and thus missing the fiscal space for investments in climate action, especially for resilience.

Just Transition and Emissions Reductions

An agreement under the Just Transition Work Programme (JTWP) on setting up a new Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) was the success story of COP30, and in Bonn in June further progress was made on drafting the framework and guidance on how the BAM would operate. A decision in Antalya would fully operationalize the BAM, which was deliberately not set up as a separate fund but as a coordination, technical assistance and knowledge sharing body to help developing countries with an inclusive and equitable just transition not just of their energy sector, but their society and economies more broadly. Language on the BAM noted the importance of social dialogue, human rights, and the inclusion of care and informal work in such considerations, and was a bright spot in a process where integration of human rights language in other negotiation strands has faced significant pushback.

On emissions reductions, negotiators in Antalya will have to decide if they are going to extend the Mitigation Work Programme, which technically concludes at COP31. Efforts under this work programme have been contentious and underwhelming, and there might be no appetite to continue with a similar format. This comes as the ambition of bottom-up emissions reduction commitments under nationally determined contributions (NDCs), the cornerstone of the Paris Agreement, remains quite lackluster. So far 150 countries covering 75% of global emissions have submitted their third five-year NDCs, which show a significant ambition gap between intended climate protection efforts and what would be necessary for a 1.5°C pathway. An updated synthesis report by the UNFCCC Secretariat was published just before COP31. The link to (a lack of) climate finance is important, as many countries in the Global South are making the level of ambition of their national efforts dependent on whether financial support is provided by developed countries as historic emitters.

Loss and Damage: Renewed Focus After Himalaya Glacier Collapse?

The horrific flood with thousands of victims following a glacier collapse in the Himalaya in Nepal and Tibet has refocused global attention in the lead-up to COP31 in Antalya on loss and damage, including continued advocacy push by civil society to establish a separate COP agenda item. It has also highlighted both the resource challenges and the implementation delays of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The FRLD is significantly underfunded with its start-up financing phase limited to US$342 million against US$2.8 billion in initial funding requests received, and it has still to figure out its long-term operational policies and priorities, which have to include rapid response finance release after climate disasters. International civil society is increasing the pressure with a #FillTheFund campaign.

In Antalya, there will be also further discussion on the governance of the Warsaw Mechanism on Loss and Damage and its work, including a mandate from Belém to move ahead with preparing a global ‘State of Loss and Damage’ report which would highlight support needs of developing countries, including for capacity building, technical assistance and finance to address increasingly catastrophic losses and damages.

Carbon Markets in an Era of Overshoot: The Risks of Article 6

Article 6 is moving from negotiating the rules of international carbon markets toward implementing the systems that will make those markets operational. Key areas of contention are related to who sets the standards, what kinds of activities can generate credits, how those credits are accounted for, and whether the rules can prevent inflated climate claims and protect affected communities from exploitation and harm.

Interlinked developments at COP31 include: the continuing integrity and transparency problems in Article 6.2; and the operationalization of Article 6.4 with critical discussion on CDR and overshoot, and the Sustainable Development Tool (SDT) safeguards. The tension at the heart of the new emerging carbon markets is between wasting more time and finance on “improving” the machinery for measuring and trading carbon, and how these long and involved processes shift us even farther away from phasing out and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. Using the very limited amount of feasible or potentially feasible CDR – whether through biological or ‘engineered’ approaches – for purposes of carbon offsetting also flies in the face of wanting to remove excess CO2 from the atmosphere after 1.5°C overshoot.

Article 6.2: Reporting, Transparency, and International Accounting

Article 6.2 allows countries to transfer mitigation outcomes toward their climate commitments based on nationally determined contributions (NDC). Its operation depends on countries authorizing transfers, reporting, tracking transactions, and applying corresponding adjustments to avoid double-counting.

Environmental-integrity issues were reported in every Article 6.2 country report examined in a June 2026 analysis of the UN technical reviews. Existing rules leave too much discretion to participating countries and insufficient transparency for independent scrutiny leaving countries to make up their reporting and trading processes as they go along.

Further, blockchain and AI are increasingly used for building and tracking registries. Big technology companies are increasingly claiming space and power in this process raising questions around transparency and power.

The Article 6.2 Ambition Dialogue will begin on Day 1 of COP31. In addition, the Article 6 Technical Expert Review (TER) dialogue will take place. Funding for Article 6.2 will also be discussed.

Article 6.4: Cdr, Lock-in and Safeguards

COP31 will be an important checkpoint. The UNFCCC has published the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body's annual report for consideration at the eighth session of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA8). The Supervisory Body's annual report to CMA8 covers its governance, implementation progress, work programme, and finances. Its recommendations provide a space for countries to give further direction to the mechanism. The SBM will formally report back to the CMA at COP31. Parties at COP31 will review the report's progress updates and address its specific recommendations to issue further structural guidance for the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM).

Meanwhile, the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body's October 2026 meeting approved updated standards and tools addressing issues such as non-permanence, reversals, leakage, additionality, and lock-in risks.

Standards for carbon dioxide removals (CDR) remain shaky. Serious questions remain regarding permanence, reversals, and the expansion of eligible activities. These rules are particularly important for distinguishing between biological (‘nature-based’) CDR and engineered CDR. Forest carbon can be released through wildfire, drought, or land-use change; engineered removals depend on energy, infrastructure, storage, and long-term monitoring. Currently, accounting rules do not adequately address these different risks.

Safeguards continue to be the most contested issue surrounding Article 6. A coalition of civil society organizations, Indigenous Peoples, community advocates, labor unions, and human rights experts called for stronger safeguards in September 2026, arguing that the Sustainable Development Tool does not adequately protect communities affected by carbon projects. From insufficient recognition of customary and informal land tenure, weakening requirements for free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) to inadequate benefit-sharing and grievance mechanisms, the process does not allow transparency or meaningful decision-making for impacted Indigenous Peoples and frontline communities.

Transitioning Legacy Clean Development Mechanism Projects Into Article 6.4

The transition of projects registered under the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) into the new Article 6.4 Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) remains a significant concern. The CDM's history includes longstanding criticism of additionality, inflated crediting, and questionable climate benefits. Ongoing concerns about environmental and human rights shortcomings in early batches of projects seeking to transition to the PACM remain unaddressed.

Backlash Against Gender and Human Rights

COP31 comes at a time of continued significant backlash against human rights and gender equality in the UNFCCC negotiations. While Belém adopted a nine-year gender action plan (GAP), the inclusion of human rights and gender language and references to intersectionality and gender diversity was challenged, and it lacks a clear link to resources for implementation. So far, most countries have largely resisted efforts to bring a more comprehensive recognition of human rights as obligatory considerations for all climate actions as mandated by the ICJ advisory opinion into the various negotiation rooms.

The negotiations in Antalya are also facing possible restrictions for international human- and gender-rights advocates coming to Türkiye as the UNFCCC host country agreement with the Türkiye COP31 Presidency includes an explicit passage that participants must respect local laws and avoid interfering in the host country’s ‘internal affairs’. In light of the recent crackdown of the Turkish government against domestic LGBTI+ groups and gender organizations – with more than 80 people currently in custody –, international human rights groups and climate activists warn that this clause could have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the right to peaceful assembly. This could include the traditional climate protest march outside of the UNFCCC venue, which was a highlight of civil society convening in Belém at COP30 as the previous three COPs were hosted in authoritarian countries, as well as separate civil society convening outside the conference halls in the People’s Summit.

Domestic Politics in Türkiye Ahead of COP31

Since March 2025, the Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, has been in custody. He is accused of corruption and other offences; the prosecution is seeking a prison sentence of up to 2,430 years. İmamoğlu’s detention marked the start of an unprecedented campaign to literally dismantle the largest opposition party, the CHP. Hundreds of elected representatives and party officials have been detained, whilst mayors have been removed from office and replaced by appointed administrators. What had previously only befallen the pro-Kurdish DEM party is now tearing the CHP apart. According to many political analysts, İmamoğlu had simply become too dangerous a rival for the President, as his popularity was soaring. To make matters worse for the government, inflation has fallen but still stands at 30 per cent officially – and is likely to be significantly higher in reality. Above all, for years now, most people’s incomes have been losing purchasing power, as prices are rising faster than wages. items.title: COP31: Overshoot, Financial Injustice and the Fight for a Fossil-Free Future Analysis Intensifying climate impacts—including the deadly glacier collapse that struck Nepal and Tibet in late August—and growing debate over the increasingly imminent prospect of “overshooting” the 1.5°C limit will shape climate negotiations in Antalya. Linda Schneider , Liane Schalatek, Dawid Danilo Bartelt, Tamra Gilbertson
items.summary:
Content
Approaching 1.5°C Overshoot: Fossil Fuel Phase-Out, Not Speculative Technology
COP31 Presidency Arrangement: Türkiye & Australia
Electrification Done Right: A Just, Renewable-Powered 35x35 Target 
Climate Finance Remains at the Centre of the Debate
Global Goal on Adaptation (Gga) Must Address Adaptation Finance Shortfall
Just Transition and Emissions Reductions
Loss and Damage: Renewed Focus After Himalaya Glacier Collapse?
Carbon Markets in an Era of Overshoot: The Risks of Article 6
Backlash Against Gender and Human Rights
Domestic Politics in Türkiye Ahead of COP31

At the heart of COP31 lies the growing contradiction between the escalating climate crisis and governments’ continued failure to deliver the decisive action needed to keep the 1.5°C limit within reach, including an immediate and equitable phase-out of fossil fuels rather than reliance on speculative technologies. Deeply unequal access to climate finance, the persistent failure to adequately fund adaptation and address loss and damage, and the continued burdening of the Global South with debt expose the structural injustices undermining global climate action. Meanwhile, the expansion of carbon markets risks entrenching false solutions and prolonging fossil fuel dependence.

Yet COP31 also presents opportunities to make tangible progress: a genuinely just electrification agenda, powered exclusively by renewables and backed by public climate finance, could reduce fossil fuel dependence, expand access to affordable energy and ensure that communities currently left behind benefit from the transition. Fully operationalising the Belém-Antalya Mechanism could likewise strengthen international cooperation and provide developing countries with the technical assistance, knowledge-sharing and support needed to advance inclusive and equitable transitions across their economies and societies. Whether these opportunities translate into meaningful progress will depend on confronting entrenched inequalities and fossil fuel interests, rather than allowing false solutions, inadequate finance and political resistance to undermine an inclusive and just transition.

Approaching 1.5°C Overshoot: Fossil Fuel Phase-Out, Not Speculative Technology

Overshoot of 1.5°C and its wider implications will likely loom large over COP31 – and possibly even find its way into a potential COP31 cover decision. The UNEP Limiting Overshoot Report, published in early September 2026, has shaped and shifted the debate on overshoot of 1.5°C by establishing a trajectory of “overshoot, peak and decline” as the best remaining option to address the climate crisis. The report is unequivocal that this is far from a benign scenario – overshoot of 1.5°C will mean excessive harm for communities, ecosystems and economies, and in part those impacts will be irreversible on human timescales.

However, the ‘decline’ part of the equation implies very large amounts of CO2 being removed from the atmosphere and stored away permanently. Even just reducing temperature by 0.1°C requires around 200 Gigatonnes of CO2 removals from the atmosphere – which is equivalent to 4-5 years of total global annual emissions. The technologies to implement such large-scale Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) do not exist at any meaningful scale; and it is highly uncertain if it will ever be possible to effectively remove CO2 from the atmosphere at the Gigatonne scale.

All of the proposed CDR technologies, if implemented at climate-relevant scales – in addition to doubts about their feasibility and effectiveness – would come with serious detrimental impacts on people and communities, land, ecosystems, water availability and resource extraction. Large-scale CDR would likely exacerbate other global ecological crises, like ecosystem and biodiversity loss. The impacts of such technologies would once more fall on those already hit hardest by the climate crisis, while allowing continued fossil fuel extraction and consumption decades into the future.

For many communities and ecosystems, 1.5°C is an existential limit. So what does approaching 1.5°C really mean? Scaling up support for adaptation actions, as well as paying up for loss and damage and climate reparations. It must also mean moving much faster on the known and tested solutions to the climate crisis – phasing out all fossil fuels (oil, gas, and coal) immediately in the rich producing and consuming countries across all sectors, and globally in an equitable, fair and funded way, shifting to renewables, agroecology and circular economy approaches as well as protecting and restoring our global ecosystems in a rights-based way.

In this context, the Santa Marta Conference on Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels (TAFF), co-convened by Colombia and the Netherlands in April 2026, provides a glimmer of hope. The second International Conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels, hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland, will take place in the Pacific in July 2027 – creating a space to make progress on a just and equitable decline of fossil fuels in line with the international legal obligation to limit warming to 1.5ºC. Importantly, the process also aims to tackle some of the structural barriers and challenges – like excessive debt burdens, high costs of capital, limited fiscal space, technological barriers and investment frameworks – facing the Global South in the transition away from fossil fuels.

COP31 also comes on the heels of another failed attempt to reach agreement on the schedule for the IPCC’s 7th Assessment Report (AR7) – a sustained negotiation deadlock that will likely cast another shadow over COP31, including in the discussions on the preparation of the second GST in 2028. Whichever final publication timeline will eventually be agreed upon by governments in the IPCC (hopefully when the suspended session is resumed in the very near future), it is crucial that IPCC scenarios centre climate justice and equity, show what an accelerated fossil fuel phase-out can contribute to keeping 1.5°C within reach, and stop overrelying on speculative and unproven technology like Carbon Capture (Use) and Storage (CC(U)S) and CDR.

COP31 Presidency Arrangement: Türkiye & Australia

For the first time, COP31 has a shared presidency split between Türkiye as the official and logistical host and Australia as the president of negotiations. This arrangement was agreed after a long and deadlocked standoff between the two countries vying for COP31 presidency.

The Action Agenda of the Turkish-Australian presidency revolves around a number of priorities, including electrification, zero waste, climate-resilient cities and oceans, while trying to sideline debates about fossil fuel phase-out, which risks turning not just the electrification agenda into a trojan horse for continued fossil fuel consumption.

According to the bilateral agreement between Türkiye and Australia, in case of difference, “consultations will take place until the difference is resolved to mutual satisfaction.” To what extent that complicates negotiation dynamics in practice remains to be seen. In order to keep front and centre the profound challenges faced by Pacific Island nations in Australia’s neighbourhood, the Pre-COP was held in Fiji, Tuvalu and Palau.

Whether this year’s split presidency arrangement sets a precedent for future COPs is also open. COP32, however, is scheduled to take place in Addis Ababa, under the solo presidency of Ethiopia.

A legacy from last year’s presidency - COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago – are two Presidency-led Roadmaps that were announced at the closing of COP30 in Belém and will have to report back at COP31 on progress made: one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly, and equitable manner” (TAFF Roadmap) and another on “halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation by 2030” (Deforestation Roadmap). For both Roadmaps, contributions and submissions by governments and non-government stakeholders were invited; the TAFF Roadmap also draws on deliberations and outcomes of the Santa Marta TAFF Conference, and the Deforestation Roadmap is accompanied by the Brazilian-led initiative for a Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF, for a critical assessment see here).

Electrification Done Right: A Just, Renewable-Powered 35x35 Target 

The COP31 Presidencies are proposing as a key element of COP31 – possibly as part of an anticipated cover decision – a global target of 35% electrification of final energy demand by 2035. Political momentum is picking up around electrification through initiatives like the COP31 35 by 35 Global Electrification Pledge and the Electrify Now campaign. Civil society has largely welcomed a focus on electrification as renewables-based electrification can be a powerful tool to address both the climate crisis and the fossil energy crisis that has led to price shocks and shortages around the world. Importantly, civil society has also drawn attention to crucial guardrails to ensure electrification serves the objective of climate justice: Electrification has to be built on renewables, reduce fossil fuel dependence, and deliver for people without energy access, without repeating the harms of extraction.

An open letter, signed by 90+ civil society networks and organisations, argues that electrification targets must be exclusively based on renewable energy, and exclude both fossil and nuclear power, as well as go hand in hand with the commitments of tripling renewable energy and doubling energy efficiency by 2030, and transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, as agreed under the first Global Stocktake (GST). In high-income countries in particular, energy efficiency and sufficiency should be prioritised, for instance by shifting to public transport rather than private electric vehicles. Also: People should come before data centres.

655 million people worldwide have no access to electricity, and many more remain without reliable or affordable supply. Electrification must also serve to close the energy access gap by supporting distributed and community-based renewable energy, including off-grid solar and mini-grids, to reach unserved communities faster and at lower cost than waiting for grid extension, and ensuring affordability. Electrification must be implemented in a just, equitable and rights-based way, and backed by public climate finance and means of implementation.

Finally, critical energy transition minerals must not create new technological dependence or reproduce the harms of fossil fuel extraction and existing mining: The transition must respect rights and due diligence, including the rights of Indigenous Peoples and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) and the rights of affected communities and workers, as well as protect ecosystems, water and biodiversity and exclude deep-sea mining. Primary demand for critical minerals has to be reduced through sufficiency, efficiency, reuse, recycling and circular design. Signatories also call for multilateral implementation of the principles of the UN Secretary-General's Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals.

In times of drastically sinking official development assistance and record military expenditure by developed countries, the focus in Antalya will remain on climate finance as a cross-cutting enabler of progress in other negotiation streams, such as for the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA), progress in operationalizing the Belém Antalya Mechanism (BAM) under the Just Transition Work Programme or preparing the second Global Stocktake (please see our detailed technical analysis on climate finance issues at COP31).

While the new collective quantified goal on climate finance (NCQG) agreed at COP29 with promises of delivering US$ 300 billion per year by 2035 to developing countries is now technically under implementation, there is still no clarity on a stepwise action plan to scale up climate finance, nor on how much would be public versus private finance and how the money would be allocated for mitigation, adaptation and to address loss and damage. An even more ambitious, ‘Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3 Trillion’ counting on massive private sector mobilizations and growing carbon revenues, which was presented in Belém, is pushed forward by the outgoing Brazilian COP30 Presidency, which will report back on its implementation progress in Antalya. According to the OECD, in 2024 only US$31.7 billion was provided for adaptation, most of it in the form of loans, many even at market rates. “Climate change is becoming more severe with each passing year and will continue to do so. That is why we are taking further measures. We must not forget that this is a struggle. Everyone should know that, in the face of this insidious enemy, we are doing everything necessary and will continue to do so.” 

Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, host of COP31 and President of Turkey, spoke in no uncertain terms in July 2025 when asked about the devastating forest fires in the Aegean region. Murat Kurum, Minister for the Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change and President of COP31, also did not hesitate to link the severe flooding in Istanbul in October 2026 to climate change. In the weeks leading up to COP, Kurum has made increasingly ambitious statements, calling on several occasions for the 1.5°C limit to be upheld and even – unlike his President – speaking of moving away from fossil fuels. He has publicly committed to shaping COP31 into a “strong implementation process”, thereby continuing the process initiated by the Brazilian COP Presidency in 2025.

Turkish Politicians Acknowledge the Challenges Posed by Climate Change

When asked about criticism of the government’s inadequate measures against forest fires and flooding, both reacted in a similar manner: one accused his political opponents in the opposition of spreading misinformation and seeking only to gain political capital from the fires. The other blamed the Istanbul city administration for uncontrolled urban growth, a lack of infrastructure and blocked riverbeds, which he said had cost lives.

The UN Climate Change Conference is coming to a country that has learnt to grasp the gravity of the climate crisis. 

These episodes illustrate well where Turkey stands politically at present. The UN Climate Change Conference is coming to a country that has learnt to grasp the gravity of the climate crisis. According to surveys, more than three-quarters of Turks believe that climate change is real and dangerous. Turkey ratified the Paris Agreement in 2021. Since then, it has revised its NDC twice, passed a climate law in 2025, set a net-zero target for 2053 and launched the pilot phase of its first emissions trading scheme (2026–27).

This is also a response to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which requires EU importers of certain carbon-intensive goods to pay for the greenhouse gas emissions contained therein. If they have already paid carbon prices for these emissions in the country of origin, these costs can be deducted. This would then preserve the competitiveness of their export goods.

Is the Largest Opposition Party Being Crushed?

On the domestic front, however, the battle against the opposition has dominated the political landscape in Turkey, ever since that March morning last year when the head of Istanbul’s city administration, Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, was arrested. He has been in custody ever since. İmamoğlu faces charges of corruption, espionage and much more. Even most AKP supporters have no doubt as to the real reason for his detention: he is – or rather, was – a threat to the President’s political future. His popularity had been soaring for months. In 2024, he won the Istanbul mayoral election again with an even better result than four years earlier; he was the designated candidate for the next presidential elections and was already leading in the polls. 

Turkey’s political system has long been evolving towards ‘competitive authoritarianism’

In the weeks and months that followed, not only were hundreds of officials from the Istanbul administration dismissed, but mayors from İmamoğlu’s party – the main opposition CHP – and senior officials across the country were also removed from office and detained on charges of corruption, embezzlement of public funds and similar offences. Others are being co-opted; several CHP mayors have already switched sides. In the 2024 nationwide local elections, the CHP won all the major cities, including many AKP strongholds, and became the country’s strongest party once again for the first time since Erdoğan came to power. Political observers at home and abroad say that the AKP is now reclaiming the municipalities it lost by means of a subservient judiciary. 

They see this process as taking on a new dimension. Turkey’s political system has long been evolving towards ‘competitive authoritarianism’: the government controls the vast majority of the judiciary. Under the super-presidential system, parliament has largely lost its powers of oversight, and its role is now confined mainly to rubber-stamping bills introduced by the executive with a government majority. The separation of powers continues to exist on paper, but has been effectively suspended in practice. The situation is no better with the ‘fourth estate’: even the largest TV channels and newspapers no longer dare to openly criticise the government on which they depend.

Where Is the Peace Process With the PKK Heading?

The analyses go on to suggest that, as the largest opposition party is being systematically dismantled, the element of competition is being lost. In other words: the government is attempting to ensure that, in the next elections – which must take place by May 2028 at the latest – an opposition candidate stands no chance and the ruling AKP party secures another clear victory.

The negotiations in the peace process between the banned Kurdish Workers’ Party (PKK) and the Turkish state also point in this direction. In parliament, the second-largest opposition party, DEM, is negotiating on the Kurdish side in this process. After 40 years of armed struggle, the significance of this process cannot be overstated.

The government, however, reduces it to the disarmament of the PKK. It holds all the cards and appears to be ignoring the DEM’s demands for greater democracy and more rights for Kurds in Turkey. So far, the government has merely agreed to suspend investigations and criminal proceedings against PKK fighters for five to ten years. Despite everything, the process represents a major opportunity for the DEM. Consequently, its behaviour as an opposition party is rather cautious.

From the Ongoing Economic Crisis to the Biggest Financial Scandal

The government currently appears to be pulling all the strings. Yet it is losing public support. The ongoing economic crisis is the main factor here: for years, high inflation – well into double figures – has been eroding the purchasing power of the wage-earning majority of the population. Although gross domestic product is growing, it is primarily people with investment income and large companies who are benefiting from this. And now even investors are affected: in what is believed to be the biggest financial scandal in recent Turkish history, fraudulently inflated investment funds worth 18 billion USD have collapsed as too many investors sought to withdraw their money. Leading AKP politicians are directly or indirectly involved. The government is promising a full investigation and compensation. Observers do not believe the government can play this down: thousands of small investors fear for their savings. They come mainly from the AKP’s own ranks. The ‘Fon’ scandal is shaking the very foundations of the party’s support base.

Pressure on the government is therefore mounting, and it is attempting to divert it. Unlike many of its northern and eastern neighbours, Turkey has an active and diverse civil society. The pressure on organisations and individuals who oppose the government has never ceased, particularly since the so-called Gezi protests in 2013 and then following the attempted coup in 2016. But it has increased significantly again over the past year and a half. At universities, rectors’ posts – and indeed professorships – are being filled on the basis of political loyalty rather than academic qualifications, whilst critical academics are being removed or driven abroad. Yet climate protection policy, perhaps more than any other policy sector, requires free and critical research.

The Pressure on Critical Civil Society Is Mounting

Critical lawyers, journalists, artists and activists are being detained with increasing frequency. So far, however, it is not only environmental organisations but also human rights, women’s and LGBTI organisations that are operating within the law. The massive raids against LGBTI organisations and members of this community in September 2026 came as no surprise in themselves – the President and the government have long been publicly and vehemently criticising the LGBTIQ community as ‘enemies of the Islamic family’. However, the fact that nearly 80 people have remained in detention ever since, that they face the prospect of imprisonment, and that key LGBTIQ organisations are now set to be banned did come as a surprise. Many in civil society see this as a warning directed at themselves as well. A sense of resignation is spreading throughout these sectors of society.

Critical lawyers, journalists, artists and activists are being detained with increasing frequency. 

The COP is therefore taking place at a time when civil society, the party-political opposition and even the government itself are under immense pressure, whilst the future of Turkey’s political system stands at a crossroads. The Turkish government is now hosting 85 heads of state and government in Turkey. The fact that the Turkish government was so determined to bring the COP to the country stems primarily from the geostrategic significance of this moment.

It may also alleviate domestic political pressure by serving as a catalyst for a positive development: Turkey enjoys good relations with Trump’s USA; it maintains a complex but functioning relationship with Putin’s Russia; it has no major geopolitical overlaps with China; it certainly feels courted by the EU, which regards Turkey as indispensable for its security and refugee policies; it is firmly established within NATO, which held its summit in Ankara a few months ago. The PKK is weakened and ready to disband; in Syria, the Kurdish groups have had to relinquish their sole control of the autonomous region of Rojava and have placed themselves under the authority of the new Syrian central government, with which Turkey, in turn, maintains good relations. Finally, its long-standing rival, Iran, has lost regional influence. Were it not for Israel’s growing ambitions and advances in Syria and the region, Turkey, as a middle power, would stand out as a leading regional power with an unblemished record.

A Commitment to Multilateralism?

The COP comes at just the right time. On the other hand, by hosting the COP, Turkey is also committing itself to UN multilateralism and to serious efforts to combat climate change under this umbrella. And it has set an example itself: it was only in 2021 that the Turkish parliament ratified the 2015 Paris Agreement. As President of COP31, Murat Kurum has embraced the mandate set out at COP30 that implementation must take centre stage. Turkey’s climate policy in practice will be judged against this in 2027 – not only in terms of its stated priority of zero-waste management, but also in terms of replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy. For only in this way does the goal of increasing the electrification of energy generation make sense for climate protection. 

This is not necessarily consistent with Turkey’s continued granting of a large number of licences for mining and other extractive projects, which are causing considerable upheaval and conflict on the ground. Such voices will come together during the COP at a ‘People’s Climate Summit’ in Antalya, organised by three environmental platforms and more than a hundred non-governmental organisations and associations.

For Turkey, therefore, COP31 will be a COP of internal contradictions: it accepts rule-based procedures, yet for the most part acts outside the rule of law when dealing with any opposition. It has recognised the dangers of dependence on oil and gas and is working to become the most important hub for the transport of oil and gas between Russia, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Europe. At the same time, Turkey’s energy demand is rising enormously. Turkey has overtaken Germany as the largest producer of electricity from coal and plans to increase its capacity at coal- and gas-fired power stations by around 30 per cent by 2035. At COP31, too, the word ‘fossil’ will probably not make it into the final declaration.
items.title: Turkey Ahead of Cop 31: Climate Ambitions Overshadowed by Authoritarian Politics Analysis Turkey is facing a COP full of contradictions: its climate ambitions and geopolitical strength are overshadowed by authoritarian politics and economic crisis. Dawid Danilo Bartelt

items.content_html:
CAIRO, EGYPT – 1 NOVEMBER 2026

The Jameel Index, the first index to combine current food trade vulnerability with climate-scenario projections, has unveiled Lens, a new tool linking import vulnerability directly to dietary health.

Using Lens across more than 180 countries, analysis shows that around 557 million people live in countries where the food supply supports a healthier-than-average diet but depends on food imports that conflict, drought, or trade shocks could disrupt. Two-thirds of them live in the Middle East and North Africa.

Lens was launched by Professor Kenneth Strzepek, technical lead of the Jameel Index, at a lecture titled ‘Weighing the shock’, part of Jameel Center Talks, a programme of events organised by Community Jameel at the Jameel Center in Cairo, Egypt.

Two measures, one picture

Lens brings together two distinct measures: The Jameel Index – which assesses a country’s vulnerability to disruptions in food imports – and the Healthy Diet Basket Index (HDBI), which measures whether a country’s national food supply is sufficient to meet the targets of a healthy diet.

Developed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS) with the Food and Climate Systems Transformation (FACT) Alliance, International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Oxford Martin School at the University of Oxford, the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research, and United Arab Emirates University, the Jameel Index draws on data from the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), UN Commodity Trade Statistics Database (Comtrade), the Oxford Programme for Sustainable Infrastructure Systems, and Harvard University’s Atlas of Economic Complexity. 

The HDBI was developed by researchers at Tufts University, the Food Prices for Nutrition project and IFPRI. Using FAO food balance sheets, it compares each country’s national food supply, measured in calories per person per day, with the targets of the Healthy Diet Basket. The FAO and the World Bank have used the basket since 2022 to monitor the cost and affordability of a healthy diet.

The HDBI scores run from 0 to 1, where 1 means no food group falls short of its healthy diet target. The Jameel Index works the other way round: it classifies vulnerability into five bands from Very Low (1) to Extreme (5), so a higher score means greater exposure to food import disruption.

The two measures capture different risks. In 2020, their correlation was approximately −0.04, so how well a country’s food supply meets healthy diet targets reveals almost nothing about how exposed that supply is to trade disruption. A well-supplied country can be highly exposed, while a country with low import vulnerability may still fall short of dietary requirements.

Libya shows the gap clearly. As of 2020, it ranked 10th of 184 countries on the HDBI, yet the Jameel Index placed it in its highest band of exposure to food import disruption.

Four situations, four policy responses

Using the two measures together, the analysis places each country in one of four situations:

  • Well supplied and less vulnerable to import disruption

  • Well supplied but dependent on fragile imports

  • Poorly supplied but less vulnerable to import disruption

  • Poorly supplied and dependent on fragile imports

Lens tracks countries moving between the four quadrants over four decades. Each situation calls for a different response, whether that means diversifying import sources and strengthening supply chains, improving the availability of nutritious foods, or both.

Professor Kenneth Strzepek, technical lead of the Jameel Index, said: “Food security is essential for SDG 2's goal to end hunger by 2030, yet hunger has risen since 2015. In 2024, 8.2 percent of people faced hunger, and 2.3 billion (28 percent) were food insecure. Resilient policy uses self-sufficiency or imports; the Jameel Index assesses exposure to import disruptions.”

Nathaniel Daudrich, Head of Product at Community Jameel, speaking at the event said: “By reading diet quality and import vulnerability together, Lens gives analysts and policymakers a tool to examine the paths nations and regions have taken to improve food security and assess the role of food trade and imports.”

Building on the Jameel Index

Lens’ cross-analysis not only opens the possibility to compare the Jameel Index with other complimentary indices in the food, trade and nutrition, but also builds on the core product update in August 2026 that extended the Jameel Index’s predictive model to 2050, while adding climate change and population growth scenarios. The Jameel Index not only shows how exposed a country's food supply is, but also what that exposure puts at risk.

The Jameel Index was launched in 2025 to help policymakers, investors, and development practitioners better understand exposure to global food trade risks, synthesising previously isolated food trade indicators into a single composite framework assessing countries’ vulnerability to disruptions across the global food trade network.

By translating complex trade and nutrition data into actionable insights, the Jameel Index supports more targeted responses to the challenges facing global food systems, from resilient sourcing strategies to long-term investment planning.

To try out Lens, visit: jameelindex.mit.edu/lens.

A multi-disciplinary platform for global voices

Today's event was the second session of Jameel Center Talks, a programme of events that showcases the work of scientists, technologists, humanitarians, and artists from around the Community Jameel network. 

The programme is anchored at the Jameel Center, the modernist building in Downtown Cairo designed by Palestinian architect Suhayl Bathish and supported by a gift from the Jameel family.

Opened in 1989 to house The American University in Cairo (AUC) department of management studies until the AUC moved to New Cairo, the Jameel Center is today part of the GrEEK Campus, Cairo’s first technology and innovation park established in 2013.

The last climate conference was shaped in large part by a multibillion-dollar fund intended to deliver the breakthrough that global rainforest protection so urgently needs: with USD 25 billion in public money and USD 100 billion in loans from private investors, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) was to speculate on global financial markets on behalf of the rainforest and pay rainforest countries USD 4 a year for every hectare of forest out of the returns. 

Just under a year after its launch in Belém, less than a third of the public money has been pledged. Following public criticism, the financial model, which provides for annual costs in the hundreds of millions for administration and asset managers alone, has been under revision behind closed doors for the better part of a year. In the fund's FAQ, the promised $4 has since become an "indicative payment objective".

The basic idea of the TFFF is compelling. Paying for standing forest and deducting at least $400 for every hectare cleared is a promising approach. Where previous programmes pay for avoided deforestation, the TFFF aims to reward forest countries for their standing forest.

That is precisely why the current financing must be scrutinised. Together with Aidan Hollis, professor of economics at the University of Calgary, I presented the first independent stress test of the financing model ahead of the last climate conference in Belém. Our finding: the returns that are meant to pay for the forest are not a reliable source of income but a premium for the risk that debtor countries will default – and that premium swings with the markets from year to year. In the extreme case, the fund can collapse before any meaningful payments reach the forest countries: public billions for the rainforest then compensate private investors for their losses – and are lost in the process.

How the Fund Is Supposed to Pay for the Forest

The idea is Brazilian: Tasso Azevedo, the founder of MapBiomas, conceived the payment per hectare in 2010. The idea of paying for the forest out of investment returns, by contrast, goes back to the former World Bank treasurer Kenneth Lay. At first, Brazil called the fund an endowment, "because we expected there to be grants and people donating money", as João Paulo de Resende, then state secretary at the finance ministry, said in Davos. The donations never came. As late as 2023, in Dubai, Brazil was soliciting $250 billion, mainly from sovereign wealth funds. Only in 2024 did this become today's model, in which every public billion is leveraged with four further billion in private loans, which it insures against losses.

The principle is easily explained. The TFFF invests its money mainly in emerging-market government bonds, which promise higher interest than the fund pays the donor countries for the money it has borrowed. From this difference, the TFFF first pays the interest to its lenders and its administrative costs. Only what is left goes to the forest countries. According to TFFF Watch, the full $4 per hectare would currently require around $2.7 billion a year. At least 20% of every payment goes directly to Indigenous peoples and local communities; the share was designed with their representatives and is enforceable. The German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) describes in detail how it works.

Why the Payment Is Not Reliable

1. The spread the forest is supposed to live on is the price of a real risk. Emerging markets pay higher interest because they cannot always service their debts. In the crisis years 2020 and 2022 alone, Argentina, Ecuador, Zambia, Sri Lanka and Ghana defaulted. Since the summer of 2025 we have therefore been asking the same core question: if it were reliably possible to borrow cheaply and invest at a substantial excess return – why confine the approach to a few billion for rainforest protection? If it were that easy to generate billions in returns with borrowed money, the same model could be set up for every global public good, from the oceans to pandemic preparedness. And the governments of the Global North could even have eased the pressure on their national budgets with such a "magic money tree" long ago.

2. Taxpayers' money insures private creditors – with nothing in return. For every dollar from the donor countries, the fund borrows four from private investors (p. 41). Losses hit the public money first: if the TFFF loses a fifth of its investments, the public billions are wiped out entirely. By the fund's own calculations for the past twenty years, that would have happened twice, in 2008 and 2020. The donor countries then act as the private investors' insurance, yet despite taking on this massive risk they receive only the low interest rate of safe US Treasuries (p. 35).

3. The forest is paid last and cut first. If the investments lose just around 6% of their value, the forest payments are cut, according to the concept note of October 2025. Those cuts would come precisely when rising interest rates are also straining the forest countries' budgets. Arrears are paid only if the fund's finances later improve (p. 10).

In the end, little arrives. According to the calculations in our book on the rainforest fund (Missing Billions), even the full $125 billion fund, with the returns since 2008, could have paid only about 60 cents per hectare instead of the envisaged $4. Of the fifth for Indigenous peoples and local communities, only a few cents would remain. And that applies to the large fund, financed with $25 billion of public money. What currently seems realistic, however, is a Mini-TFFF of around $10 billion: while the running costs would still be around $100 million a year, the potential rainforest financing shrinks with every missing billion. A large part of those costs would go in fees to the financial industry, which publicly backs the fund but has so far not addressed the open questions about its financial model.

Reliability in Rainforest Policy

The incentive model only works if the $4 flows reliably every year. Forest protection costs money every year: for forest rangers and protected areas, for Indigenous peoples and local communities, and for state enforcement against illegal clearing. Brazil, for instance, cut deforestation in the Amazon by more than four fifths between 2004 and 2012. Forest countries, however, can only budget for the promised payment if they can influence its amount themselves by clearing less. 

If the payment fails to materialise despite all their efforts because financial markets turn, recipient countries cannot budget for the promised payments, and the incentive the TFFF is designed to create is largely lost. The governments of the forest countries then bear not only the political risks of forest protection but ultimately its costs as well. The concept note knows this: long-term forest policy, it says, is only possible if "long-term, predictable financing" is in sight (p. 69). Four pages later, it announces that the payments will be cut in times of crisis.

The fund was nonetheless sold as safe. At the launch in Belém, Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, declared that the fund could give forest countries "secure financing that lasts". In the same statement, Norway tied its money to "a sustainable financing model with acceptable risk". Therein lies the current danger: a fund that invests more safely also earns less. The result would be a zombie fund: a Mini-TFFF that starts with significantly less capital, takes on less risk and, on top of that, retains part of its profits each year as a cushion instead of paying them out to the forest countries. It could reach the political minimum target of $10 billion and would hardly ever go bankrupt, but it would fob the forest off with cents. That would save face for all those who committed to the model too early – but possibly not a single hectare of rainforest.

The Charge of Exploitation

Some accuse the TFFF of profiting from the high interest rates of poorer countries. After decades of debt crises, the suspicion is understandable. The interest on a government bond, though, is owed regardless of who holds it. If the TFFF buys additional bonds from emerging and developing countries, that should, if anything, marginally lower those countries' interest burden and so relieve their public budgets. 

The fund's problem lies elsewhere: in the risk, which forest countries and donor countries bear first. The TFFF also does not bring about the often-feared "financialisation" of the rainforest: rather, the model provides forest countries with the means to fund measures against commercial clearing.

Doubts Are Growing

Experts now share our concerns, each by their own route. Bård Harstad, professor of economics at Stanford, reminds us, with reference to the TFFF, that there is no "free lunch" in international capital markets. Robert Nasi, director general of the Center for International Forestry Research (CIFOR), writes that the yield the design depends on is "not free money". Azevedo, the inventor of the payment per hectare, also asks publicly why anyone should put money into the TFFF rather than into US Treasuries, which are "safer and guaranteed".

Even donor countries are demanding a sustainable financial model. And this despite having largely co-developed the current design themselves before it was publicly questioned: Germany, Norway and the United Kingdom sat on the working groups that drafted it. Norway has nonetheless not earmarked a single krone for the fund in its 2027 budget and is having the model reviewed by two pioneers of its oil fund, including its founding chief executive Knut N. Kjær. The oil fund itself caps emerging-market bonds at no more than 5% of its bond holdings. In contrast, the TFFF plans to invest predominantly in such bonds – and with borrowed money at that. Further, the Netherlands has tied its latest contribution to a review and does not intend to decide until mid-2027. Germany's billion-euro pledge is also conditional: the Bundestag will decide at the end of November. Andreas Mattfeldt, the CDU budget committee member responsible for the file, wants to block the first instalment because, he says, the government has issued a "blank cheque".

What Is at Stake

A failure of the fund would be a political catastrophe. In our simulations, in which we ran the fund on actual market data for every start year from 2000 to 2018, sixteen out of nineteen funds would have lost more than half of the donor countries' money by today, and one would have lost everything. The TFFF is currently regarded as the flagship project of forest protection, was presented in Belém as a central initiative of the climate conference, and is to be counted, at least in part, as climate finance. 

Herein lies an enormous risk: the failure of such a massive financial-market speculation with billions in public money would hand the opponents of international cooperation a ready-made narrative that could, in the short and medium term, pose a real political danger to future rainforest protection, but also to climate finance and global cooperation as a whole. Especially at a time when climate finance and development cooperation are already under enormous political pressure, that is a potentially fatal scenario.

The Change Needed

The promising core of the TFFF must be preserved: the payment of $4 per hectare, the deduction of at least $400 for every hectare cleared, and the fixed share for Indigenous peoples and local communities. Two things are missing. 

First, transparency: before further public money flows, the revised financial model must be published; the vote in the Bundestag and COP31 are the right moment for that. 

Second, stable financing that does not depend on the risk premium of emerging markets. Aidan Hollis and I proposed TFFF 2.0 for this ahead of Belém: the donor countries lend the fund money interest-free. The fund uses this money to buy safe government bonds of the donor countries, and the interest on those bonds finances the payments for standing forest. In essence, the donor countries only pay the interest and get their money back in full. The key difference: this time without default risks and without risky leverage through private loans. At a 5% yield, $50 billion of such loans would generate $2.5 billion a year for the forest.

Several such proposals are currently under discussion, and none of them rests on financial-market speculation with rainforest money.

Brazil has delivered the right idea. It would be up to the donor countries to provide the necessary financing.
items.title: Tropical Forests Forever? An Important Idea With Questionable Financing Analysis The basic concept behind the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) is compelling: paying for existing forest cover and deducting penalties for every hectare cleared is a promising idea. This is precisely why the current financial model needs scrutiny. Max Alexander Matthey
