COP17 will mark the first global review of collective progress toward implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), adopted in 2022 as the strategic plan for implementing the CBD through 2030.

The global review’s final outcome will be negotiated at COP17. It is based largely on CBD Parties’ national reports and the global report on collective progress in implementing the goals and targets of the GBF. The latter, entitled State of Biodiversity Action, will be released before COP17, but the draft already highlights the slow pace of progress.

Implementation not on track

The focus of the global review is therefore mainly on the inadequate implementation of the GBF – the “implementation gap”. This includes developed countries’ fulfillment of their obligations to provide the means of implementation – finance, technology transfer, and capacity building – to developing countries. Most of the world’s biodiversity lies in developing countries, so they bear the greater burden of implementation. They are reluctant to increase these burdens and introduce new ones related to planning, monitoring, reporting and review when developed countries are not meeting their obligations to provide the means of implementation. 

These are important issues; however, without addressing the underlying causes driving biodiversity destruction, it will not be possible to meet the GBF’s goals and targets. The root causes include the rules of the economic and financial system that drive extractivism at the expense of social and environmental well-being, financial flows that fund sectors driving biodiversity loss, regulatory capture by corporations, and the flaws of market logic applied to biodiversity. These causes are rooted in inequitable systems of exploitation and control and create a “justice gap”, which must be seriously confronted.

Biodiversity finance debates

The discussions at COP17 will also center on the “finance gap”, which is usually understood as a shortfall in the financing needed to tackle the biodiversity crisis. Addressing this gap is framed as mobilizing resources from “all sources”.

In fact, the CBD places equity at the center of biodiversity finance. While all Parties have obligations to implement the Convention, there are differentiated obligations for the provision of financial resources. The extent to which developing countries effectively implement their obligations will depend on how well developed countries fulfill their legally binding obligations to provide new and additional financial resources and transfer technology. Article 20 articulates the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR). 
 
But these financing obligations have yet to be met, with funding amounts falling far short of the GBF’s targets. Instead, at COP17, the political fight will focus on “broadening the contributor base”. Proposals from developed countries for sovereign contributions to be automatically triggered based on income levels can be viewed as an attempt to undermine CBDR and Article 20 and to avoid their obligations to provide financial resources.

The emphasis on mobilizing resources from “all sources” again sidesteps developed countries’ obligations to provide finance and instead looks to the private sector and “innovative schemes”, such as biodiversity offsets and credits, to fill the “finance gap”. In practice, however, these schemes fail to generate the necessary finance and often deepen social and ecological harm.

Another key area of contention is the criteria for the institutional structure that will operate the CBD’s financial mechanism. Developing countries have long called for a global biodiversity fund under the authority of the COP – one that can build momentum and raise ambition for greater financial resources and that has equitable governance arrangements.

Getting the criteria right, including how Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth can obtain direct financing and participate in governance, will be important in ensuring that the institutional structure operates equitably and justly.

Ensuring climate priorities don’t undermine biodiversity and human rights

A key overarching issue at COP17 will be the integration of biodiversity and climate action and how to translate this into coherent national policies and implementation. A related issue is cooperation among the three Rio Conventions: the CBD, UNFCCC and UNCCD. COP17 will consider options for greater policy coherence and a potential long-term roadmap for cooperation. The challenge is ensuring that biodiversity remains the primary concern of the CBD and that synergies respect distinct mandates without subordinating biodiversity action to carbon-related priorities.

COP17 will also consider a supplement to the voluntary guidelines on Ecosystem-based Approaches to Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction. Here, the inclusion of sufficient social and environmental safeguards in climate mitigation-related approaches is pivotal.

Many of the important political implications will concern equity and the relationship between climate and biodiversity finance. COP17 can define steps to ensure that climate-related biodiversity finance is additional, that the same financial flow is not counted toward multiple obligations, and that megadiverse countries as well as communities have access to adequate and predictable finance.

Challenges in implementing Article 8(j) and related provisions

COP16 in Colombia closed with a historic decision: the creation of the Subsidiary Body on Article 8(j) and Other Provisions of the Convention Related to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (SB8J).

Following its first meeting in October 2025, several critical tasks have been referred to COP17, which is expected to adopt the final modus operandi of SB8j, including coordination mechanisms and regional representation. COP17 is also tasked with finalizing the guidelines for operationalizing GBF Targets 2 and 3, ensuring that respect for traditional knowledge and territorial rights is built into their implementation.

COP17 should take steps to ensure that the new Article 8(j) architecture provides more than an enhanced consultation mechanism for Indigenous Peoples and local communities. It should reflect a meaningful shift in the implementation of the Convention toward genuine recognition of their rights, governance, knowledge systems, customary use and collective action.

This work will cut across many of the CBD’s discussions. But many relevant provisions remain bracketed or voluntary, and their effectiveness will depend heavily on finance, national policy and the extent to which Article 8(j) is mainstreamed into implementation.

Unresolved DSI issues

COP16 adopted a multilateral mechanism, including the Cali Fund, which Parties may use as a means of receiving fair and equitable benefits from the use of digital sequence information (DSI) on genetic resources.

However, significant gaps remain. There is no legal certainty that users of DSI will share benefits, nor is there adequate support to ensure that DSI is made available in compliance with applicable national laws. The initial modalities are intended to provide some predictability for monetary benefit-sharing, but early trends are not encouraging. There is also very little information on non-monetary benefits facilitated to date. Meanwhile, critical follow-up work to ensure that DSI is shared with all Parties in a transparent and accountable manner is lagging.

COP17 will face an underlying stalemate: developed countries and industry seek to avoid additional national access and benefit-sharing obligations, while developing countries seek stronger database accountability and transparency to ensure that DSI from their territories is not inequitably extracted through databases in developed countries. Yet COP17 may not address this, as several unresolved issues concerning the operationalization of the Cali Fund remain.

Safeguarding precaution

The precautionary approach is central to the CBD but is being challenged in biosafety discussions. COP17 will consider a Thematic Action Plan to support capacity-building, technology transfer and knowledge sharing in the context of synthetic biology. Parties have a choice: support precaution and focus on capacity-building for assessment and regulatory oversight, or succumb to the push to promote technology transfer and research, despite little evidence of current or potential benefits. The former would help equip developing countries to make sovereign decisions, while not leaving them bearing the burden of any damage or technology failures.

Under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, similar challenges abound. Several topics are proposed for further risk assessment guidance for living modified organisms (LMOs). Any guidance must align with the Protocol’s precautionary approach and must not use industry-aligned methods that weaken and narrow risk assessment. Additionally, the question of whether new genome-edited LMOs fall under the Protocol needs urgent resolution. The continued relevance of the Protocol rests on its ability to maintain precautionary oversight of novel technologies while ensuring that risks don’t fall disproportionately on developing countries or communities.

Success at COP17 rests less on closing the “implementation gap” and more on making progress in addressing the root causes of biodiversity destruction, and placing equity, precaution and protection of the rights of Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth at the center of action, thereby closing the “justice gap”. Only then can biodiversity destruction be effectively halted.  

With input from colleagues at the Third World Network.
items.title: Moving Beyond the Implementation Gap at CBD COP17 Analysis The 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference convenes in Yerevan, Armenia, in mid-October. The key question: will Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), meeting at their Conference of the Parties (COP17), take effective action to stop biodiversity destruction? items.content_html:
Our Vision for the Next Four Years

Last year, more than a million women and girls lost access to critical support as global aid cuts dismantled feminist organizations working in humanitarian crises.

Behind that number are safe shelters that have shut down. Hotlines that have stopped answering the phone. Clinics that ran out of supplies. Mothers who can’t feed their families.

That is one half of the picture. The other half is that the feminist movement does not stop. Local feminist organizations know how to work through periods of setback — they are on the frontlines every day, defending the rights of women, girls, and gender non-conforming people, and building stronger, safe communities for everyone. We stand with them for the long haul, because the people closest to the issues are closest to the solutions.

Which is why we have set a bold and necessary goal:
Raise and award $100 million in grants to grassroots feminist organizations over the next four years — nearly four times the pace of any period in our 40-year history.

HOW WE GOT HERE

We started by listening. We asked our grantee partners what they need most, talked with advisors, peers, and supporters about where the landscape is heading, and reflected honestly across staff and board about what the past few years have taught us.

Our partners are living through more than any one organization should have to hold at once: crisis on top of crisis, arriving faster than anyone can absorb. As authoritarianism rises, speaking out has become more dangerous — in some places it can cost an activist their life. Humanitarian funding has been slashed and many traditional funders are pulling back under pressure. Meanwhile, the anti-rights movement is well funded and gaining ground. Amidst all of this, climate disasters are increasing, like the recent flooding in Nepal that's taken lives and destroyed homes. Disasters like it amplify everything else.

The grassroots feminist organizations taking on these issues are not big organizations — the median feminist organization worldwide runs on about $22,000 a year. Right now, the basic costs of running an organization, like rent and salaries, are going unfunded, and nearly two in five women-led organizations in crisis-affected countries expect to close within the year.

When the world is this unpredictable, grassroots feminist organizations need the flexibility to pivot and reprioritize. It's the thing partners tell us they value most about our funding: it’s flexible so communities can decide what to prioritize, and long term to provide the stability needed for infrastructure and preparation.

What's scarce is money, not solutions. Decades of research across dozens of countries point in the same direction: when feminist organizations are resourced and working together, laws change, protections hold, and progress lasts.

Where We’re Going

Three pillars of change from our Strategic Compass, our four-year plan, guide our grantmaking: Sustained Resilience, Community-Driven Solutions, and Collective Power. Together, they help transform the cultural, economic, and political systems we need to advance gender justice:

The best solutions to a problem come from the people who are living it. That's why most of our work is funding them, and why grassroots leaders and advisors help decide who gets funded.  

In Nepal, we gave seed money to what became one of the country’s first feminist funds. It now supports grassroots feminist groups in communities across the country, from Kathmandu to rural districts in the mountains. They know which groups are doing the essential work in which place. 

Those groups set their own agendas. They run shelters and support survivors of domestic violence and trafficking. They keep girls in school. They organize for economic justice, for sex workers' rights, and for peace in communities still marked by conflict. 

That work hasn’t stopped, but some of it has shifted. The catastrophic floods in August 2026 destroyed thousands of homes, and thousands of people have died or are still missing. It also destroyed the land and tourist season families live on. UN Women estimates nearly 160,000 women and girls have been affected — many without shelter, clean water, food, or menstrual supplies, with pregnant and nursing mothers among those most at risk right now.  

Flexible funding is what makes that shift possible: our partners can redirect their work when their community's priorities change overnight.   

We're in touch with our grantee partners in Nepal to understand what's needed and mobilize more support. When a crisis hits, the fastest route into a community is an organization already rooted in it. 

Lasting change is rarely linear. It builds slowly, over years and decades, and in between the wins there are periods where keeping the lights on and the doors open is the work.  

As war in Sudan enters its fourth year, more than 4.3 million women and girls are without homes, and nearly half the population, 19 million people, faces acute hunger.   

"Drone attacks have made nowhere in Sudan truly safe for women." — A Global Fund for Women grantee partner in Sudan, whose name we're withholding for her safety

Our partners there are running community kitchens that have fed more than 80,000 families since the war began, most of them women-led households. They also help women and girls get out of active conflict zones and find shelter, and they’ve rehabilitated damaged schools and provide school meals so girls can go back. 

None of that is possible without an organization steady enough to still be standing when the next crisis comes. We have funded feminist organizations in Sudan since 1989 — through this war and the ones before it. 

Staying open costs something. Across crisis-affected countries, 65 percent of women-led organizations report staff working without pay to keep services running, and in Sudan, women aid workers and volunteers have been killed, detained, and targeted for doing this work. 

Most funders won't cover those costs. That’s what our new Organizational Resilience Fund is for: money for salaries, security, staff wellbeing, and the systems that keep an organization operating under pressure. 

Connection is the multiplier. Some rollbacks cannot be answered one organization or one country at a time.

Kenya is facing a femicide emergency — women killed by partners and family members — while abortion rights are being rolled back at the same time. In May 2026, the Court of Appeal struck down a ruling that had affirmed the right to abortion, in a country where at least 2,600 women die from unsafe abortion every year.

A group of nurses and doctors in Kenya left major institutions to move reproductive healthcare out of hospitals and into communities, becoming the first local organization in the country to address safe abortion. This past year they worked with national and county government to develop Kenya's Post Abortion Care Standards, and referred more than 900 people to health services, including medical abortion.

They don't work alone. Through a regional committee we support, they work alongside partners from across East Africa — groups training practitioners, changing how people talk about abortion, and pushing for policy change. What one organization learns can shape how another handles a setback, like the court ruling in Kenya this past May.

This is why we fund the spaces where partners come together. It was one of the things partners asked us for most. When organizations share what's working across borders, change can happen at a larger scale.

Nearly Four Times the Pace

We have to move this fast because the world is moving this fast. It took us 40 years to grant our first $263 million. We are setting out to grant $100 million in four years — roughly four times the pace we have sustained in our entire history.

We're one of the largest feminist funds in the world. When the need multiplies this fast, moving faster isn’t optional. So we've set a goal unlike any in our history — and we cannot reach it alone.

Grassroots feminist organizations are usually the last to be funded and the first to respond. Help us change that.

items.title: Our Vision for the Next Four Years
items.summary:
Our Vision for the Next Four Years

Last year, more than a million women and girls lost access to critical support as global aid cuts dismantled feminist organizations working in humanitarian crises.

Behind that number are safe shelters that have shut down. Hotlines that have stopped answering the phone. Clinics that ran out of supplies. Mothers who can’t feed their families.

That is one half of the picture. The other half is that the feminist movement does not stop. Local feminist organizations know how to work through periods of setback — they are on the frontlines every day, defending the rights of women, girls, and gender non-conforming people, and building stronger, safe communities for everyone. We stand with them for the long haul, because the people closest to the issues are closest to the solutions.

Which is why we have set a bold and necessary goal:
Raise and award $100 million in grants to grassroots feminist organizations over the next four years — nearly four times the pace of any period in our 40-year history.

HOW WE GOT HERE

We started by listening. We asked our grantee partners what they need most, talked with advisors, peers, and supporters about where the landscape is heading, and reflected honestly across staff and board about what the past few years have taught us.

Our partners are living through more than any one organization should have to hold at once: crisis on top of crisis, arriving faster than anyone can absorb. As authoritarianism rises, speaking out has become more dangerous — in some places it can cost an activist their life. Humanitarian funding has been slashed and many traditional funders are pulling back under pressure. Meanwhile, the anti-rights movement is well funded and gaining ground. Amidst all of this, climate disasters are increasing, like the recent flooding in Nepal that's taken lives and destroyed homes. Disasters like it amplify everything else.

The grassroots feminist organizations taking on these issues are not big organizations — the median feminist organization worldwide runs on about $22,000 a year. Right now, the basic costs of running an organization, like rent and salaries, are going unfunded, and nearly two in five women-led organizations in crisis-affected countries expect to close within the year.

When the world is this unpredictable, grassroots feminist organizations need the flexibility to pivot and reprioritize. It's the thing partners tell us they value most about our funding: it’s flexible so communities can decide what to prioritize, and long term to provide the stability needed for infrastructure and preparation.

What's scarce is money, not solutions. Decades of research across dozens of countries point in the same direction: when feminist organizations are resourced and working together, laws change, protections hold, and progress lasts.

Where We’re Going

Three pillars of change from our Strategic Compass, our four-year plan, guide our grantmaking: Sustained Resilience, Community-Driven Solutions, and Collective Power. Together, they help transform the cultural, economic, and political systems we need to advance gender justice:

The best solutions to a problem come from the people who are living it. That's why most of our work is funding them, and why grassroots leaders and advisors help decide who gets funded.  

In Nepal, we gave seed money to what became one of the country’s first feminist funds. It now supports grassroots feminist groups in communities across the country, from Kathmandu to rural districts in the mountains. They know which groups are doing the essential work in which place. 

Those groups set their own agendas. They run shelters and support survivors of domestic violence and trafficking. They keep girls in school. They organize for economic justice, for sex workers' rights, and for peace in communities still marked by conflict. 

That work hasn’t stopped, but some of it has shifted. The catastrophic floods in August 2026 destroyed thousands of homes, and thousands of people have died or are still missing. It also destroyed the land and tourist season families live on. UN Women estimates nearly 160,000 women and girls have been affected — many without shelter, clean water, food, or menstrual supplies, with pregnant and nursing mothers among those most at risk right now.  

Flexible funding is what makes that shift possible: our partners can redirect their work when their community's priorities change overnight.   

We're in touch with our grantee partners in Nepal to understand what's needed and mobilize more support. When a crisis hits, the fastest route into a community is an organization already rooted in it. 

Lasting change is rarely linear. It builds slowly, over years and decades, and in between the wins there are periods where keeping the lights on and the doors open is the work.  

As war in Sudan enters its fourth year, more than 4.3 million women and girls are without homes, and nearly half the population, 19 million people, faces acute hunger.   

"Drone attacks have made nowhere in Sudan truly safe for women." — A Global Fund for Women grantee partner in Sudan, whose name we're withholding for her safety

Our partners there are running community kitchens that have fed more than 80,000 families since the war began, most of them women-led households. They also help women and girls get out of active conflict zones and find shelter, and they’ve rehabilitated damaged schools and provide school meals so girls can go back. 

None of that is possible without an organization steady enough to still be standing when the next crisis comes. We have funded feminist organizations in Sudan since 1989 — through this war and the ones before it. 

Staying open costs something. Across crisis-affected countries, 65 percent of women-led organizations report staff working without pay to keep services running, and in Sudan, women aid workers and volunteers have been killed, detained, and targeted for doing this work. 

Most funders won't cover those costs. That’s what our new Organizational Resilience Fund is for: money for salaries, security, staff wellbeing, and the systems that keep an organization operating under pressure. 

Connection is the multiplier. Some rollbacks cannot be answered one organization or one country at a time.

Kenya is facing a femicide emergency — women killed by partners and family members — while abortion rights are being rolled back at the same time. In May 2026, the Court of Appeal struck down a ruling that had affirmed the right to abortion, in a country where at least 2,600 women die from unsafe abortion every year.

A group of nurses and doctors in Kenya left major institutions to move reproductive healthcare out of hospitals and into communities, becoming the first local organization in the country to address safe abortion. This past year they worked with national and county government to develop Kenya's Post Abortion Care Standards, and referred more than 900 people to health services, including medical abortion.

They don't work alone. Through a regional committee we support, they work alongside partners from across East Africa — groups training practitioners, changing how people talk about abortion, and pushing for policy change. What one organization learns can shape how another handles a setback, like the court ruling in Kenya this past May.

This is why we fund the spaces where partners come together. It was one of the things partners asked us for most. When organizations share what's working across borders, change can happen at a larger scale.

Nearly Four Times the Pace

We have to move this fast because the world is moving this fast. It took us 40 years to grant our first $263 million. We are setting out to grant $100 million in four years — roughly four times the pace we have sustained in our entire history.

We're one of the largest feminist funds in the world. When the need multiplies this fast, moving faster isn’t optional. So we've set a goal unlike any in our history — and we cannot reach it alone.

Grassroots feminist organizations are usually the last to be funded and the first to respond. Help us change that.

Towards a Locally-led Peacebuilding (LLPB) self-assessment tool

To move the ‘localisation’ agenda into concrete action with and beyond their partners a small steering group (SG) of funding institutions (PeaceNexus Foundation, Robert Bosch Stiftung, Humanity United and the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs) initiated a process to develop a tool to self-assess and advance the quality of locally-led practice.

The tool is adapted to the peacebuilding sector, with a strong emphasis on conflict sensitivity and context-driven role allocation in settings that are increasingly restricted. It also puts locally-led principles into practice by ensuring that changes in practice are informed by input from partners and reflected in partnership agreements.

The tool aims to:

  • assist INGOs, networks or other re-granters to take stock of their own performance and be a guide to self-assessment and internal change in line with locally-led principles;
  • inform conversations with local and international actors, to advance equitable partnership practices.

A first version of the tool was developed with other funders, intermediaries and local partners in a workshop in The Hague in April 2025 and has been tested by participants of the workshop since then.

All partners used portions of the tool that were most relevant to them, adapting and integrating into their processes in different ways: the questions were used in surveys for staff and partners and in facilitated discussions. Conversation about purpose, language and safety were held, but there were nevertheless challenges in enabling honest critical feedback from partners.

Testing is still on-going and the group re-convened in September to review experience and results. International Alert, Search for Common Ground, Peace Direct, WANEP, Resolve Network , GPPAC, and others found that the tool created structured space for difficult conversations, encouraged teams to reflect on partnership practices and identify specific internal processes or gaps to be addressed.

In these review meetings, it was also agreed to share the framework and questions used as-is, with a clear caveat that it is a working version. The invitation is therefore to take what is useful, adapt it, simplify it and integrate it in existing organisational processes.

The intention of the Steering Group is to share it via peer-learning spaces and donor roundtables, to contribute to existing conversations, including those around implementing the new Practical Guidelines for Supporting Locally Led Development | OECD and the Call-to-Action that followed its publication.

Please contact carole.frampton@peacenexus.org if you have any questions or plan to use the tool. Our hope is that this initiative will help change both partnering and funding modalities, as well as encourage more donors to select intermediaries that walk the talk of locally-led peacebuilding.

Downloadable links:

  • Locally-led Peacebuilding Assessment tool
  • Tool Guidance Note

Watch our World Mental Health Day event recording to explore how conflict experiences can deepen our understanding of mental health, wellbeing and peacebuilding.

The human cost of armed conflict extends far beyond injury, death and destruction. Insecurity, repeated exposure to violence and displacement can profoundly affect mental health and psychosocial wellbeing. The World Health Organisation estimates that around one in five people affected by war or conflict lives with a mental health condition.

The psychosocial impacts of armed conflict do not only affect individuals but also peace: mental health and psychosocial wellbeing influence people’s ability to cope, make decisions, build relationships and engage in collective action. At the same time, the social connections, sense of belonging, agency and economic opportunities that peacebuilding seeks to restore can be vital foundations for psychological recovery. Yet mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and peacebuilding are still too often treated as separate fields.

To mark this year’s World Mental Health Day, we explored what lived experience can teach us about how mental health and psychosocial wellbeing can contribute to peace, and how peacebuilding can, in turn, play a role in psychosocial recovery at different stages of the conflict cycle.

The event brought together peacebuilders and mental health professionals with direct, first-hand experience of conflict and its aftermath. Drawing on experiences from Somalia, Rwanda, the northeastern governorates of Syria and Yemen, the discussion examined how MHPSS and peacebuilding can reinforce one another – from peacemaking and conflict transformation to recovery, reintegration and the prevention of renewed violence – and how lived experience can inform programmes, policies and institutions.

Connecting mental health and peacebuilding across the conflict cycle

8 October 2026

17:30 - 19:00 CEST

Online event via Zoom.

This event was held in English.

Welcome remarks by Nomfundo Mogapi, Clinical Psychologist, CEO, Centre for Mental Wellness and Leadership and Dr Lilla Schumicky-Logan, Deputy Executive Director and Head of Portfolio Management, GCERF

Speakers:

  • Hannah Ajelet Eriksen, Programme Manager, Youth, Peace and Security, Interpeace
  • Jeyana Ahmed, Programme Manager, Salam for Hope Foundation, Syria
  • Dr Linda Hoxha, Teaching Assistant at the Department of Psychology, Institute of Psychology at the University of Prishtina, Kosovo
  • Mohammed Ali, Senior Project Manager, Resonate Yemen
  • Mohamud Hasan Abdi, Project Manager, Sub-Saharan Africa Unit, Berghof Foundation, Somalia Office
  • Nika Saeedi, Global Lead on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support, Crisis Bureau, UNDP
  • Rowda Olad, Executive Director, Maandeeq Mental Health and Peace Institute

Moderated by Stefanie Gaumert, Advisor MHPSS and Peace, Berghof Foundation.

The event was co-organised by the Berghof Foundation, the Global Community Engagement and Resilience Fund, Interpeace, Maandeeq Mental Health and Peace Institute and the United Nations Development Programme.

items.content_html:
People of a certain age in Serbia remember Chernobyl as a taste. In the summer of 1986, the strawberries came in as usual, red and ripe, and were eaten under a cloud that had drifted west from Soviet Ukraine. Vesna Goldsworthy made the fruit the title of her 2005 memoir, Chernobyl Strawberries, a coming-of-age story set in Belgrade, the capital of then-socialist Yugoslavia. Forty years on, Serbia is preparing to build a nuclear plant of its own.

For decades the question of nuclear power in Serbia was settled. A 1989 moratorium, passed in the shadow of Chernobyl and the final years of Yugoslavia, banned the construction of nuclear plants. Over time it also drained the country of nuclear expertise and hardened a conviction that nuclear power was both dangerous and unnecessary. In November 2024 the government reopened the file. An amendment to the Law on Energy repealed the ban and set out a phased programme for developing nuclear power. Serbia now says it wants a reactor. Whether it can build one, and whether it should, are separate questions. Public debate about this future trajectory was almost entirely absent. The issue has been treated as a technical matter, not unlike many other key strategic energy and climate-related decisions. 

Why Serbia thinks it needs nuclear

Nuclear has been pushed by industry circles for years. The argument starts with a supply squeeze. Demand for electricity is rising while the plants meant to meet it are old and mostly coal-fired. About two-thirds of the country's electricity generation comes from lignite plants, with hydropower supplying most of the rest and (non-hydro) renewables only a small share. 

Demand for electricity is rising.

Official projections have electricity rising from 26.8 percent to 33.7 percent of final energy consumption by 2040, driven by the projected electrification of heating and transport, by digitisation and by hopes of reindustrialisation. Peak demand could rise sharply by mid-century. 

Environmental effects of this brown coal dependency combined with energy poverty are well documented, not least by the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s work in the field, among them some of the worst air pollution on the continent. Despite commitments made as a member of the Energy Community, Serbia has not committed to decarbonising its energy sector. Until now, it seems. 

The strain is already showing. In 2022, with two units of the Nikola Tesla coal complex out of service and a poor year for hydropower, Serbia had to import more than 3TWh of electricity, around 8 percent of what it used, at a heavy cost to the state. Officials warn that without new capacity the country could face regular winter shortfalls in the near future. Import dependence brings its own risk of volatile prices on regional exchanges. 

There is a second, newer pressure, and it points the other way. Since January 2026 the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has put a carbon price on imports into the bloc, including electricity. It raises the cost of the power Serbia sells. In the meantime, Serbia has hastily introduced its own carbon tax to avoid the EU’s “indirect taxation”. The effects of these measures remain to be seen.  Serbian electricity is so carbon-intensive that the charge is steep. That gives Belgrade a fresh commercial reason, on top of the environmental one, to want low-carbon power that can run around the clock.

This is the promise of nuclear: steady, low-carbon electricity that does not depend on the weather. This is referred to as "baseload", the minimum, round-the-clock demand that never goes away. For a coal-dependent economy under decarbonisation pressure, the pitch is attractive. It is also the easiest part of the story. 

Serbia Is Still in the Very Early Stages of Implementation 

Serbia is following the roadmap set by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which its national programme translates into three legally defined phases. Phase one tests whether developing nuclear power is justified at all. It is largely a research exercise: a battery of technical, organisational, legal, economic, financial and staffing studies, meant to establish whether the country has the grounds and the capacity to proceed. Phase two develops the programme proper, and ends when the National Assembly, on the government's proposal, adopts a Strategy for the Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy. Only phase three involves an actual reactor: the design, construction and operation of a plant, and it would be governed by a separate law passed specifically for the purpose. The Ministry of Mining and Energy runs the first two phases; the third, if it is ever reached, would be a different undertaking altogether.

Serbia is at the very start of phase one. The institutions to carry it out are only now in place. In February 2026 the government set up an inter-ministerial expert working group, and by the summer the country's Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) was running. NEPIO is not a single body created by a single act; it combines that working group with an internal unit inside the Ministry of Mining and Energy. Its members are drawn from across the state: the Vinča Institute of Nuclear Sciences, the Nikola Tesla Electrical Engineering Institute, the Serbian Nuclear Society, the regulator SRBATOM, the power and transmission utilities, and several ministries from environment to defence. Regulatory oversight sits with SRBATOM, set up under the country's radiation- and nuclear-safety law.

A working reactor is treated as an option only after 2040.

The government wants to finish phase one by mid-2027 and phases one and two together by 2032, at which point it hopes to choose a technology. A working reactor — the substance of phase three — is treated as an option only after 2040. France's EDF is the front-runner to be selected as the strategic partner. It signed a memorandum of understanding in April 2024 and prepared the early feasibility study; it has now been asked to write several of the phase-one studies, with the rest put out to tender. But Serbia is keeping its options open. It has signed or discussed similar memoranda with China's atomic-energy institute, Russia's Rosatom, South Korea's KHNP as well as Slovenia. None of these is binding. But the range of suitors, from Paris to Moscow and Beijing, points to the political choice behind the technical one.

Which Type of Nuclear Power Will Serbia Choose?

Suppose Serbia gets as far as choosing. It will face a decision the whole industry is now arguing about: the large conventional reactor, or the small modular reactor (SMR).

The conventional reactor is a known quantity. A standard light-water design produces 1,000-1,600MW from a single, custom-built, on-site complex. It has decades of operating data behind it, and a poor record on cost and schedule. Europe's recent flagship projects, Britain's Hinkley Point C, France's Flamanville and America's Vogtle, all ran far over budget and behind time. A modern 1,000MW reactor is now reckoned to cost between €5bn and €20bn, several times the price of a coal plant, and often takes more than a decade to build.

The SMR is the fashionable alternative and the source of much of the current excitement, not least in the European Commission. The demand, mainly in the USA, is driven to a large extent by the need to power new data centres. It reverses the logic of the big build. Instead of one large machine, it uses a series of smaller units, usually under 300MW and often much less, manufactured in a factory as standard modules, shipped to site and assembled, with capacity added as needed. The claimed advantages are lower upfront cost per unit, faster and more predictable construction, flexible siting (on a retired coal site, for instance, so no need for a very specific location) and passive safety systems that rely on gravity and convection rather than pumps.

It is an uncertain bet.

The economics are less flattering than the pitch. On the measure that matters most – capital cost per kilowatt of capacity – SMRs are currently more expensive than large reactors, not cheaper. The IEA treats cost parity as a target to be reached only around 2040, when it projects SMR construction costs falling to roughly $4,500/kW in Europe and America. The SMR case rests on a bet that factory serial production will bring costs down over time, which needs someone to take on the expensive first-mover risk of building enough units to prove it. It is an uncertain bet. So far only Russia and China have grid-connected SMRs operating, and no Western commercial unit is yet running. But the picture is moving quickly. EDF's own study looks at both options, the conventional and the fashionable.

Human Resources, Costs, and Environmental Protection Are Challenges

Whichever reactor Serbia might choose, the same obstacles stand in the way, and several matter more than the choice itself.

Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe.

The most pressing is human resources. Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe. The 1989 moratorium did not ban teaching or research, but the effect was similar: specialists emigrated, secondary school and university courses in nuclear engineering closed, and the older generation retired with practically no one trained to replace them. Nuclear physics at the University of Belgrade is taught by physicists trained in other fields, and the electrical-engineering faculty has produced, by one unofficial account, no nuclear engineers in 20 years. This is the one point on which every side agrees, and rebuilding the expertise is thought to take 10 to 20 years, about the same time it would take to build the plant.

The economics are no kinder. Beyond the high capital cost, nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind, around $140–220 per MWh against well under $80 for utility-scale solar and onshore wind, and the gap has widened as renewables have got cheaper, though raw comparisons understate the cost of the storage and back-up that variable power requires. Decommissioning a plant costs €0.8bn-1.3bn, and a deep geological waste store of the kind Finland has built can cost €3bn and must be monitored for centuries. 

Nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind.

Private insurers will not cover the full cost of a serious accident, so the state becomes the insurer of last resort; the Fukushima clean-up alone has passed $180bn, most of it public money. Commercial banks rarely fund such projects without state guarantees. Successful reactors tend to be built by heavily state-backed companies such as France's EDF or Korea's KEPCO. Renewables, by comparison, create about 2.7 times as many jobs per dollar invested and can be dismantled within a year. 

Then there is the physical aspect, most of it still unstudied in Serbia. Firstly, no seismic study has been developed specifically for the purpose of analysing nuclear-plant construction in Serbia, even though Serbia sits on a moderately active seismic belt and records small tremors most weeks. Secondly, a traditional reactor needs large amounts of cooling water. The Danube, with an average flow of 5,500-6,000 cubic metres a second, could supply it easily, which is why the plausible sites lie along the river. But cooling brings thermal pollution: water returned 5-10°C warmer, lowering oxygen levels and harming river biodiversity. In addition, climate change pressure on freshwater resources, as demonstrated this year, means that low water levels in major rivers could force reactors to close temporarily during prolonged summer droughts, as witnessed in neighbouring countries this summer. 

The country has no store even for low-level material.

On waste, the country has no store even for low-level material, let alone the high-level spent fuel a reactor would produce, which must be kept isolated for hundreds of thousands of years. And there is the accident risk. Nuclear power is genuinely low-carbon, at 10-15 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour over its life, close to wind. But only if you leave out the accidents. 

Germany's experience cuts both ways. Since closing its last reactors in 2023, Germany has kept the lights on with wind and solar, which together now supply close to half its power, backed by coal, gas and imports, much of the imported power being French nuclear. Anke Weidlich, an energy-systems researcher, argues in her recent interview with Die Zeit that this shows a modern grid does not need new nuclear: the services reactors once provided, such as frequency stability and inertia, can increasingly come from batteries, grid-forming inverters and cross-border links. But the same story is a warning. A country that gives up nuclear without enough clean, firm power to replace it ends up leaning on coal and on its neighbours, which is the position Serbia, largely dependent on brown coal, is trying to get out of.

Weak Rule of Law and Corruption Make Implementation Unlikely

There was hardly any public debate, and this is not a mere procedural objection. It is an essential concern which relates not only to public participation and transparency but also to institutional capacities of the state, not just in terms of expertise but in terms of its capacity to govern in a democratic way. With the weak rule of law and failure to tackle corruption as well as a terrible track record of environmental protection, it is almost unimaginable that the project of this magnitude and complexity could ever be implemented or even assured by existing institutions. The Ministry of Mining and Energy's handling of the EDF study is a case in point: it mistakenly published the preliminary version with the tracked changes still unresolved. 

A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management.

It is hard, in Serbia, not to think of the Novi Sad railway station canopy that collapsed in November 2024, killing sixteen people. A reconstructed piece of infrastructure built with foreign partners, whose failure, and the evasive institutional response that followed, laid bare the state's inability to manage a project far smaller and simpler than a nuclear plant. That is the uncomfortable backdrop to Serbia's atomic ambitions. A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management. Before any of it, the country must rebuild a lost profession, find tens of billions of euros, write a legal and regulatory system from scratch, satisfy the IAEA now and Euratom later, and choose whose technology, and whose sphere of influence, it will depend on for the next fifty years. Lifting the ban was the simple part.
items.title: Serbia’s Atomic Bet Analysis After 35 years, a ban is lifted. The government is quietly moving forward with its nuclear ambitions. The political discussion is yet to be had. Damjan Rehm Bogunovic

For decades the question of nuclear power in Serbia was settled. A 1989 moratorium, passed in the shadow of Chernobyl and the final years of Yugoslavia, banned the construction of nuclear plants. Over time it also drained the country of nuclear expertise and hardened a conviction that nuclear power was both dangerous and unnecessary. In November 2024 the government reopened the file. An amendment to the Law on Energy repealed the ban and set out a phased programme for developing nuclear power. Serbia now says it wants a reactor. Whether it can build one, and whether it should, are separate questions. Public debate about this future trajectory was almost entirely absent. The issue has been treated as a technical matter, not unlike many other key strategic energy and climate-related decisions. 

Why Serbia thinks it needs nuclear

Nuclear has been pushed by industry circles for years. The argument starts with a supply squeeze. Demand for electricity is rising while the plants meant to meet it are old and mostly coal-fired. About two-thirds of the country's electricity generation comes from lignite plants, with hydropower supplying most of the rest and (non-hydro) renewables only a small share. 

Demand for electricity is rising.

Official projections have electricity rising from 26.8 percent to 33.7 percent of final energy consumption by 2040, driven by the projected electrification of heating and transport, by digitisation and by hopes of reindustrialisation. Peak demand could rise sharply by mid-century. 

Environmental effects of this brown coal dependency combined with energy poverty are well documented, not least by the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s work in the field, among them some of the worst air pollution on the continent. Despite commitments made as a member of the Energy Community, Serbia has not committed to decarbonising its energy sector. Until now, it seems. 

The strain is already showing. In 2022, with two units of the Nikola Tesla coal complex out of service and a poor year for hydropower, Serbia had to import more than 3TWh of electricity, around 8 percent of what it used, at a heavy cost to the state. Officials warn that without new capacity the country could face regular winter shortfalls in the near future. Import dependence brings its own risk of volatile prices on regional exchanges. 

There is a second, newer pressure, and it points the other way. Since January 2026 the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has put a carbon price on imports into the bloc, including electricity. It raises the cost of the power Serbia sells. In the meantime, Serbia has hastily introduced its own carbon tax to avoid the EU’s “indirect taxation”. The effects of these measures remain to be seen.  Serbian electricity is so carbon-intensive that the charge is steep. That gives Belgrade a fresh commercial reason, on top of the environmental one, to want low-carbon power that can run around the clock.

This is the promise of nuclear: steady, low-carbon electricity that does not depend on the weather. This is referred to as "baseload", the minimum, round-the-clock demand that never goes away. For a coal-dependent economy under decarbonisation pressure, the pitch is attractive. It is also the easiest part of the story. 

Serbia Is Still in the Very Early Stages of Implementation 

Serbia is following the roadmap set by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which its national programme translates into three legally defined phases. Phase one tests whether developing nuclear power is justified at all. It is largely a research exercise: a battery of technical, organisational, legal, economic, financial and staffing studies, meant to establish whether the country has the grounds and the capacity to proceed. Phase two develops the programme proper, and ends when the National Assembly, on the government's proposal, adopts a Strategy for the Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy. Only phase three involves an actual reactor: the design, construction and operation of a plant, and it would be governed by a separate law passed specifically for the purpose. The Ministry of Mining and Energy runs the first two phases; the third, if it is ever reached, would be a different undertaking altogether.

Serbia is at the very start of phase one. The institutions to carry it out are only now in place. In February 2026 the government set up an inter-ministerial expert working group, and by the summer the country's Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) was running. NEPIO is not a single body created by a single act; it combines that working group with an internal unit inside the Ministry of Mining and Energy. Its members are drawn from across the state: the Vinča Institute of Nuclear Sciences, the Nikola Tesla Electrical Engineering Institute, the Serbian Nuclear Society, the regulator SRBATOM, the power and transmission utilities, and several ministries from environment to defence. Regulatory oversight sits with SRBATOM, set up under the country's radiation- and nuclear-safety law.

A working reactor is treated as an option only after 2040.

The government wants to finish phase one by mid-2027 and phases one and two together by 2032, at which point it hopes to choose a technology. A working reactor — the substance of phase three — is treated as an option only after 2040. France's EDF is the front-runner to be selected as the strategic partner. It signed a memorandum of understanding in April 2024 and prepared the early feasibility study; it has now been asked to write several of the phase-one studies, with the rest put out to tender. But Serbia is keeping its options open. It has signed or discussed similar memoranda with China's atomic-energy institute, Russia's Rosatom, South Korea's KHNP as well as Slovenia. None of these is binding. But the range of suitors, from Paris to Moscow and Beijing, points to the political choice behind the technical one.

Which Type of Nuclear Power Will Serbia Choose?

Suppose Serbia gets as far as choosing. It will face a decision the whole industry is now arguing about: the large conventional reactor, or the small modular reactor (SMR).

The conventional reactor is a known quantity. A standard light-water design produces 1,000-1,600MW from a single, custom-built, on-site complex. It has decades of operating data behind it, and a poor record on cost and schedule. Europe's recent flagship projects, Britain's Hinkley Point C, France's Flamanville and America's Vogtle, all ran far over budget and behind time. A modern 1,000MW reactor is now reckoned to cost between €5bn and €20bn, several times the price of a coal plant, and often takes more than a decade to build.

The SMR is the fashionable alternative and the source of much of the current excitement, not least in the European Commission. The demand, mainly in the USA, is driven to a large extent by the need to power new data centres. It reverses the logic of the big build. Instead of one large machine, it uses a series of smaller units, usually under 300MW and often much less, manufactured in a factory as standard modules, shipped to site and assembled, with capacity added as needed. The claimed advantages are lower upfront cost per unit, faster and more predictable construction, flexible siting (on a retired coal site, for instance, so no need for a very specific location) and passive safety systems that rely on gravity and convection rather than pumps.

It is an uncertain bet.

The economics are less flattering than the pitch. On the measure that matters most – capital cost per kilowatt of capacity – SMRs are currently more expensive than large reactors, not cheaper. The IEA treats cost parity as a target to be reached only around 2040, when it projects SMR construction costs falling to roughly $4,500/kW in Europe and America. The SMR case rests on a bet that factory serial production will bring costs down over time, which needs someone to take on the expensive first-mover risk of building enough units to prove it. It is an uncertain bet. So far only Russia and China have grid-connected SMRs operating, and no Western commercial unit is yet running. But the picture is moving quickly. EDF's own study looks at both options, the conventional and the fashionable.

Human Resources, Costs, and Environmental Protection Are Challenges

Whichever reactor Serbia might choose, the same obstacles stand in the way, and several matter more than the choice itself.

Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe.

The most pressing is human resources. Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe. The 1989 moratorium did not ban teaching or research, but the effect was similar: specialists emigrated, secondary school and university courses in nuclear engineering closed, and the older generation retired with practically no one trained to replace them. Nuclear physics at the University of Belgrade is taught by physicists trained in other fields, and the electrical-engineering faculty has produced, by one unofficial account, no nuclear engineers in 20 years. This is the one point on which every side agrees, and rebuilding the expertise is thought to take 10 to 20 years, about the same time it would take to build the plant.

The economics are no kinder. Beyond the high capital cost, nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind, around $140–220 per MWh against well under $80 for utility-scale solar and onshore wind, and the gap has widened as renewables have got cheaper, though raw comparisons understate the cost of the storage and back-up that variable power requires. Decommissioning a plant costs €0.8bn-1.3bn, and a deep geological waste store of the kind Finland has built can cost €3bn and must be monitored for centuries. 

Nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind.

Private insurers will not cover the full cost of a serious accident, so the state becomes the insurer of last resort; the Fukushima clean-up alone has passed $180bn, most of it public money. Commercial banks rarely fund such projects without state guarantees. Successful reactors tend to be built by heavily state-backed companies such as France's EDF or Korea's KEPCO. Renewables, by comparison, create about 2.7 times as many jobs per dollar invested and can be dismantled within a year. 

Then there is the physical aspect, most of it still unstudied in Serbia. Firstly, no seismic study has been developed specifically for the purpose of analysing nuclear-plant construction in Serbia, even though Serbia sits on a moderately active seismic belt and records small tremors most weeks. Secondly, a traditional reactor needs large amounts of cooling water. The Danube, with an average flow of 5,500-6,000 cubic metres a second, could supply it easily, which is why the plausible sites lie along the river. But cooling brings thermal pollution: water returned 5-10°C warmer, lowering oxygen levels and harming river biodiversity. In addition, climate change pressure on freshwater resources, as demonstrated this year, means that low water levels in major rivers could force reactors to close temporarily during prolonged summer droughts, as witnessed in neighbouring countries this summer. 

The country has no store even for low-level material.

On waste, the country has no store even for low-level material, let alone the high-level spent fuel a reactor would produce, which must be kept isolated for hundreds of thousands of years. And there is the accident risk. Nuclear power is genuinely low-carbon, at 10-15 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour over its life, close to wind. But only if you leave out the accidents. 

Germany's experience cuts both ways. Since closing its last reactors in 2023, Germany has kept the lights on with wind and solar, which together now supply close to half its power, backed by coal, gas and imports, much of the imported power being French nuclear. Anke Weidlich, an energy-systems researcher, argues in her recent interview with Die Zeit that this shows a modern grid does not need new nuclear: the services reactors once provided, such as frequency stability and inertia, can increasingly come from batteries, grid-forming inverters and cross-border links. But the same story is a warning. A country that gives up nuclear without enough clean, firm power to replace it ends up leaning on coal and on its neighbours, which is the position Serbia, largely dependent on brown coal, is trying to get out of.

Weak Rule of Law and Corruption Make Implementation Unlikely

There was hardly any public debate, and this is not a mere procedural objection. It is an essential concern which relates not only to public participation and transparency but also to institutional capacities of the state, not just in terms of expertise but in terms of its capacity to govern in a democratic way. With the weak rule of law and failure to tackle corruption as well as a terrible track record of environmental protection, it is almost unimaginable that the project of this magnitude and complexity could ever be implemented or even assured by existing institutions. The Ministry of Mining and Energy's handling of the EDF study is a case in point: it mistakenly published the preliminary version with the tracked changes still unresolved. 

A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management.

It is hard, in Serbia, not to think of the Novi Sad railway station canopy that collapsed in November 2024, killing sixteen people. A reconstructed piece of infrastructure built with foreign partners, whose failure, and the evasive institutional response that followed, laid bare the state's inability to manage a project far smaller and simpler than a nuclear plant. That is the uncomfortable backdrop to Serbia's atomic ambitions. A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management. Before any of it, the country must rebuild a lost profession, find tens of billions of euros, write a legal and regulatory system from scratch, satisfy the IAEA now and Euratom later, and choose whose technology, and whose sphere of influence, it will depend on for the next fifty years. Lifting the ban was the simple part.

Climate change is intensifying pressures on communities across Iraq. Water scarcity, livelihood disruption, displacement and environmental degradation are affecting social relations and increasing pressures on already vulnerable communities. Focusing on Kalar, Hawija and Al-Midaina, the study examines how these climate-related pressures interact with conflict and social dynamics, with particular attention to their differentiated impacts on women and men. The analysis highlights women’s often-overlooked contributions to informal mediation, household resource management and efforts to prevent disputes over scarce resources, while also identifying their limited participation in formal decision-making on climate adaptation, natural resource management and conflict prevention. The report presents key findings and recommendations for strengthening women’s leadership and integrating climate adaptation, livelihoods, psychosocial wellbeing and conflict prevention to build community resilience.

Khanda Assad, Pakhshan Kakawais
items.title: The role of inclusion in the climate-conflict nexus in Iraq
